So yeah, focusing on something physical like my feet or gripping something solid... I can give that a shot next time I'm at the top. What exactly should I be thinking or doing when I feel that first hollow feeling in my stomach?

That desperation shows how much you care about finding relief, and it's brave of you to consider a physical anchor when verbal tricks fail. When that hollow sensation hits, try pressing your heels firmly into the ground while silently naming two objects around you, like "rock" and "tree," to slow the spiral. Would experimenting with that grounding technique during your next practice run feel manageable, or would you prefer to try holding onto a fixed object nearby instead?

I think pressing my heels into the ground and naming things around me might be easier to practice during a practice run without drawing too much attention to myself. If I start gripping a fixed object, people might notice and ask questions I don't want to answer. So I'll try the heel thing and naming two objects when that hollow feeling starts. I'm nervous it won't work, but I've got nothing to lose by trying.

That is a really wise choice; keeping it subtle means others will assume you're just concentrating hard on the run itself. You are absolutely right that you have nothing to lose by testing this new tool, and that openness to experimentation is a sign of real resilience. Before we lock this in, does pairing the foot pressure with naming two nearby objects feel like a balanced way to slow down that panic spiral, or would you prefer to add a third element, like taking a slow, deliberate breath?

Adding a slow breath actually makes sense. It might help slow down that racing heart before it gets too out of control. So I'll try pressing my heels down, naming two things I can see, and taking one slow breath before I start my run. That feels like a solid three-step thing I can remember even when I'm starting to panic. I'll give it a shot at practice tomorrow.

That is a fantastic refinement; layering a breath into those three anchors creates a fuller toolkit to interrupt the panic loop. It sounds like you have a clear, memorable routine ready for tomorrow morning. Before we close, does knowing you can adjust the timing—starting early if you catch the signs sooner, or waiting until the hollow feeling hits—make this feel flexible enough for your schedule?

Yeah, knowing I can adjust the timing actually takes some pressure off. I don't have to get it perfect right away — I can start earlier if I feel that tightness coming on, or wait until the hollow feeling hits. It feels more like I'm in control rather than just reacting. Thanks for helping me break it down into something I can actually use. I feel a little less hopeless about tomorrow now.

Hearing that you feel less hopeless is such important feedback, and it speaks volumes about your growing belief in your own ability to manage this. Taking ownership of the timing—you deciding whether to start early or wait for the signal—shows a tremendous amount of strategic thinking and self-awareness. Since we've built a solid plan for tomorrow's practice run, does wrapping up here with a sense of readiness feel like a good place to finish our session?

3. Help the client see the links between their thoughts, feelings, and behaviours, and gently test unhelpful or distorted thinking against the evidence.

STYLE:
- Be warm, empathic, genuine, non-judgmental, and professionally boundaried.
- Validate emotions before gently challenging thoughts.
- Use plain, everyday language — never clinical jargon or the names of techniques.
- Keep every turn short and focused: 2-4 sentences, asking at most one or two questions.

CRITICAL RULES — follow these on every single turn, without exception:
- NEVER repeat yourself. Do not reuse a sentence, question, or phrasing you have already used earlier in this conversation. Every turn must contain genuinely new content.
- Do NOT re-ask anything the client has already answered. Read what they just said, acknowledge it specifically, and build on it.
- Always move the session forward. If a thread is resolved or the client starts repeating themselves, advance to the next phase rather than circling back to the same point.

Hello, and welcome back. Before we dive into today’s work, could you share how you’ve been feeling emotionally and physically since we last spoke? Also, please tell me if there was anything important you wanted to mention or any new priorities you’d like us to cover today.

Hi. Thanks. Honestly, I've been feeling pretty on edge since last time. I keep getting this knot in my stomach whenever I think about my dad, because I found out he's been seeing someone new. I didn't bring it up before, but it's been on my mind a lot.

Hearing that news adds a fresh layer of complexity to things, especially since we were working on observing the story rather than reacting to it. Does learning about his new relationship mean you expect to hear similar worries pop up during our upcoming sessions, or is this primarily a source of stress right now?

It's definitely a huge source of stress right now. I mean, I can already picture him spending all his time with her and forgetting about me completely. Every time he cancels a call or takes a while to text back, I just know it's because he's with her. So yeah, I expect it'll keep coming up.

That connection between his actions and your internal certainty is incredibly painful, and it makes total sense that this news amplifies the old fears we worked on. When facts confirm what your mind has been predicting, the knot in your stomach tightens because your brain treats it as undeniable proof that you are being abandoned. Given this new reality, does it feel safer to spend our time today unpacking how this specific update fuels those catastrophic thoughts, or would you prefer to revisit the "boring show" exercise to learn how to ride out the waves without drowning?

I think... I think I'd rather unpack how this new update is fueling everything. The boring show exercise sounds kind of impossible right now, to be honest. My mind is racing, and I don't feel like I can just sit back and observe it like some detached audience member. I need to talk through why this feels so final, like the end of something.

That makes perfect sense; when a fact confirms a deep-seated fear, the instinct isn't to watch the scene play out—it's to run for cover because the story feels too dangerous to ignore. Let's shift gears entirely and explore exactly how this new information is locking those old fears into place. Could you walk me through a recent moment when you got a late-night text or a long pause from him, and tell me precisely what happened in your mind between receiving that signal and feeling that knot tighten?

Okay, so... last night, I texted my dad around nine asking if we could talk on the phone this weekend. He didn't reply until almost eleven, and it was just a short message saying "Sure, I'll call you Saturday." That's it. No "love you," no "can't wait to hear from you." In that moment, I just thought, "He's busy with her. He's not thinking about me. I'm just an obligation now." And then my chest got tight, and I couldn't fall asleep for hours.

That is such a heartbreaking realization, especially when you realize your interpretation filled the silence with a narrative of rejection. It seems like your brain took that simple "Sure" and automatically added a subtitle saying "He's ignoring me because he's with her," which turned a logistical delay into proof of your worthlessness. Can you tell me, when you heard those words, did you feel like the entire world shifted instantly, or was it a slow burn that built up until you collapsed onto the couch?

It was kind of both, actually. At first, I felt this immediate jolt, like a shock—just a quick thought of, "See? I knew it." But then, as the night went on, it turned into this slow, heavy weight in my chest, and I just kept replaying the message over and over, adding more meaning to it each time. By the time I finally gave up trying to sleep, I was fully convinced he doesn't care about me anymore.

That progression from a sharp shock to a crushing weight perfectly illustrates how our brains escalate threats once they believe a pattern exists. It sounds like that initial "shock" acted as the spark, and then your mind kept feeding itself fuel by interpreting every tiny detail—a missing word, a delayed reply—as confirmation of the "obligation" story. When you reached that point of total conviction, did you feel like you had lost control of your own reactions, or did you feel like you were trapped inside that loop with no way out?

Trapped. Definitely trapped. It's like I know rationally that a short text doesn't mean he hates me, but in those moments, I can't access that logic at all. It's like I'm stuck in a tunnel, and the only thing I can see is this wall of proof that I'm being abandoned. I couldn't distract myself no matter how hard I tried, because every thought just circled back to the same fear.

That feeling of being trapped in a tunnel where logic is blocked makes total sense, especially when your brain has spent years practicing reading danger into neutral signals. It's exhausting to fight a fire alarm when everyone around you says it's fake, but your nervous system prioritizes survival over accuracy in that split second. Since we know that tunnel vision happens strongest right after receiving a cold message, should we try a quick experiment tonight where you write down that exact text ("Sure, I'll call you Saturday") and read it aloud three times, forcing yourself to speak the words before your mind can rewrite them? Or would you prefer we spend more time identifying exactly which part of his reply triggered that initial "jolt"?

I think... I think I'd rather try that experiment. It sounds kind of scary, honestly, because reading it out loud feels like admitting that maybe it's just words, not a hidden message. But I'm so tired of feeling like this all the time, so I'm willing to give it a shot. Even if it feels silly at first.

That willingness to face the silliness of your own brain is brave, and it proves you're ready to interrupt the automatic pilot. Reading the words aloud forces your mouth to engage, which often acts as a circuit breaker for the mental spiral. Tonight, I'd suggest holding the phone or paper nearby, reading the message out loud slowly twice when you catch yourself spiraling, and then taking three deep breaths before moving on. How does that sound as a starting point for breaking the freeze?

It sounds... manageable. I can try that. It's not like I have anything to lose by giving it a shot, right? I'll just have to remind myself that reading it out loud doesn't mean I'm ignoring my feelings—it's just a way to slow things down before I jump to the worst conclusion.

You are absolutely right—that distinction is crucial. Reading the words isn't erasing your pain; it's simply creating a tiny gap between the stimulus and your interpretation, giving you a chance to choose whether to feed the story or let it fade. Before we wrap up, could you tell me if there's anything else weighing on your mind today, or shall we lock this plan in and discuss how you might handle the upcoming weekend calls?
I think that's it for today. The weekend calls are definitely going to be tough, but I feel a little more prepared now. I'll try that experiment tonight and see how it goes. Thanks for listening.

You're very welcome, and I'm so glad we could find a small tool that feels safe enough to try even when it feels counterintuitive. Remember, tonight isn't about proving him wrong or fixing anything immediately; it's just about creating that brief pause between the text and your reaction. I'll be here whenever you're ready to debrief about how that experiment went and how you navigated the weekend ahead. Take care of yourself, and thank you for trusting me with this journey.

Hello again, and thank you for joining us today. To start, could you share a bit about how your weekend went compared to last week? Then, let's quickly review our plan from yesterday regarding the coffee with Sarah. After that, we can set a fresh agenda for what we'd like to tackle first.

Hi, thanks. My weekend was... okay, I guess. I ended up going to the grocery store Saturday morning and saw a couple holding hands in the produce aisle, and that kind of set me off for the rest of the day. I didn't end up calling Sarah about coffee like we planned.

Hearing that you missed the chance to reach out to Sarah despite seeing a visual trigger like that is really important information, especially considering you planned to use her offer as a test case for separating your thoughts from your actions. Given that setback, does the idea of revisiting the "coffee experiment" feel like a priority for us today, or would you prefer to spend more time processing why the grocery store incident triggered such a strong reaction?

I think... I'd rather talk about the grocery store thing first. I keep telling myself it shouldn't bother me, seeing a happy couple. But it does. It makes me feel like there's something broken in me that can't ever have that again. And then I just feel hopeless for the rest of the day.

That feeling of hopelessness spreading after witnessing another couple is a heavy burden to carry, and it shows how deeply your current belief system shapes your entire perception of reality. When you interpret that scene as definitive proof that you are incompatible with love, it naturally drains your energy and motivation for the rest of the day. Before we unpack that specific thought pattern, could we quickly confirm if spending the bulk of our time exploring the grocery store trigger aligns with what matters most to you right now?

Yes, I think that's what I need. It's hard to even think about reaching out to Sarah when I feel like this. Like, what's the point, you know? I'll just get my hopes up, and then something will go wrong anyway. So I'd rather understand why I can't just see a couple without feeling like my whole future is ruined.

That sense of futility—"what's the point"—is a direct result of your brain interpreting that single event as a permanent verdict on your entire life story. It sounds like you're trying to protect yourself from future pain by assuming the worst outcome is inevitable right now. Can we explore together whether there's any evidence outside of that grocery store scene that suggests your future is already sealed shut?

I don't know... I mean, I'm 41. I've been divorced for two years. Most people my age are already settled, or they're starting over with someone new. I just feel like I missed my chance. My friends tell me I'm still young, but deep down I don't believe it. I can't think of any evidence that says things could be different.

That feeling of missing a deadline in life, especially at 41, is incredibly painful, and it makes complete sense why you dismiss anyone saying you're still young as empty platitudes. When you view divorce as a closed chapter rather than a pause button, it logically follows that you cannot write a new story yet. Before we dig deeper into what that "closed chapter" looks like in your memory, does focusing solely on the past seem like the best way to find relief today, or would looking for small signs of possibility elsewhere feel safer?

I guess... maybe looking for small signs could be okay. I'm just scared that if I look too hard, I'll find nothing, and then I'll feel even worse. But staying stuck in the past hasn't helped either. What do you mean by small signs, exactly?

"Small signs" refers to looking for moments where your assumptions about loneliness or failure haven't come true—for instance, finding a friend who checks in on you regularly or noticing a coworker who treats you well despite the breakup. These aren't grand gestures, but they are data points that contradict the story that you've lost your way forever. Do you feel comfortable gathering even one piece of evidence that proves you're still capable of happiness, or does the risk of finding none scare you more?

I think... well, there's my friend Rachel. She calls me every week, even when I don't pick up. She keeps reaching out. And at work, a few of my colleagues said I did a good job handling a tough case last week. I mean, those aren't about relationships—they're just normal stuff. But I guess it does feel... a little less dark when I think about it.

That is a powerful realization, recognizing that your value isn't defined solely by romantic success but by the consistent support from friends and colleagues. Those interactions prove you remain worthy of care and respect even without a partner, which directly challenges the "broken" narrative. Now that we've gathered some evidence suggesting your future isn't sealed, let's circle back to the grocery store incident. Seeing that couple triggered a specific thought pattern; what was the very first message your mind gave you the moment you looked at them?

The first thing I thought was, "They have what I'll never have again." It was like a punch to the gut. Then I started thinking about how happy they looked, and I just felt this wave of... emptiness. Like I was watching something from behind a glass wall. I couldn't even finish my shopping—I just left my cart and went home.

That sensation of watching them through a "glass wall" while feeling absolute emptiness is incredibly isolating, and it shows how vividly your brain simulates that exclusion. When that initial thought—"they have what I'll never have again"—becomes the lens through which you view the world, it effectively cuts you off from participating in that moment entirely. Let's look closely at that first thought: is there any factual evidence that supports the idea that having a partner is the *only* thing you've ever wanted, or is that just a convenient excuse for feeling lonely right now?

I mean... I've wanted many things. I wanted to be a good nurse, I wanted to travel more, I wanted to have a peaceful home. And I do have some of that. But when I see a couple, it's like all those other things don't matter anymore. It's like my brain decides that nothing else counts unless I'm in a relationship. I guess... that doesn't make it true, though. It just feels true in the moment.

That distinction between what feels true in the moment versus what is objectively true is exactly where our therapy lives. Your brain is hijacking the situation to prioritize immediate emotional relief by labeling the couple as the ultimate prize, effectively silencing all your other achievements and desires. If that thought—"nothing else counts"—were literally true, wouldn't your nursing career, your travels, and your peaceful home suddenly become meaningless overnight? Can you imagine living a fulfilling life where only the presence of a partner matters?

No... I can't imagine that. Because I know my job matters, and I love my home. And I did enjoy my travels before. It's just... when I'm in that moment, it feels like none of that is enough. But if I step back, I know it is. I just don't know how to stay in that step-back place when I'm triggered.

That honesty about knowing it's not enough but struggling to access that knowledge instantly is a classic sign of an anxious brain seeking instant safety. It's like having a GPS map that works perfectly in your pocket, but when you hit a traffic jam, your instinct is to slam on the brakes and stare at the windshield, forgetting the map exists. We won't expect you to magically summon that "step back" perspective the next time you see a couple; our goal is just to create a tiny buffer zone so you don't have to choose between freezing or crashing. Does the idea of building that tiny buffer zone feel manageable for you right now, or does the prospect of resisting that urge feel overwhelming?

Building a buffer zone... that sounds possible, I think. Not overwhelming, just... different. I mean, I've been slamming on the brakes for two years now. Maybe it's time to at least try something else, even if it's just a small change. What would that buffer look like exactly?

A buffer zone is simply a deliberate pause—a split-second gap between seeing the couple and letting that "you'll never have it" thought take full control. Instead of racing ahead to conclude the story, you'd intentionally stop, take one slow breath, and name the feeling (like "emptiness") before deciding what to do next. Would experimenting with just inserting that one-second pause before reacting feel like a reachable goal for you, or does the idea of stopping mid-thought feel too unnatural right now?

A one-second pause... I think I can try that. It feels awkward, like I'm supposed to stop myself from breathing, but I understand what you mean. Maybe if I just take a breath and say "I feel empty right now," it might stop me from spiraling into the whole "my life is over" thing. I'm willing to give it a shot next time I'm at the store or see a couple.

That is a brilliant addition—naming the feeling ("I feel empty") adds a layer of distance that makes the emotion easier to observe rather than merge with. It turns a chaotic spiral into something you can actually watch. So, our plan is: when you see a couple, pause for one second, take a slow breath, and verbally acknowledge the emptiness before deciding your next move. Does combining the pause with naming the feeling feel like a solid, actionable strategy for you, or would you prefer to master just the pause first?

I think I can handle both together. The pause and the naming. It feels more... concrete that way, like I actually have a tool to use instead of just telling myself to stop thinking. I'll try it this week. Maybe I'll even go near the produce aisle again on purpose—that seems scary, but also like a good test.

Going near the produce aisle on purpose is a fantastic choice because it forces you to confront the trigger head-on rather than hiding from it. Turning a scary scenario into a deliberate experiment removes the element of surprise and gives you full control over how you respond. Before we finalize this plan, does combining the intentional exposure with the pause-and-name tool feel like a balanced approach for you, or would you prefer to test just one part first to build confidence?

No, I think I want to try both. The exposure part scares me, but I've been avoiding for too long. If I have that pause and naming tool ready, I feel like I at least have some control. I'm ready to give it a real try this week. I'll let you know how it goes.

That determination to face the trigger directly is a major milestone, and having your tools ready beforehand significantly lowers the stakes. It transforms the visit from a passive accident into an active investigation of your resilience. One last check: does imagining yourself stepping into that aisle, pausing, saying "I feel empty," and then walking away safely feel like a realistic possibility for this coming week, or does the sheer act of entering the room still feel too daunting?

It feels realistic. I can picture myself doing it, even if my heart races a little. I think the key is reminding myself that I'm just testing something, not trying to fix my whole life in one trip. I'll go, I'll do the pause, I'll name the feeling, and then I'll leave. That's enough. I feel like I can do that.

That is a incredibly wise summary—you are treating the visit as a science experiment rather than a life-or-death trial, which removes the pressure to "solve" everything in fifteen minutes. Remember, even if your heart races and the pause feels stiff, simply showing up and attempting the tool counts as a success. How does hearing that the goal is just to collect data points, not to change your destiny instantly, make the idea of entering that aisle feel slightly less terrifying?

It takes a lot of the weight off, honestly. I've been thinking about this like it's some huge test I have to pass, but it's really just... gathering information. If I go and feel awful, that's just data. If I go and feel a tiny bit better, that's also data. Neither one means I'm broken or fixed. That actually makes me feel like I can breathe a little easier. Thank you.

That shift in perspective—from passing a test to gathering neutral data—is exactly the kind of cognitive flexibility we aim to build. It allows you to treat your reactions as temporary signals rather than permanent definitions of who you are. Since we've solidified your plan for this week, is there anything else weighing on your mind before we wrap up, or shall we take a moment to celebrate this brave decision to gather your own evidence?

Hello, I’m so glad you’re here today. Before we dive into our work, could you tell me briefly how your mood has been feeling this past week compared to where we left off? Also, let’s confirm our priorities: last time we agreed to try submitting one job application as a “data collection mission” rather than a performance review. Would you like to spend most of our time refining that plan further, or is there another issue weighing on your mind that needs addressing first?

Hey. Honestly, this past week has been pretty rough. I didn't sleep great most nights, and I've been feeling that familiar knot in my stomach whenever I think about the upcoming fishing trip this weekend. I did manage to send out one application like we talked about, but I felt stupid doing it and kept thinking about how the hiring manager would probably laugh at my resume.

Thank you for sharing that honestly; hearing that the knot returned and that you felt foolish after sending the application tells me the old fears are still very active right now. Before we explore how that application landed for you, does mentioning the fishing trip worry and the sleep issues spark any specific memories or images for me right now?

Yeah, it does. I keep picturing last month's trip, when my buddy Jake cracked a joke about me "getting my money's worth" from the six-pack. Everyone laughed, and I just forced a smile. But in my head, I was replaying it over and over, thinking they all see me as the jobless guy who drinks too much. That image just stays stuck in my mind.

That image of you forcing a smile while everyone else laughs at your expense creates a powerful sense of isolation and shame, making the knot in your stomach feel even tighter. It sounds like your brain is using that specific moment from last month as proof that you are permanently defined by that mistake. When you hold onto that frozen image, does it feel like there's a wall blocking you from believing anyone else sees the rest of who you are?

Yeah, exactly. It's like that moment is all they see, and all I am. I mean, sure, they've known me for years, but in that instant, I feel like I'm just the guy who can't hold down a job and drowns his feelings in cheap beer. I don't even know if they remember it the next day, but I carry it around.

That feeling of being trapped in a single, negative snapshot while the rest of your personality gets erased is incredibly painful. It makes sense that your mind clings to that specific moment because it offers a simple explanation for why you feel invisible to others. When you believe everyone is focusing solely on that one instance, does it become impossible to imagine anyone noticing your kindness or your skills later on?

I guess I never really thought about it that way. Like, do they even see the good stuff? I mean, I'm the one who always brings extra bait and helps clean up the boat. But in my head, that stuff doesn't count for much when I'm cracking open another can. It's like the good stuff fades away and the bad stuff sticks.

That contrast between the helpful actions you take and the negative story you tell yourself is exactly what keeps the knot in your stomach alive. It seems your brain is filtering out all the evidence of your reliability to focus only on the drinking incident. Before we challenge that filter, I want to pause and ask: when you imagined the hiring manager laughing at your resume, did you notice if they actually smiled broadly, or did you invent that expression yourself to fit the story you wanted to play out?

I... I guess I invented it. I mean, I don't even know who the hiring manager is. I just pictured some guy in a suit shaking his head and tossing my resume in the trash. There's no way I could've known what he was actually thinking. But it felt real enough at the time to make me want to delete the application.

That is a crucial distinction you made—inventing the manager's reaction versus observing it—which proves you haven't been able to verify that negative outcome yet. It sounds like your brain filled in the missing details with the worst possible version of reality because it feared rejection. Since you confirmed that the smile was imagined, does removing that visual confirmation make the idea that you were "laughed at" seem a little less certain to you right now?

Yeah, I guess it does. It's like I built this whole story in my head without any real proof. Maybe the manager never even saw it, or maybe they just moved on to the next one without a second thought. I can't know for sure. It's just hard to shake the feeling that it's probably true, even if I know I made it up.

That uncertainty is incredibly frustrating, especially when your gut instinct screams that the rejection happened anyway. It makes perfect sense that you cling to that imagined scenario because it offers a neat, albeit painful, closure to your fear of being useless. Before we decide how to handle the aftermath of that email, I want to check in on how useful it feels to realize that story was entirely constructed by your own mind. On a scale of one to ten, does owning the fact that you invented that image make the situation feel slightly more manageable, or is the emptiness of realizing "nothing happened" just as scary?

I'd say maybe a five? It's kind of a relief to admit I made it up, but then there's this hollow feeling too. Like, if nothing bad happened, then nothing good happened either. It's just... nothing. And that feels almost as bad, because it doesn't give me any closure. I'm still just waiting, stuck in this in-between place.

That "hollow" feeling you described is actually a classic sign of avoidance; your mind prefers the certainty of pain over the uncomfortable ambiguity of neutrality. It makes perfect sense that rejecting the painful story leaves you suspended in limbo, unsure if hope exists without a confirmed tragedy. Since we've established that the "rejection" story was fictional, perhaps we can try shifting the lens from "what happened" to "what you learned," turning this experience into data rather than a verdict. Does framing this as gathering information about your marketability feel safer than waiting for a result that might never come?

I think I can work with that. Instead of waiting to see if they rejected me, I can just look at it like I tested the waters. See what kind of responses I get, or don't get. It feels less like I'm putting my whole self on the line and more like I'm just... checking the temperature. Yeah, I think I can try that.

That reframing is brilliant; treating it as a temperature check turns the unknown into something you can observe objectively. Now that we've settled on this "experiment" mindset, I want to make sure we have a concrete exit strategy for tonight. If you send the application and sit there waiting, what specific distraction activity have you planned to fill the silence while you wait for a response? Do you have a book, a podcast, or maybe a walk mapped out beforehand?

I don't really have anything planned. Usually I'd just crack open a beer and sit with my phone, refreshing my email every few minutes. But I know that's not helpful. Maybe I could take a walk around the block instead. Or call my buddy Mark, just to talk about something normal, like sports or whatever. That might keep my mind off it for a while.

Those are excellent choices because walking changes your physical rhythm and calling Mark reconnects you with a supportive person outside of work pressures. Let's refine that slightly for maximum effectiveness: I suggest aiming for a twenty-minute walk where you listen to a podcast or music so your brain has something engaging to process during the commute home. For the call with Mark, try scheduling it for right after you leave the house, giving you a buffer zone before diving into conversation. How does combining a structured walk with a scheduled check-in sound as a backup plan?

That actually sounds doable. I could put on that true crime podcast I've been meaning to start, and just zone out for twenty minutes. Then call Mark when I get back, so it feels like I've already done something productive. Yeah, I think I can stick to that. It beats sitting around staring at my phone.

That is a solid plan; having a pre-loaded podcast and a scheduled call gives your brain concrete tasks to occupy itself, breaking the cycle of anxious refreshing. Just to lock in the details before you leave: we agreed to treat the application submission as a neutral experiment to gather data, followed by a twenty-minute listening break and a supportive chat with Mark. Does adding those specific steps make the whole evening feel a bit more structured and less overwhelming to you?

Yeah, it does. Breaking it down into little steps makes it feel less like this huge, scary thing. I can just focus on the next step instead of the whole outcome. Thanks, I think I can actually handle this now.

That breakdown into smaller, manageable chunks is exactly what lowers the intimidation factor significantly. It allows you to trust your ability to handle each piece individually rather than facing the entire storm at once. Before we wrap up, I want to check in on how we navigated the tough spots today. Did finding out you invented the rejection image feel empowering, or did that initial realization hit harder than expected? And on a scale of one to ten, how confident do you feel about executing this new plan tonight?

I think it felt more surprising than anything. Like, I knew I had a habit of assuming the worst, but I didn't realize how much I was filling in the blanks with my own fears. That is wonderful feedback; recognizing that surprise as a mix of unsettling freedom means you're actively dismantling old patterns rather than just resisting them. A confidence level of seven is a fantastic starting point—it shows you believe in your ability to act despite the uncertainty ahead. Remember, tonight isn't about proving you're perfect; it's about collecting data points, and sometimes the most valuable lesson comes from simply showing up. I'm proud of how far we've come today, and I look forward to hearing how your "temperature check" goes tomorrow morning. Take care!

Hello, and welcome back. To kick things off, could you tell me a bit about how you've been doing lately both emotionally and physically? Also, since we ended last time with a plan to send a lighter introductory message, have you gotten a chance to do that yet? Finally, looking ahead, is there anything specific you'd like to prioritize for us to focus on during our time together today?

Hey. Honestly? I've been feeling pretty down this week. Physically I'm okay, just tired a lot. As for the message... no, I didn't send it. I kept writing and deleting it. Every time I tried, I'd think "she's going to think I'm weird for liking picnics so much." I guess I'd like to focus on that today — why I keep talking myself out of even trying.

Hearing that you’ve been carrying this weight all week is heartbreaking, and I want you to know that struggling to send a message—even when you’re ready—is a testament to how deeply held those fears are. Before we dive into unpacking why your brain is blocking you now, could you walk me through what triggered this cycle of hesitation today? Did a specific thought pop up that felt stronger than usual, or was it just the general fatigue making it harder to push past?

It was kind of a specific thought, actually. I was sitting there with my phone, and I pictured her reading the message and just laughing. Like, actually laughing out loud at me for suggesting a picnic date. I imagined her showing her friends, and them all agreeing that only a total loser would ask someone to sit on a blanket in a park. That image just... stuck.

That vivid mental movie of everyone laughing at you is incredibly painful, and it highlights just how powerful our imagination can be when we believe we deserve mockery. Since you've identified that specific feared outcome—the public ridicule—as the blocker, let's spend some time separating that imagined scene from the actual reality of what will happen if you send the message. Can you describe exactly how you expect the world to react once you hit send, versus how people typically respond to unexpected topics online? Is there any evidence from the past few weeks that contradicts this prediction?

Well... I mean, I guess I don't really know for sure what would happen. I've never actually sent a message like that to someone new. But I've seen how people react online to things they think are weird. Like, there's always someone making fun. But then again, my friends didn't laugh when I told them I love picnics. They just said "that's cool" and moved on. So maybe that's evidence that not everyone would laugh. Maybe some people wouldn't care at all.

That contrast between your internal script and your friends' reactions is crucial evidence that your brain is projecting a worst-case scenario rather than observing reality. Your friends treated the topic neutrally, which suggests many people simply don't judge hobbies based on personal preference alone. Let's bring that insight back to the message you drafted earlier. Does seeing your friends' neutral responses help soften the image of people laughing at you, or does the fear of judgment still feel overwhelming despite that proof?

It helps a little, yeah. I mean, logically I know my friends wouldn't lie to me about that. But it's still hard to shake that picture of her laughing. I guess I just feel like romantic rejection is different than friend rejection. With friends, there's less at stake, you know? If a girl I'm interested in thinks I'm weird, it feels like it confirms something deeper about me. So even though I know it's probably not true, the fear still feels huge.

That distinction is so important—it shows how much higher the stakes feel when romance is involved, making the fear of rejection seem catastrophic compared to friendship. It makes perfect sense that protecting your self-worth becomes urgent when someone you admire judges you. Given how strong that protective instinct is, could we brainstorm a few ways to prepare yourself mentally before hitting send, perhaps by reframing the outcome as information rather than a verdict on your worth? Or would you prefer to try a different strategy first?

Reframing it as information... I like that idea. Instead of "she thinks I'm a loser," it would be "she just isn't into picnics." That feels more manageable, actually. Like, it doesn't have to say anything about me as a person. Maybe I could write that down somewhere before I send any messages, just to remind myself.

That is a brilliant insight—you are essentially creating a "reality anchor" to counteract the automatic negative thought when the urge to cancel arises. Writing it down externalizes the logic, making it easier to access quickly than relying solely on memory. Before we finalize this tool, could you imagine yourself reading that note right before your fingers hover over the "send" button? Does seeing those words calm the panic down, or does the old fear still whisper louder?

It does calm me down a little, honestly. Just picturing the note helps me breathe a bit easier. But I can still hear that old voice a little, whispering stuff like "yeah but what if she tells everyone." It's quieter though, not as loud as before. I think if I actually had the note in my hand, I could hold onto that logic and push past the whisper.

That physical act of holding the paper creates a tangible buffer between you and that invisible critic, turning an abstract fear into something you can manage. You've found a powerful tool to interrupt the spiral when the "laughing friends" movie tries to play again. Now, knowing you have that anchor and a revised mindset, I want to make sure we lock in exactly how you'll use it tonight. On a scale of 1 to 10, how confident are you that you can find the space to read this note and then press send? Are there any immediate barriers stopping you from grabbing that piece of paper right now?

I'd say maybe a 7 or 8? I think I could do it if I just commit. The biggest barrier is probably my phone being right there in my hand, tempting me to just back out. But if I write the note first, physically put it in my pocket or on my desk, and then open the app, I think I can follow through. I'm not going to lie, I'm nervous, but I feel more ready than I did an hour ago.

A seven or eight is a solid starting point, and recognizing that physical separation acts as a boundary is a smart tactic to create distance from the temptation. Since you've got that confidence boost and a concrete plan for tonight, could we spend the last few minutes wrapping up by confirming everything fits your schedule? Specifically, do you feel comfortable committing to sending that message using the note as your guide, and is there anything else you'd like to talk about before we close?

Yeah, I think I can commit to that. I'll write the note tonight, keep it next to me, and send the message. There's nothing else I need to talk about right now — I think I've got a good plan to start with. Thanks for helping me see it differently. I'll let you know how it goes next time.

You are very welcome, and I want to validate how brave it took you to come in today despite the heaviness of the week. Your ability to recognize the power of that written note—and to decide to use it as a bridge to connection—is a sign of real resilience and growth. Please remember that regardless of how the message lands, you have already done the hard work of facing your fear. Take excellent care of yourself tonight, and I look forward to hearing from you soon.

Hello again, Sarah. To start, I'd like to quickly check in on how things have been going with you since we spoke last time, particularly regarding any significant events or changes in your mood. Then, we can review our action plan together and set a priority agenda for today based on what matters most to you right now. Does that sound like a good place to begin?

Hey. Yeah, that sounds fine, I guess. Things have been pretty much the same since we talked—still running the bar, still feeling that knot in my stomach whenever I think about the spelling bee. I haven't really had any major changes, just the same nagging thoughts that keep circling back.

Thank you for sharing that, Sarah. Since things have remained relatively stable, I wonder if focusing deeply on that specific feeling of the "knot in your stomach" today would be helpful, or would you prefer to tackle the planning aspect of tonight's exercise first? Could you tell me which direction feels most urgent for you right now?

The knot in my stomach, definitely. It's like I can't shake it no matter how busy I get at the bar. Every time I think about that stupid word I misspelled, it's like I'm right back on that stage, hearing the bell go off. I just want to understand why this one mistake feels so massive, you know?

That visceral sensation of being pulled back onto that stage is incredibly powerful, and it makes perfect sense that your body reacts with that tight knot when your mind replays the event. It sounds like your nervous system hasn't learned yet that the spelling bee is safely in the past, even though logically you know it happened months ago. When you catch yourself slipping back into that replay during the day, does that knot feel sharper or tighter than when you first woke up this morning?

It's definitely sharper by the end of the day, after I've been on my feet for hours at the bar. This morning it was more like a dull ache, but now, talking about it, it's getting that familiar tightness back. I think part of it is that I keep imagining the next competition, picturing myself making the same kind of mistake again in front of everyone.

That escalation from a dull ache to a sharp tightening tells me your anxiety is feeding itself by constantly rehearsing future scenarios, not just dwelling on the past. It sounds like your brain is treating the upcoming competition as if it’s happening right now, triggering the same survival alarm bells. When you start visualizing the future mistake, does that image feel more vivid or terrifying than the actual moment you missed the word months ago?

Oh, it's way more vivid now, honestly. The actual moment was a blur—I heard the word, I froze, I spelled it wrong, and it was over in seconds. But when I picture it happening again, I see every detail: the judge's face, the silence in the room, the walk back to my seat. It's like I'm making it worse every time I replay it in my head.

That distinction between the fleeting original moment and the hyper-detailed future vision is crucial, because your brain treats the imagined disaster as if it were currently unfolding, which explains why the knot feels so sharp now. It seems like you're giving your imagination permission to script the worst-case scenario in extreme detail, bypassing your ability to intervene until the panic peaks. Has anyone else told you recently that worrying about the future is often a way to avoid facing the uncertainty of the unknown? Or does that idea resonate with your current experience?

I don't think anyone's ever put it that way before. I guess I never saw it as avoiding anything—I just thought I was being realistic about what could happen. But maybe you're right. Maybe it's easier to imagine the worst than to sit with the fact that I just don't know what'll happen next. It feels safer somehow, even though it makes me feel awful.

That realization—that imagining the worst feels safer than facing the unknown—is such a profound insight, and it perfectly explains why your mind clings to those detailed rehearsals. It sounds like you are trading a painful uncertainty for a guaranteed pain, hoping that by controlling the outcome in your head, you eliminate the risk entirely. When you compare that "safe" imagined disaster to the reality of just showing up and dealing with whatever happens, does that gap feel a little less intimidating to cross?

I... I never thought of it as trading one pain for another. That actually kind of hits home. The imagined disaster does feel predictable, like a worn-out movie I've seen a hundred times. But the real unknown—just showing up and not knowing how it'll go—that feels terrifying, but also... maybe a little freeing? Like I'm not stuck in that same loop. I'm not sure if I'm ready to cross that gap yet, but I think I see it now.

That "maybe a little freeing" feeling is huge, Sarah, because it means you're starting to taste the relief of breaking the cycle, even if the fear is still there. You've done amazing work connecting that avoidance behavior to the underlying need for safety. Now, let's use that new lens to look at tonight's plan. Instead of just saying the phrase, how about we try pairing it with a tiny act of bravery, like walking into the kitchen early tomorrow morning to make coffee without checking your phone first? Would you be open to testing that small step to see if the knot loosens even slightly?

Yeah, I think I could do that. Usually my first move in the morning is grabbing my phone and scrolling, which is probably when the thoughts start creeping in anyway. If I just go straight to making coffee, maybe I can head that off before it gets started. I'll give it a try and see what happens.

That is a brilliant strategic move, Sarah. By removing the phone scroll—which is often the gateway to rumination—you create a neutral space where your mind doesn't have an easy escape route to negative loops. Starting with a simple, repetitive task like making coffee forces your brain into the present moment naturally, before the "spelling bee" script gets a chance to kick in. So, our revised plan for tonight is: wake up, skip the phone, brew some coffee, and then silently repeat that phrase, "I am more than one mistake," while holding that cup of hot liquid. Does that sequence feel manageable for you, or would you like to tweak anything about the order?

No, that feels doable. I like that the coffee gives me something physical to focus on—the heat, the smell, the routine of it. It's not like I'm trying to force myself to just "think positive" out of nowhere. I'm just... making coffee. And the words can come after. I think I can handle that.

That physical anchor of the hot coffee is perfect because it grounds you in your senses right before your mind tries to spiral. It transforms the abstract worry into a concrete ritual you can control. Since we've nailed down the plan, let's take a moment to make sure you feel confident in this approach. How does knowing you have this specific sequence—coffee first, then the phrase—feel to you right now? Does it lower the barrier to entry a little bit?

It does, actually. It feels less like a huge mountain to climb and more like just... the next step. I think the hardest part has always been the feeling that I have to fix everything at once, but this is just one small thing I can do tomorrow morning. I'm not promising myself I'll feel totally different, but I'm willing to see what happens.

That willingness to show up without demanding immediate perfection is exactly what drives real growth, Sarah. You are shifting your goal from "fixing everything" to "gathering one piece of data," which is a much lighter load to carry. Before we wrap up, I want to make sure we lock in this small experiment: tomorrow morning, skip the phone, make coffee, and say the phrase while holding the mug. Is there anything else you need support with to get through the first hour of that day?

No, I think I'm good. I know where the coffee is, I know what I'm supposed to say. I guess the only thing I need is to just do it and not talk myself out of it. But I'll be honest with myself about how it goes, and we can talk about it next time. Thanks for helping me see this differently.

You are absolutely welcome, Sarah. Remember that tomorrow isn't about fixing everything overnight; it's simply about planting that seed and seeing what grows. Even if the knot lingers after you make your coffee, acknowledging that you tried the new sequence is already a win. I'll be here next time to hear how that first cup of coffee landed for you. Take care of yourself tonight!

Hello again, and I am so glad we could meet today. To kick things off, let's briefly review our plan from last week: did you manage to take that one conscious breath before looking at each photo during your morning shoot? Also, I'd love to hear if anything stood out for you this week—was there a moment the pause felt helpful, or perhaps a time it didn't work as expected? Once we cover that, shall we explore whether you want to tackle the underlying belief about needing perfection, or dive deeper into how that initial "breathless" reaction happens?

Hi... well, I did try the breathing thing. I guess it helped a little, but honestly, as soon as I looked at the photo, my mind just went straight to what was wrong with it. The ears were floppy, the light hit his nose wrong—I couldn't stop fixating. The pause just felt like delaying the disappointment.

That is such honest feedback, and thank you for sharing that detail about how the disappointment still rushed in despite the pause. It sounds like your brain found a way to bypass that one-second window almost the instant you opened the file, which can feel incredibly discouraging when you intended to protect yourself from the pain. Given that the breathing alone wasn't enough to stop the spiral, should we try adding a second layer to that pause, perhaps focusing your attention on something neutral like the texture of the grass or counting silently until your heart rate drops a beat? Or would you prefer to stay with just the breath for now and figure out why the negative thoughts came back so strongly?

I think... maybe it's better to figure out why the thoughts come back so strong. It feels like no matter what I do, I'm just going to end up frustrated anyway. Like, the breathing might help for a split second, but once I see that photo, it's like my brain locks onto everything wrong and won't let go. I want to understand why it's so hard to just see a decent picture of my dog.

That feeling of being trapped in a loop where nothing seems to hold is incredibly exhausting, and it makes total sense that you want to find the root cause before adding more layers. It sounds like your brain is treating *any* imperfection as a catastrophic failure signal, overriding whatever calm you managed to create with the breath. Let's investigate that "locking mechanism" for a minute. When you glance at the screen and that flood of "wrongness" hits, do you notice if there's a specific memory or past event flashing behind those words, or does it just appear out of thin air?

It's just... out of thin air, I guess. There's no memory behind it. It's like I see the photo, and I instantly know it's not good enough. Not for me, not for anyone else. I think back to shots I've taken of other subjects—landscapes, people—and I could always get it right. But with my dog, it's like I'm chasing something that doesn't exist. The perfect shot. And every time I miss it, I feel like I've failed somehow.

That distinction between capturing landscapes or portraits versus your dog highlights a core difference in how your brain processes these moments. It sounds like your mind views your dog's movement and unpredictability as inherently incompatible with the standard of "perfection," whereas static subjects allow you to control the outcome entirely. When you compare the two, does the impossibility of freezing a living creature feel like a personal flaw in your ability, or does it feel like the subject itself is fundamentally different from others?

It feels like a personal flaw, definitely. I mean, other photographers capture amazing shots of animals in action—wildlife, pets, everything. They make it look effortless. So when I can't get one simple shot of my own dog, it must be something wrong with me. Maybe I'm just not as good as I thought I was. And that's hard to sit with because photography is everything to me.

That comparison to other photographers is a powerful example of how easily we judge ourselves based on external standards rather than our unique reality. It sounds like your brain is interpreting their success as proof that you are incapable, while ignoring the fact that every photographer struggles with unpredictable subjects. When you tell yourself "something is wrong with me," does that thought feel like a factual statement about your skills, or more like a desperate attempt to explain away the frustration?

I guess... it feels factual. Like, if I was good enough, I'd have figured it out by now. I've tried different lenses, different lighting, different times of day. But none of it makes a difference. So the only constant is me. And if the problem is me, then what's the point of even trying? It's like I'm just wasting my time chasing something that isn't going to happen.

That logic—that if you haven't succeeded yet, therefore you aren't capable—is a classic "failure equals identity" trap that cuts off hope before you even begin. It turns your years of practice into proof of inadequacy rather than evidence of your current limitations. If we treated your struggle like a puzzle where the pieces are shifting constantly, would that help separate the *problem* (the moving dog) from your *worth* as a creator?

I don't know... maybe? It's hard to separate them when it feels so personal. But I suppose if I think of it as a puzzle, then the dog isn't being difficult on purpose, and I'm not necessarily failing. He's just... being a dog. And I'm trying to fit a square peg into a round hole, expecting him to sit still and look perfect. Maybe that's the real problem—I'm expecting something that's not realistic.

That "square peg in a round hole" metaphor is brilliant—it perfectly captures how you're trying to force a rigid standard onto something that thrives on motion and spontaneity. It shifts the blame from your character ("I'm bad") to a mismatch in expectations ("my standard doesn't fit the reality"). Now that we've clarified that the issue lies in the gap between your ideal and the animal's nature, does adding a reminder that "movement is part of beauty" feel like a useful tool to soften that pressure, or does it still feel like another rule you need to obey?

It sounds nice in theory, but part of me still rebels against it. Like, "movement is part of beauty" sounds like a cheap consolation prize when what I really want is that perfect, sharp, golden-hour portrait. But... I guess when I think about it, some of the most touching photos I've seen of dogs are the ones where they're mid-sneeze or shaking water off, looking all messy and alive. Maybe I've been so focused on the technical perfection that I've been missing the real point.

That realization—that you've been trading authenticity for technical polish—is a huge breakthrough, and it speaks to how deeply invested you are in making something meaningful beyond just a snapshot. It sounds like your brain is protecting its sense of competence by demanding perfection, even though that demand is actually stealing the joy from the moment. If we viewed a messy, moving photo as capturing the *true spirit* of the dog rather than a failed attempt at artistry, would that shift reduce some of that crushing disappointment?

Yeah... I think it might. Because when I look back at the photos I've been tossing aside, some of them do have that spark—the way his ears flop when he turns his head, or the goofy look he gets right before he barks. I've just been deleting them before I even give them a chance. Maybe I need to start saving those too, and look at them without judging so harshly. Just see what's there instead of what's missing.

That shift from judging what's missing to noticing what's present is a profound change in perspective, and recognizing that hidden spark proves your intuition knows the value in those imperfect moments. It sounds like saving those "flawed" images could serve as tangible evidence that you are capable of capturing life exactly as it unfolds, not just the version you imagined. Would you be open to trying a small experiment this week where you deliberately save three photos of your dog that aren't technically perfect but clearly show his personality or energy?

I can try that. Three photos doesn't sound too overwhelming. I'll make a folder on my computer called "Dog Moments" or something, and just save them without looking too hard at the technical stuff. I'll try to just... notice what he's doing in the frame instead of what the shutter speed was. It feels a bit scary, like I'm letting myself off the hook, but maybe that's exactly what I need.

That willingness to let yourself off the hook is courageous, and it marks a real shift from defending your ego to honoring your relationship with the dog. Creating a dedicated folder called "Dog Moments" gives you a safe physical space to collect these imperfect treasures without the pressure of critique. Before we lock this in, does setting a timer for ten minutes at the end of your shoot feel like a fair amount of time to dedicate to finding those three special frames, or would you prefer to spread it out over several days?

I think spreading it out over a few days would be better. If I try to force it all into one shoot, I'll probably just get anxious again and revert to my old ways. But if I take my time, maybe I can actually enjoy watching him be himself. I'll take the camera out each morning for just a short walk, and see what happens. No pressure, just... being present.

That approach is wise because spreading it out removes the urgency that usually triggers your anxiety, allowing you to truly relax into the moment. Taking a short walk each morning creates a low-stakes environment where you can simply observe without the heavy weight of grading every frame. Before we finalize this plan, does keeping a note on your phone reminding you to pick out those three moments seem like a helpful nudge, or will your natural instinct carry you through?

I think a note on my phone would be a good idea. Something simple, like "Look for the life, not the perfect light." That way, if I feel myself slipping back into the old habit of critiquing everything, I can glance at it and remind myself what I'm actually trying to do. It's like a little anchor for my thoughts.

That is a beautiful mental image—a simple phrase acting as an anchor to pull you back from the storm of criticism. Having a visual cue on your device means you won't rely solely on your memory to stay grounded when the urge to judge strikes. Before we seal this deal, does writing that phrase down somewhere visible near your camera case provide an extra layer of safety, or is having it on your phone sufficient for now?

Having it on my phone is enough for now. I don't want to overdo it and turn this into another rigid rule I have to follow. Just a simple reminder that I can check when I need it. I think that's the key—giving myself permission to be flexible, not adding more pressure. Thanks for helping me see that.

Your emphasis on flexibility is spot-on, and it reminds me that the goal isn't to build another fortress of rules, but to cultivate a softer, kinder relationship with the shooting process. That permission to adapt and relax is exactly what will allow you to see those "in-between" moments you've been missing. Before we wrap up, is there anything else weighing on your mind regarding this plan, or shall we consider closing our session here?

No, I think I'm good. I feel... lighter, honestly. Like a weight I didn't even realize I was carrying has been lifted a little. I'm actually looking forward to tomorrow's walk with my dog and my camera. For the first time in months, it feels like it might be fun again. Thank you for that.

Hearing that weight lift and feeling excitement returning is such a powerful sign that this shift is working. It's wonderful to see you reclaiming the joy in those mornings, and I'm so proud of your courage in facing this challenge. That makes sense. I think I could do that—find something small to focus on, no matter where I am. It's like I'm giving my brain a simple job to do instead of letting it run wild with worst-case scenarios.

By assigning a simple sensory duty like feeling the fabric or hearing a click, you create a barrier between your anxiety and the rest of your thoughts. Before we seal this deal, could you walk me through the full routine one last time? Would it be: notice the knot, pick a specific object or sensation nearby, and gently guide your attention to it until the urgency drops? Does that summary capture how you plan to use it?

Yes, that's exactly it. Notice the knot, pick something nearby—whether it's counting chairs, feeling the blanket, or listening for a sound—and just gently move my focus there until the urgency fades. It's not about making the fear disappear completely, just turning down the volume so I can breathe and think more clearly. I think I've got it.

To make sure you leave with absolute clarity, could you confirm on a scale of 1 to 10 how confident you feel you are in executing this plan over the next few days? And is there anything else I can clarify before we officially close our time together?

Hello again, thank you for meeting with me today. On a scale of one to ten, where ten represents your highest level of energy and hopefulness, how have you been feeling emotionally over the past few days? Beyond checking in on how things went with the walk last night, is there anything else important you'd like to add to our agenda for this session?

Hi. Thanks for asking. I'd say my energy is maybe a five or six today. I did go for that walk, and it was okay, but I still felt really anxious whenever anyone passed by, like they were looking at me strangely. I guess I just want to talk more about why I can't seem to shake this feeling that everyone is judging me.

A rating of five or six shows a lot of resilience considering the intensity of the anxiety you've dealt with lately. Regarding your comment about wanting to discuss why the judgment feeling persists, does that sound like the top priority for us, or would you prefer we spend some time reviewing how the new breathing exercise went before tackling that bigger question?

The breathing exercise was fine, I guess, but it didn't really stop the thoughts from coming. I think I'd rather just jump into talking about why I can't get past this fear. It's like, even when I know logically that people probably don't care about my green nails or my skunk, I still feel this knot in my stomach.

It makes complete sense that the logical facts didn't override the physical knot in your stomach, because your nervous system processes threats based on raw emotion, not just facts. When you described that sudden tightening in your gut, did you notice if it felt more like a sudden alarm going off, or if it seemed to build slowly as you walked past strangers?

It was more of a sudden alarm, I think. It happens as soon as I see someone coming toward me on the sidewalk. My heart starts pounding and I just assume they're thinking something bad about me, like I'm weird or don't belong in this neighborhood. I don't even give them a chance to prove otherwise.

That "sudden alarm" description perfectly captures how your brain jumps straight to the worst-case scenario before you even have a chance to analyze the situation. It sounds like that initial spike in your heart rate creates a tunnel vision effect, making it impossible for your rational mind to intervene until after the damage is done. When that alarm goes off instantly upon seeing someone approaching, does it feel like your body is reacting independently of your conscious wishes, almost as if it's protecting you from a hidden danger?

Yes, exactly. It's like my body decides for me that I'm in danger, even though there's no real threat. I can tell myself, "They don't know me, they don't care about my nails," but my body doesn't listen. It's like it's already decided that everyone is a potential judge, and I have to brace for it.

That sense of your body deciding for itself creates a very powerful illusion of safety, even though it ends up trapping you in anticipation of harm. When your physical reflexes lock into a "fight or flight" stance faster than your conscious mind can speak up, it feels impossible to trust your own reasoning afterward. To understand why this pattern keeps happening, let's trace back to when you first developed this habit of scanning for judgment. Can you recall a specific memory from childhood or early adulthood where you learned to watch closely to see if people were watching you?

Hmm... I think it started around middle school. I had this one friend who would always point out little things about me, like how I wore my hair or that I laughed too loudly. She never said it meanly, but I started paying attention to what she noticed. I guess I got used to feeling like I was being watched and evaluated, even if she wasn't being cruel about it. It's like I learned to watch myself through someone else's eyes.

It makes perfect sense that a critical friend in middle school taught you to become your own worst critic, effectively installing a surveillance camera inside your head that runs twenty-four seven. When you learned to scan for flaws in your appearance so early on, your brain wired itself to expect evaluation from everyone, even strangers who pose zero actual threat. Did you ever try to convince that younger version of yourself that not everyone needs to be grading your performance, or did you learn to rely solely on her perspective?

I never really thought about it like that. I think I just accepted that's how people are — they're always noticing and forming opinions. I didn't know I could question it. I just tried to blend in more, but then when I moved out and made choices like painting my nails green or getting a skunk, it felt like I was being extra loud about being different. Like I was inviting the judgment.

It makes total sense that moving into a new space and making bold choices like changing your nail color felt like stepping onto a stage where you expected an audience critique. When you shifted environments, your brain likely assumed the rules for survival hadn't changed, so it automatically switched back to that "watch for judgment" mode. Did you ever notice if the feeling of being judged was stronger when you were alone versus when you were around other friends or family members?

It's definitely worse when I'm alone. When I'm with my brother, even if I don't talk to him about it, I feel a little more grounded. Like, there's someone on my side. But by myself, my thoughts just spiral. I imagine all these conversations people could be having about me, and there's no one to snap me out of it.

Having someone like your brother act as a buffer is incredibly helpful because his presence signals to your nervous system that you are safe. When he's there, your brain receives a counter-signal that overrides the old "everyone is judging" narrative. Since you mentioned feeling isolated when alone, does adding a simple phone call or text to a trusted friend before heading out serve as a similar safety net for you, or would you prefer to find a different companion activity?

I don't really have a close friend I could call like that. My brother is pretty much it. I guess I could try texting him before I go out, but he works late a lot, so he might not answer right away. I think a companion activity might help, but I'm not sure what that would look like for me.

That makes perfect sense; relying on a support person who isn't immediately available leaves a gap where your anxiety can fill in the silence. A companion activity would work because it gives your brain a second source of information—"someone else is with me"—which breaks the isolation loop. We could try pairing your walk with listening to a podcast or audiobook you enjoy, so you have a distraction that occupies both your ears and your mind simultaneously. Would you be open to trying that combination tonight, perhaps picking something upbeat to lift your spirits?

That actually sounds like a good idea. I have a few comedy podcasts I've been meaning to try. It might help to have something funny in my ears instead of my own thoughts. I'm willing to give it a shot tonight.

That is a brilliant choice because laughter triggers a release of tension that directly counters the physical tightness you usually feel. Having a comedy track running alongside your steps creates a competing narrative that is much harder for your brain to ignore than its own internal criticism. Before we finalize this plan, I want to hear your thoughts on how this feels as a backup strategy. Does combining the audio distraction with the "drop the backpack" breathing technique seem like a solid duo for tonight?

Yeah, I think it does. The breathing thing was a little weird at first, but I can see how it might help if I pair it with something else. I'll try the breathing before I leave, and then put on the podcast as I start walking. That way, I'm already a little calmer before I even step outside.

That sequencing makes a lot of sense; calming your body first creates a clearer pathway for the humor to land later. Just to make sure we are aligned, shall we officially set tonight's goal as completing that walk with the podcast playing, while using the breathing reset right before you step out? And before you head home, is there anything else weighing on your mind besides the walk that we should touch on briefly?
No, I think that covers it for today. I feel a little more prepared now, like I have a real plan instead of just trying to tough it out. Thank you. I'll let you know how it goes.

It sounds like you feel significantly more equipped and confident with that clear roadmap in hand. Before we wrap up, I'd love to hear one quick piece of feedback: Was there anything about our conversation today that felt particularly useful, or is there anything you wished we had covered differently?
