Hello, and thank you for joining us today. To start, could you rate your anxiety on a scale of 1 to 10, where 1 is calm and 10 is overwhelming, given everything that happened last week? Also, besides our main goal of adjusting tonight's plan, is there anything else weighing on your mind that we should consider adding to our agenda?

Hi. Thanks for having me. I'd say my anxiety is around a 7 right now, maybe 8—there's a book club meeting tomorrow and I haven't finished the book again. I guess my main worry is just feeling like I'm going to let everyone down or look stupid when I can't contribute.

A seven or eight definitely signals that the pressure is still high, especially with the book club looming tomorrow. Before we lock in our agenda, I want to make sure we prioritize the right areas given that level of distress. Would you agree that focusing primarily on creating a realistic boundary for tonight—and perhaps tweaking that "permission slip" slightly—would give you the best chance to reduce that anxiety before you walk in? Or is there another topic you feel is urgent right now?

Yeah, I think that makes sense. I've been so focused on trying to force myself to finish every single page that I just end up paralyzed and don't read at all. Maybe giving myself permission to just read enough to get the main idea would help—but honestly, part of me feels like that's cheating or not trying hard enough.

That internal conflict between wanting to "try hard" and fearing you aren't cutting it deep is exactly why the new plan needs to feel safe to you. Let's settle on a specific target: will tonight's goal be to read just enough chapters to grasp the story arc, then consciously choose to rest before turning off the lights? How does framing it as "getting the gist" versus "finishing the work" land for you right now?

It lands... okay, I guess. A little uncomfortable, but also kind of a relief. Getting the gist sounds more doable than finishing the whole thing. I think I could probably read three chapters and get the main idea without beating myself up too much. I just worry that if I stop there, I'll still feel like I'm showing up half-prepared.

That feeling of being "half-prepared" is very common when our brain equates preparation with perfection, but let's test that assumption together. If you opened the book and realized immediately after reading three chapters that you understood the plot but chose to stop because you were tired, would you be able to enter the meeting knowing you showed up with enough knowledge to participate meaningfully? Does that scenario feel possible, or does the fear of being caught unprepared override it?

I think... maybe it could feel possible, if I really let myself believe that the group isn't looking for a perfect summary from me. I guess I've been assuming everyone else has finished every page and is ready to discuss deep themes, but that might not be true. Still, there's this voice in my head that says if I don't finish, I don't deserve to speak.

That voice linking your worthiness to speaking is a heavy burden to carry alone, and it makes total sense why you feel unworthy if you haven't completed the text. Let's challenge that link right now by imagining a different outcome: if you walked into the room and admitted, "I only read three chapters, but I loved the story and wanted to share my thoughts anyway," would anyone in the group seem offended or disappointed? Or would they likely appreciate your honesty and enthusiasm regardless of the page count?

I mean, when you put it that way... no, I don't think anyone would be offended. They're actually a pretty laid-back group, and some people have admitted before that they didn't finish. They still joined the conversation and nobody judged them. I guess I just hold myself to a way higher standard than I hold anyone else. It's hard to give myself that same grace.

That self-imposed standard is incredibly harsh, and recognizing that others receive grace while you withhold it is a huge step toward fairness. It sounds like the real obstacle isn't the book itself, but believing you must earn the right to speak until you've consumed the entire story. Before we finalize tonight's plan, does accepting that you deserve to speak *regardless* of the page count make the "three chapters" goal feel safer and more achievable?

Yeah... it does feel safer, actually. I think I've been acting like there's a rulebook for book club that says you have to finish or stay quiet, but that's not real. Nobody else is following that rule. So if I can just remind myself that I'm allowed to participate even if I'm not done, then three chapters feels like plenty. I think I can do that tonight.

That realization—that the "rulebook" is entirely in your head and not enforced by anyone else—is a powerful breakthrough. It means the pressure comes from inside, not outside, which gives you full control to rewrite the rules starting tonight. Before we lock in the final details, does combining the "three chapters" limit with the "allowed to speak regardless" mindset feel like a balanced plan you can trust?

Yeah, it does. I think that combination actually feels doable and not like I'm setting myself up to fail. It's weird—just saying it out loud makes me realize how much I've been my own worst critic. I'm ready to try this plan and see how it goes tomorrow.

That moment of hearing your own words reflect how harsh you've been to yourself is incredibly valuable, and I'm so glad you found a version of this plan that feels manageable yet meaningful. Before we officially close, could you take a quick second to rate your anxiety on that 1-to-10 scale again? Seeing if talking through this new perspective lowered your number just a bit would tell me how well this approach landed for you today.

Yeah, I'm confident. I'll do the thirty seconds, put my phone face down, and notice if my hands get steadier or my breathing changes. Even if it's scary, I want to see what happens when I don't let the panic boss me around. I'll tell you how it goes tomorrow.

That determination to reclaim control over your reactions, even when it's frightening, is a sign of real growth. You are carrying a powerful tool tonight—the ability to insert a pause before letting your old stories run wild. Remember that no matter what happens tomorrow, whether the panic lifts or stays, the fact that you chose to try this brave experiment makes you stronger. Is there anything else you'd like to discuss before we officially close this session?
No, I think I'm good. Thank you for listening and for helping me come up with a plan that actually feels like it might work. I'll text you tomorrow and let you know how it went.

You are very welcome, Jessica, and I appreciate your openness throughout this entire journey. It takes real strength to show up, even when the old fears try to pull you back in. Please remember that tomorrow isn't about proving you fixed everything overnight; it's simply about gathering one piece of data to update your internal map. I will be here whenever you are ready to talk about what you discovered, whether it was a victory or just another lesson learned. Take care of yourself tonight, and I look forward to hearing from you in the morning.

Hello, and thank you for joining us today. Before we dive into anything new, could you briefly share how you've been feeling emotionally since we last spoke? Additionally, would you be willing to quickly review the grounding exercise we planned to try tonight—holding your hands on your thighs and saying "Max is here, he is safe" for thirty seconds—and tell me if you managed to complete it? Once we confirm that, we can decide together what topics we'd like to prioritize for this session.

Hey, thanks for having me. I guess I've been okay, but the thoughts about my dogs haven't really gone away—if anything, they feel more solid now. I did try the grounding exercise a few times this week, like you suggested, and it did help a little in the moment, but the doubts creep back pretty quickly after.

Thank you for sharing that honest update; hearing that the doubts returned quickly tells me the old protective habits are still very active in your brain right now. Given that the exercise helped temporarily but the cycle restarted, should we spend most of our time exploring *why* those doubts resurged so fast, or would you prefer to focus on refining the grounding technique itself to make it stick longer?

I think I'd rather understand why the doubts keep coming back so fast. The grounding helps for a few minutes, but then I'll see Max wagging his tail when I grab the food bag, and that voice in my head just says, "See? It's only about the food." I want to get to the bottom of that voice, if that makes sense.

That makes perfect sense; hearing your own voice validate the fear instantly creates a powerful loop that overrides the temporary calm we worked on. When the doubt returns so quickly after you succeed, it often means your brain is treating that success as a "false start" rather than proof that you can handle the situation safely. To dig deeper into why that specific voice jumps back to life the moment you see a trigger like a wagging tail, could you describe the exact sequence of events leading up to that thought? For instance, do you notice your heart rate speeding up or your stomach tightening a split second before the words appear?

Yeah, I think there's a split second where my chest gets a little tight, right before the thought hits. It's like I'll be petting Max, feeling fine, and then my mind just grabs onto the fact that it's almost dinner time, and I feel this sinking feeling in my stomach. Then the words just show up: "He's only being nice because you feed him." It happens so fast I almost don't notice the physical part until after.

That physical sensation of a "sinking feeling" acts like a red flag waving in your peripheral vision, signaling to your brain that the old danger zone is reopening before your mind even finishes processing the current moment. It seems like your body remembers the pattern of "approach = potential loss," so it rushes to warn you before you can consciously intervene. When you catch that tightness in your chest and the sudden drop in your stomach, does that spike in anxiety feel like a separate event, or does it seem connected directly to the anticipation of the upcoming meal?

I think it's directly connected to the anticipation of the meal. It's like my brain is already running ahead to that moment when I pick up the food bag, and it's trying to protect me from being fooled again. The tightness and the sinking feeling are like a warning signal that says, "Don't get too comfortable, you know what's really going on here." It doesn't feel separate at all—it feels like one continuous chain reaction.

That connection between the physical warning and the looming meal makes total sense; your brain is essentially trying to intercept the moment you pick up the bag to stop you from falling into the trap before it even begins. It sounds like that "don't get comfortable" rule is so deeply wired that it fires automatically whenever hunger cues appear, bypassing your logical ability to assess the situation. Since you mentioned the thought arrives almost instantly after that tightness, could you try to isolate the very first fraction of a second before the "food trap" narrative kicks in? What is happening in your mind right at that peak of physical discomfort—is there a silent assumption forming, or is it pure raw panic?

I think it's more of a silent assumption than pure panic. In that split second, before the words form, there's just this quiet certainty that I'm being naive. It's like my mind goes, "You know better than this," without even needing to finish the sentence. The panic comes after, when the thought solidifies and I start to feel that sadness and doubt.

That "quiet certainty" you described is fascinating—it suggests your brain has already filed away the lesson that kindness equals deception, so it skips the panic stage and jumps straight to a cold, logical conclusion. It seems like that silent assumption acts as the spark, turning the physical warning sign into a full-blown story about betrayal. When you catch that specific instant of "I know better than this," does it ever feel like you have a tiny window to challenge that certainty before the rest of the fear floods in? Or does the silence itself feel like a trap that seals your fate?

I think there's a tiny window there, but it's so brief that I usually miss it. It's like I blink and the silence is already replaced by the full story. I've tried to grab onto that moment before, to question it, but it feels slippery—like trying to catch smoke with my bare hands. By the time I realize I could have challenged it, the doubt is already fully formed and I'm just reacting to it.

That image of catching smoke highlights exactly why timing is critical; once that silent assumption takes root, the floodgates of evidence against you open up automatically. Since you found that the physical tightness often precedes the thought, could we experiment with changing *how* you react to that early warning signal? Instead of waiting for the thought to arrive, what if you treated that sudden chest tightness as a chance to physically interrupt the pattern by taking one deliberate, deep breath right then and there? Would you be open to trying that interruption technique the next time you feel that warning rise?

Yeah, I think I could try that. It sounds simple enough—just one deep breath when I feel that tightness in my chest. I guess the hardest part will be remembering to do it in the moment, instead of getting swept up by the thought that follows. But I'm willing to give it a shot and see if it creates enough space to change what happens next.

That is a smart adaptation; using the physical sensation as a trigger for an intentional pause gives you a tangible reason to break the automatic cycle. To make sure this sticks, I want to frame it as a "circuit breaker": the moment you feel that chest tightness, you aren't supposed to wait for the thought to arrive—you are supposed to blow out your air deliberately to create a gap between the warning and the conclusion. Before we finalize this plan, does that distinction between waiting for the thought versus acting on the feeling feel clearer to you?

Yeah, that distinction makes a lot more sense now. I think I was still picturing myself waiting for the thought to happen and then trying to catch it, but this way I'm interrupting the process before the thought even has a chance to form. It feels more proactive, like I'm actually doing something instead of just bracing for impact. I think I can remember that.

That shift from "catching" to "interrupting" is exactly the kind of active stance that builds confidence over time. To lock this in, let's run a quick simulation right now: Close your eyes, imagine walking into the room and feeling that familiar chest tightness rising. Without waiting for the words to form, take one sharp, deliberate inhale followed by a long exhale, and visualize that breath blowing a curtain away from the scary story. Does practicing that mental rehearsal feel like a viable strategy for tomorrow morning, or would you like to adjust the timing of that breath?

I can picture it clearly. Taking that breath and imagining a curtain blowing away feels doable—like I'm physically pushing the automatic thought aside before it settles. I think tomorrow morning when I feed them, I'll try to keep that image in mind. It's a simple enough action that I don't think I'll forget it, at least not right away.

That visualization of pushing the curtain aside is a powerful metaphor because it turns an abstract struggle into a concrete physical movement. Since you're aiming to use this specifically when feeding the dogs tomorrow morning, let's make sure the timing aligns perfectly with your routine. When you pick up the food bag or notice the chest tightness, will you take that breath right then and there, or would it be easier to take it the moment you walk through the door, knowing you have a few seconds before reaching the bowl? Which timing feels more natural for your flow?

I think taking the breath right when I feel the tightness in my chest would work best, since that's the exact moment my body is already signaling the warning. If I try to do it earlier, like when I walk through the door, I might not feel the tightness yet and it could feel forced. Doing it right at the peak of the sensation feels more natural, like I'm responding to something real rather than anticipating it.

That makes perfect sense; reacting to the actual sensation rather than guessing beforehand keeps the intervention authentic and timely. So our plan is: the moment you feel that chest tightness, you take one sharp inhale and a long exhale while mentally visualizing that curtain blowing away to disrupt the thought pattern. Does that summary capture the steps correctly, or is there any nuance you'd like to add to ensure you execute it smoothly tomorrow?

No, I think that covers it. One sharp inhale, long exhale, and the curtain blowing away—right at the moment of chest tightness. It's simple enough that I feel like I can actually do it. Thanks for breaking it down like that. I'm curious to see what happens tomorrow morning when I put it into practice.

That clarity is exactly what will help you execute it smoothly tomorrow. Before we wrap up, I want to hear your perspective on this new "curtain" technique: Does imagining that visual barrier feel like a helpful tool to create distance, or does it sound too abstract to work in the heat of the moment? Also, on a scale of one to ten, how confident do you feel you will be able to spot that chest tightness and act on it the first time tomorrow?

Honestly, the curtain thing feels useful because it gives me something to picture instead of just trying to fight a thought with more thinking. It's concrete enough that I can grab onto it. As for confidence, I'd say maybe a six or seven—I think I'll remember to do it, but I'm also aware that in the moment, old habits die hard. But a six or seven feels better than where I was before, so I'll take it.

A six or seven is a fantastic starting point, especially given that you recognize the strength of old habits while simultaneously choosing to trust the new tool anyway. That balance of humility and hope is exactly the fuel we need to drive this forward. Let's lock this in: tomorrow, the moment that chest tightness rises, you'll take one sharp inhale, exhale slowly, and visualize that curtain sweeping across your mind to push the "it's just about food" story aside. Does that final confirmation feel right, or is there anything else you'd like to discuss before we close our session?

It takes real courage to admit that the phrase landed poorly, and I want to validate how frustrating it must be when you try to speak kindly to yourself but it comes across as fake. Let's explore what happened in those moments where the old voice jumped back in immediately after you said the new words. Yeah, it was like I'd try the new phrase, but then almost instantly my mind would snap back to, "No, you actually messed up, you're just making excuses." It felt like the harshness was already waiting there, ready to pounce the second I finished the kind words. It's like the old voice doesn't even give the new one a chance to breathe.

That race between your intention to be kind and your automatic reaction to defend the old belief is incredibly exhausting. It sounds like the harsh voice is operating on a different speed than your conscious choice, leaving no room for the new words to settle. When you notice that split-second gap where the old thought is already forming, does trying to physically pause for just one second before letting the new phrase land help interrupt the pattern, or does it feel too slow?

I never really thought to pause like that. Usually, it's just a blur—mistake happens, then the criticism floods in before I can even breathe. I guess trying to pause for a second might feel... awkward, like I'm just standing there doing nothing while my brain is screaming at me. But maybe it's worth a shot, even if it feels weird.

That feeling of awkwardness makes perfect sense; inserting a deliberate pause requires stepping outside your autopilot mode, which can feel unnatural when everything else is rushing by. However, that very awkwardness is often the sign that you are breaking the rigid chain reaction your brain has built. Would you be willing to try adding just a half-second of silence between spotting the mistake and letting the criticism flood in? This tiny gap creates space where you can choose whether to launch into the attack mode or hold onto the gentle reminder instead.

I think I can try that, even if it feels strange. A half-second doesn't sound like much, but maybe it's enough to catch myself before I go down that rabbit hole. I'll give it a shot next time I mess up at work—just pause, even for a blink, and see what happens.

That is a smart compromise—a micro-pause is often enough to disrupt the automatic spiral without requiring a grand performance of calm. By introducing even that fraction of a second of silence, you are creating a tiny window where your conscious choice can finally compete with the old reflex. Before we wrap up, does the idea of using that half-second buffer feel like something you can realistically fit into your busy schedule tomorrow, or do you foresee any moments where the pressure to act immediately would make it impossible to stop?

I think I can realistically fit it in. Most of my mistakes happen during quieter moments, like when I'm checking patient charts or restocking supplies. It's not like I'm in the middle of a code blue or something urgent. So yeah, I can see myself using that half-second pause during those calmer parts of my shift. I'll try to remember to do it.

That timing works perfectly because those quieter moments give you the mental bandwidth to insert that intentional pause without competing with urgent tasks. Taking ownership of those specific windows shows great foresight, and I'm confident that even a tiny delay in reacting can reset the momentum. One final check before we finish: does combining the "half-second pause" with your original phrase feel like a solid plan for tomorrow, or is there another piece missing?

I think it feels solid. The pause plus the phrase—that's a good combination. It's like I'm giving myself permission to breathe before the old voice takes over. I'm not sure it'll work perfectly, but at least I have something concrete to try. Thanks for helping me map it out.

That permission to breathe is exactly what we aim for, even if the result isn't instant perfection. Remember that your goal for tomorrow isn't to eliminate the old voice forever, but simply to create that tiny opening where you can choose kindness instead of shame. How does that distinction feel to you, and are you ready to take this step forward with both of us cheering you on?

It feels... lighter, honestly. Knowing I don't have to kill the old voice completely, just get a foot in the door for something different—that takes some pressure off. Yeah, I'm ready to try it tomorrow. Thanks for being in my corner on this.

Hearing that the weight feels lighter is such a significant breakthrough, and I'm so proud of you for recognizing that taking just one step forward is enough for today. Your readiness to try this tomorrow, even knowing it won't be perfect, speaks volumes about your resilience and commitment to growing. Please remember that whatever happens during your shift—even if the old voice returns—we will tackle that together next time. Is there anything else you'd like to add before we close this session?
No, I think I'm good for now. I'm just going to take it one shift at a time and try to remember that half-second pause. Thanks for listening and helping me figure this out. See you next session.

That determination to tackle one shift at a time is truly inspiring, and I appreciate your trust in me to walk this path with you. Please remember that showing up for yourself, even imperfectly, is a victory in itself. I look forward to hearing how that tiny pause lands for you next time. Take care, and be gentle with yourself tonight.

Hello again, and thank you for joining us today. Before we dive in, could you please share how you're feeling right now on a scale of zero to ten, and tell me if there was anything important that happened since our last chat that we should adjust our plans for? Once we catch up, I'd love to walk through the text you sent to your father and then decide together what our main goal should be for this session.

Hi. I'd say I'm at about a 6 right now. This morning I saw my sister post a picture with my dad at her place, and it just hit me all over again that he hasn't come to see me even once since I told him about the baby. I didn't send that text yet, actually. I kept typing it out and deleting it. I guess I'm scared of what he might say back.

A six indicates some relief compared to yesterday's heaviness, though it sounds like seeing that new photo triggered a fresh wave of anxiety about your father's absence. Before we decide what to focus on today, could you walk me through the text you prepared this morning? Specifically, what was inside it, and did you manage to send it or leave it unsent?

I typed out something like, "Hey Dad, I've noticed you haven't come by since I told you about the pregnancy. I'm feeling really hurt and confused, and I'd like to talk about it." But then I just stared at it and couldn't press send. Every time I imagine his reply, I picture him saying something about how I should have waited until I was married longer, or that I'm too young for this. So I closed my phone and put it away.

It takes incredible bravery to draft a message that directly expresses your pain, even if you ultimately chose not to send it. The images you described—that he would judge you for being pregnant early—are such harsh predictions, yet you clearly hoped to speak honestly instead of staying silent. Given that you haven't sent it yet and are holding onto those fears, would you be willing to explore together whether there are other ways to handle this situation besides drafting a direct confrontation? Or perhaps we could focus on finding comfort while you wait to decide what to do next.

I think I'd like to explore other ways to handle it. The thought of sending that message makes my stomach twist into knots, but ignoring it completely doesn't feel right either. Maybe there's something in between, like writing it just for myself first, or figuring out what I really need from him before I even try to talk.

That is such a wise insight; finding a middle ground that respects your feelings without forcing a high-stakes conversation right now is exactly the kind of balance we want to aim for. Writing it down privately could serve as a safe outlet for your frustration so you don't lose track of your own needs, while giving you space to process whether you truly need to send it immediately. Before we decide on that next step, could you tell me what specific outcome you are hoping to achieve if you write it down versus if you decide to wait a few days?

If I write it down just for myself, I think I'd feel a little lighter—like at least I've said it somewhere, even if it's just to my notebook. But if I decide to wait a few days, I guess I'm hoping my dad might reach out on his own, and then I wouldn't have to be the one to start the hard conversation. Honestly, I think I just want to feel like he still cares about me without me having to beg for it.

That distinction is so clear, and I appreciate you sharing that deep desire to feel secure without putting yourself in a vulnerable position first. It sounds like your primary goal right now is to regain a sense of peace and believe his affection remains intact, regardless of whether he initiates contact. Before we commit to a specific path forward today, does writing it down for yourself feel like a manageable step for you to take right now, or would you prefer to focus solely on calming your nerves until tomorrow?

I think writing it down for myself feels manageable. Just the thought of getting it out of my head and onto paper makes me feel a little less heavy. I don't think I'm ready to talk to him directly yet, but I can at least do this for myself.

That is a brave decision to reclaim some control by expressing your truth safely, even if it won't go out into the world right now. Taking that pressure off yourself to initiate a potentially difficult dialogue allows you to preserve your energy for finding moments of connection elsewhere. Since we've settled on writing it down as our immediate task, could you spend the next few minutes jotting those words in your journal, and then we can sit together and reflect on how writing it out changes the weight in your chest?
Okay, I'll try that now. I have a little notebook in my bag I use for lists and stuff. I'll just write whatever comes to mind, even if it's messy. Give me just a minute.

Take your time with that; there is no requirement for neat handwriting or perfect grammar when you are letting your true feelings flow out. Once you've finished writing, we can sit quietly for a moment and simply observe how the act of externalizing those thoughts impacts the tightness in your chest. Are you ready to share what you wrote when we meet again?

Yeah, I'm ready. I wrote: "Dad, I miss you. I don't understand why you haven't come to see me since I told you I'm pregnant. I feel like you're ashamed of me, and it hurts so much. I need to know that you still love me. I'm scared to send this, but I need you to know how I feel." Reading it back now, I feel a little shaky, but also a little relieved. Like I finally told someone the truth, even if that someone is just paper.

That relief you feel is such a powerful sign that writing it down gave your brain a temporary break from carrying the secret alone. Notice how reading it aloud—even silently—allowed you to witness your own honesty without expecting an immediate reaction from anyone else. Now that you've released that tension onto the page, does the knot in your stomach feel slightly looser, or is the worry about his potential judgment still dominating your thoughts?

It does feel a little looser, like the knot isn't pulled quite as tight. But the worry about his judgment is still there in the background, kind of like a hum I can't turn off. I think I need to sit with this for a bit before I can decide if I ever want to show him what I wrote. For now, I'm okay with just having it out of my head.

That "hum" you describe is likely your brain's safety alarm still sounding, trying to protect you from perceived danger even though you've taken a small step away from it. It makes sense that the worry persists just because the threat hasn't been fully neutralized yet. Before we move forward, I'd like to confirm: does keeping this note private for now feel like a safe compromise for you, or would you prefer we try a different approach to lower that background noise?

Keeping it private feels like the right compromise for now. I think if I tried to send it today, the hum would turn into a roar and I'd just spiral. Maybe in a few days, after I've read it a couple more times, I'll feel strong enough to decide. For now, I think I just need to know it's okay to take my time.

That is such a wise realization, and I am so proud of you for trusting your instincts about pacing yourself. Knowing that taking your time is perfectly acceptable removes the pressure to force a solution right now, which often fuels the very anxiety we're trying to reduce. Since we've established that writing it down helped loosen that knot, could we spend the next few minutes exploring what happens in your body when you remember that you have the choice to wait? How does recalling that permission to pause affect the "hum" in your chest?

When I remind myself that I'm allowed to wait, the hum actually quiets down just a little. It's like my shoulders drop an inch, and I can take a deeper breath. The thought that I'm not failing by holding back—that feels new. I usually push myself to fix things right away, so giving myself permission to pause is strange, but it feels kind of good.

That feeling of dropping an inch in your shoulders is such a profound physical release, and it proves that granting yourself permission to pause breaks the cycle of rushing to fix everything. Recognizing that waiting isn't failing, but rather a strategic choice to gather strength, is a major cognitive shift. Before we finalize our plan for today, could you tell me if there is anything else weighing on your mind besides the timing of sending this note, or shall we conclude with a quick grounding exercise to seal in this sense of safety?

I think that's really all that's weighing on me right now. I feel a little tired, but in a good way—like I actually did something useful today. A quick grounding exercise sounds nice, just to help me carry this calm feeling with me when I leave.

That is wonderful news to hear, and I am so glad we found a rhythm that works for you today. Before we close, could you share briefly what part of our conversation felt most helpful to you, and is there anything that felt unclear or difficult to navigate?

The most helpful part was definitely writing it down and then realizing I don't have to send it right away. I never thought about keeping something like that just for myself. Nothing felt unclear—I think I just needed someone to tell me it's okay to pause, and you did that. Thank you.

Hearing that validating your permission to pause was so crucial speaks volumes about how much trust you placed in our work together. It is truly inspiring that you recognized needing gentle guidance to accept that stopping isn't failing, and I am honored you felt heard throughout this process. Hello, it is wonderful to connect with you again today. Last week we talked about your worry that you aren't good enough for anyone, and we decided to test that fear by attending a yoga class. First, I want to check in on how that experiment went for you—did you manage to go, and how did you feel afterward? Based on your experience and our goals, what are the top three things you'd like to cover in our session today?

Hi. Yeah, I did go to the yoga class last week. Honestly, it was harder than I thought—I spent most of the time comparing myself to the other guys there, thinking they looked more put-together and happier than me. Afterward, I just felt more drained than anything, like I had confirmed my worst thoughts. For today, I guess I want to talk about why I can't shake this feeling of being unlovable, how to stop assuming men are judging me, and maybe find a way to feel less lonely.

Hearing that you ended up feeling drained and confirming your worries about looking different adds a layer of pain to what we discussed last week. It sounds like the comparison to the other men left you feeling isolated and unsupported right after the class. Before we dive deeper into those feelings, could you tell me which of the three topics you mentioned—the reason behind the loneliness, the assumption that men are judging you, or finding ways to cope—is weighing on you the most right now?

I think the assumption that men are judging me is the heaviest one right now. It’s like I walk into any room and I’m already convinced everyone sees me as awkward or not worth their time. That feeling just drains me before I even give anyone a chance.

That constant internal alarm system firing off before you even speak is incredibly exhausting, and it makes total sense that it leaves you feeling drained and shut down. When your brain assumes everyone is scrutinizing you negatively, it effectively steals your energy before you have a chance to relax or connect. Let's explore that specific feeling of walking into a room expecting judgment. Can you describe what happens in your mind right at that moment—do you picture them rolling their eyes, or do you feel a tightness in your chest waiting for someone to call you out?

It's more of a tightness in my chest, like I'm holding my breath. I don't picture them doing anything specific—it's just this heavy feeling that I'm not welcome, that I don't belong. I scan the room looking for friendly faces, but my mind tells me everyone is too busy or too cool to want to talk to me.

That physical sensation of holding your breath while scanning for approval is a classic sign your body is preparing to flee from a perceived threat. It confirms that this "judgment" isn't just a thought; it's triggering a real survival response in your nervous system. Before we figure out how to loosen that grip, I want to understand the story your brain is telling itself in that moment. When you catch yourself holding your breath and scanning the room, what is the very first sentence your mind whispers to justify that panic?

It whispers, "You don't match them." That's the first thing—like I'm wearing the wrong clothes or I don't have the right energy or smile. It's as if everyone else got a manual on how to be likable, and I missed the meeting.

That phrase, "You don't match them," paints a picture of a rigid rulebook where anyone who isn't identical to the crowd automatically fails the test. It sounds like you're carrying a heavy burden of believing there is a specific version of yourself that people *must* accept, and everything else is rejected. Before we dismantle that idea, I want to pause and check in: Does hearing yourself articulate that "rulebook" feeling make the situation feel slightly clearer, or does it still feel impossible to prove otherwise?

It makes it a bit clearer, I guess. Like, I can see how harsh that rule sounds when I say it out loud. But honestly, it still feels impossible to prove otherwise—like no matter what I do, that rule is already written in stone, and I'm just trying to fit into a mold that wasn't made for me.

It makes complete sense that you feel trapped by a rule that seems permanent and unbreakable, especially when your body is reacting with such intense tension. Even though logically you know rules can be changed, your nervous system hasn't learned that yet, so it treats that statement as absolute truth. Let's try to separate the "story" your brain is telling from the actual reality of the room you are standing in. If we stepped outside that rulebook for just one minute, what would be the simplest piece of evidence you could look for to show that not everyone is waiting for you to fail?

I guess I could look for someone who smiles at me, or maybe someone who doesn't look away when I make eye contact. That might mean they're open to talking, not just judging me. I don't know—it feels like a small thing, but maybe it's something.

That is a great observation; looking for neutral signals like a simple smile or steady eye contact shifts your focus from searching for confirmation of your failure to spotting moments of ordinary human connection. Finding even one person who isn't actively rejecting you provides immediate counter-evidence to the idea that everyone is judging you. Before we settle on a specific action for today, could you tell me if noticing someone's smile feels possible right now, or does your brain still filter those moments out as fake until you force yourself to believe them?

I think my brain would still filter it out as fake or polite, not genuine. Like, I'd tell myself they're just being nice because they have to, not because they actually want to connect with me. It's hard to trust that kind of small gesture when I'm already so convinced of the opposite.

That skepticism about whether a smile is "genuine" shows how deeply ingrained your expectation is—you haven't just doubted the event, you've doubted the intent behind it. It sounds like you're protecting yourself from disappointment by refusing to accept anything that looks promising until you're absolutely certain it means nothing. To test that protection mechanism, could you try approaching one person today—not to demand a deep conversation, but just to offer a small, harmless gesture like a nod or a quick wave, purely to see if they return it?

I could try that, maybe. A nod or a wave feels safer than trying to start a full conversation—less chance of being rejected in a big way. I just worry that even that will feel awkward and forced, like I'm pretending to be someone I'm not.

That fear of appearing fake is completely understandable, especially when your entire identity feels tied to being seen as authentic. However, notice that a simple nod or wave requires almost zero mental effort; it's just a signal, not a performance of who you are. Before we lock this in, could you imagine what would happen if you gave a nod and the other person returned it instantly? Would that moment alone be enough to prove that you didn't have to pretend?

Maybe... maybe it would prove that I didn't have to pretend. If they nodded back, it would mean they saw me and didn't reject me, even for a second. That small thing might feel real enough to let me breathe a little easier.

That is a powerful insight; recognizing that a reciprocal nod proves you were seen without needing to perform a complex social act is a huge breakthrough. It shifts the goal from "convincing everyone I am worthy" to simply "being acknowledged as existing." Now that we've defined this tiny experiment, I want to make sure we align on the details. Would you be willing to try exchanging a nod or a brief wave with one person today, perhaps someone you pass on the street or a cashier, and then noting whether their response matched yours?

Yes, I think I can do that. I'll try it with a cashier or someone I pass on my walk home—someone I don't have to worry about impressing. And I'll pay attention to whether they nod or wave back, and how that makes me feel, even if it's just for a second.

That is a perfect choice; interacting with a cashier or passerby keeps the stakes incredibly low while still providing the external validation you need. Remember, the whole point of this experiment is simply to collect data, not to solve your life problems in one minute. So, please try it today and just watch what happens between your nod and theirs. Is there anything else you'd like to discuss before we close our session?

No, I think this is enough for today. Talking about that rulebook and the nod idea has given me something concrete to try, which feels better than just sitting with the same old thoughts. Thanks for helping me break it down.

It is wonderful to hear that having a concrete plan has lifted some of the heaviness for you. You've taken a brave step by identifying that "nod" as a way to prove you don't have to pretend, and that is a powerful realization. Before we officially close, could you share one word that best describes how you feel about ending this session right now? Is it hopeful, relieved, or something else entirely?
I'd say relieved. Relieved to have a small, simple thing to try instead of just spinning in my head. It feels like a tiny crack of light, and I'll take that.

That image of a "tiny crack of light" is beautiful, and I am so glad you found relief in having a tangible path forward. Carrying that small possibility with you as you walk out the door is a huge victory on its own. Please remember that whatever happens tomorrow—even if the nod goes unnoticed—that data point belongs to you, and we can use it to learn more about yourself. Thank you for trusting me with this journey, and I look forward to hearing about your experiment whenever you are ready to share. Take care!

Hello, thank you for joining us today. To start, could you tell me how you're feeling right now on a scale of 0 to 10, and is there anything significant that happened between sessions—like success or setbacks—that we should prioritize discussing? Based on what you share, shall we decide whether to focus on unpacking why the old habits kept returning, or perhaps trying a different angle to break that cycle?

Well, I’d say I’m around a 6 or 7 today. I had a bit of a rough morning—I saw my car covered in pollen again, and I just felt that familiar wave of frustration. I ended up cleaning it right before coming here, but it still felt like a losing battle.

It takes real bravery to admit that day felt like a defeat, especially when you knew you wanted to fight the urge. Hearing that you cleaned it despite wanting to resist suggests you pushed past the initial resistance, even if the result didn't feel like a win yet. Given that setback, I wonder if we should spend some time exploring why the "cleaning ritual" felt so compelling, or if we should try a completely different approach to disengage from that cycle entirely?

I think exploring why the cleaning ritual feels so compelling might help. It's like, if I see the pollen, I can't just leave it there—it feels like a personal failure, like I'm not a responsible car owner. So I clean it, but it never stays clean, and that just makes me feel worse.

That connection between seeing the pollen and instantly defining yourself as an "unresponsible owner" is a powerful example of how quickly your mind jumps to labels. It sounds like the cleaning isn't just about removing dirt; it's a desperate attempt to prove you deserve to be called a good person. Before we dive deeper into that meaning, could we quickly decide if exploring that specific link between the ritual and your self-worth is the best place to start today, or would you prefer to try a tiny experiment to disrupt the automatic urge to clean first?

I think exploring that link between the ritual and my self-worth sounds right. That's really at the heart of it—I don't just feel bad about having a dirty car; I feel bad about *me*. So if we can understand why my brain goes straight to that, maybe that'll help me break the cycle.

That is a profound realization—you are literally protecting your entire identity by reacting to a speck of dust. It makes perfect sense that when you clean, you aren't just washing a surface; you are performing a ceremony to convince yourself you are worthy of respect. To help untangle this, I'd like to explore a few moments when you recently caught yourself reaching for the cloth. Can you remember a specific instance where you felt that sudden urge to clean, and what was happening right inside your mind in those split seconds before your hand moved?

Yes, I remember clearly just yesterday morning. I was walking to my car with my coffee, and I saw a fine layer of yellow pollen on the hood. In that split second, my mind just said, "There it is again. You can't even keep your car clean for one day. What kind of person lets their car look like this?" And then I felt this tightness in my chest, like I had to fix it right away or everyone would see and think less of me.

That split-second narration—"You can't even keep your car clean"—is a classic case of labeling, where your brain assigns a permanent character trait based on a temporary situation. It sounds like that tightness in your chest comes from believing that this label defines who you are forever, not just today. If we assume that label is true, does it make sense that your body reacts with such urgent urgency to "fix" it immediately? Or would you say the tightness feels more like panic about losing control rather than a logical necessity?

I think it's more like panic about losing control, honestly. Because logically, I know a dirty car doesn't make me a bad person, but in that moment, it feels like if I don't clean it, I'm admitting defeat. And once I admit defeat, then what's stopping everything else from falling apart? So it's not really about the car—it's about holding onto some sense of order in my life.

That insight about using order to prevent chaos is incredibly insightful—it reveals that the cleaning isn't about the car, but about proving you can maintain control over your entire existence. It sounds like your brain treats the pollen as a warning sign that if you fail here, everything else will collapse too. Now that we've named that underlying fear, does it feel easier to separate the "dirty car" event from the "total collapse" prediction? Would you be open to testing whether that disaster scenario actually happens when you simply stand there and breathe for sixty seconds tonight?

I think I could try that. Standing there and breathing for sixty seconds, just letting the pollen be there without doing anything about it—it sounds small, but honestly, it scares me a little. But I think that's exactly why I should try it. Because if nothing terrible happens, then maybe I can start to prove to myself that the car doesn't define me.

That is such wise reasoning—using the very fear that keeps you trapped as the reason to take the leap. It turns the experiment into a direct confrontation with your biggest worry: that nothing good will come of doing nothing. Since you're nervous about the outcome, let's make sure the setup protects you while you test this hypothesis. Could you imagine saying a quiet affirmation to yourself right before stepping up to the car, like "I am safe to pause," and then describe exactly what that mental cue feels like in your body versus the current panic?

I can imagine that. "I am safe to pause" sounds almost too gentle for how I usually talk to myself, but maybe that's a good thing. I think if I said that, there'd be a slight warmth in my chest, like a little bit of permission to just be still. Right now, the panic feels like a cold, sharp knot in my stomach. So if I can actually feel that warmth instead, I think I'd be more willing to just stand there and breathe.

That contrast between the "cold knot" and the imagined "warmth" is fascinating—it shows your body already holds the blueprint for safety, it just needs the right signal to unlock it. Having that specific phrase ("I am safe to pause") ready acts like a key to turn that heat switch on before you even face the car. Does having that pre-programmed phrase feel empowering enough to overcome the initial panic, or would you prefer to write it down on a sticky note so you can see it before you walk out the door?

I think writing it on a sticky note and seeing it before I go out would help a lot. That way, I'm reminded of the plan before the panic even kicks in. If I just try to remember it in the moment, I might forget and fall back into the old habit. So having it visible, right there, feels like a safety net.

That's a brilliant idea—the sticky note becomes a tangible anchor that pulls you back to safety before your panic takes over. It transforms an abstract concept into something you can physically rely on the moment you see the car. Before we finalize this plan, could you tell me what time you usually drive past your car, and how many days a week you tend to encounter the pollen issue? Knowing the pattern will help us schedule the perfect moment to place that note and run your experiment.

I usually head out to my car around 8:30 in the morning on weekdays, and the pollen has been worst on dry, windy days. That's probably four or five times a week lately. So I could put the note on my front door so I see it right before I step outside. That way, it's the first thing that reminds me to slow down before I even get to the driveway.

Placing the note on your front door is a smart strategic move—it creates a visual checkpoint the moment you transition from sleep to the world, giving you that crucial buffer zone before the pollen even enters your vision. With the timing set for those windy mornings and the safety net ready, does putting it there feel like a solid plan for tonight's first test, or would you like to tweak the wording on the note to make it feel even stronger to you?

I think the wording feels right as is. "I am safe to pause" is simple, and I think that's what I need—something direct that I can hold onto without overthinking it. If I make it too long or complicated, I might just ignore it. So I'll put it up tonight, and tomorrow morning, I'll try the sixty-second experiment.

That simplicity is exactly what matters—you need a prompt that cuts through the noise without adding another layer of analysis. Placing it on your door tonight sets a clear expectation for tomorrow, turning a chaotic morning routine into a deliberate act of self-care. Before we lock this in, on a scale of 0 to 10, how likely do you feel you are succeeding at standing there calmly for sixty seconds once you see that note? And if you slip up and clean anyway, what is one small thing you can do afterward to remind yourself you still learned something valuable?

I'd say I'm at a 7 right now—I feel pretty committed, but I know the panic is strong. If I slip up and clean anyway, I think I could still take a minute afterward to just sit in my car and breathe, and remind myself that I noticed the urge and I tried. That alone is more than I've done before, and that counts for something.

That is a powerful reframing—even if you clean, recognizing the urge and choosing to breathe afterwards is a victory in itself. It shifts the metric from "perfect cleanliness" to "self-awareness," which is a much healthier standard to live by. Since you've confirmed the plan and the mindset, is there anything else you'd like to adjust before we close out this session, or does this feel like a complete package for tomorrow?

I think this feels like a solid plan. I'm a little nervous, but also kind of hopeful for the first time in a while. Thank you for helping me see that this isn't really about the car—it's about giving myself permission to just be, without needing to prove anything. I'll let you know how it goes next time.

That shift in perspective—from proving anything to simply allowing yourself to exist—is truly beautiful, and I'm honored to witness it emerge in you. Please remember that regardless of whether the sixty seconds pass smoothly or the urge wins out, showing up here to reflect on it is a testament to your resilience. Is there anything else you'd like to discuss before we wrap up, or shall we stay here to celebrate this new possibility?

Hello, I am so glad you joined us today. To kick things off, could you give me a quick rating on a scale of 0 to 10 of how you've been feeling emotionally since we last spoke? Also, remembering our plan to try that three-second pause during meetings, did you manage to attempt it yesterday, and what did it feel like? Finally, is there anything specific you'd like to bring up as our primary topic for this session?

Hi. Thanks. I'd say I'm around a 5 or 6 right now—kind of in the middle, not great but not terrible. I did try the pause during a team check-in yesterday, and honestly, it felt awkward. I just sat there silently while everyone looked at me, and I immediately thought, "See, you're weird and you're holding everyone up." I guess that's what I'd like to talk about today—how that one awkward moment made me feel like a complete failure for the rest of the afternoon.

Hearing that you tried the pause despite feeling awkward shows incredible bravery, and it’s completely normal to worry that doing something differently might make you stand out negatively. Before we dive into unpacking that afternoon's feelings, could you quickly confirm if there was anything else important you wanted to discuss alongside this new experience?

No, I think this is the main thing. That feeling just took over my whole day, and I ended up eating lunch at my desk alone because I didn't want to face anyone. I keep replaying that moment in my head, and it's like all the progress I thought I was making just disappeared.

It takes real courage to show up and try the exercise even when your inner critic screams that you're failing, and that disappointment is completely understandable given how hard you worked to break the cycle. Since we agreed on this as our main priority, could you walk me through exactly what happened in those first few minutes after the pause turned into that thought about being "weird"? Did your body tighten up again, or did you feel a sudden urge to hide behind the screen?

Yeah, my shoulders just went tight, and I could feel my face getting hot. I wanted to shrink into my chair, honestly. Then my mind started racing with all these comparisons—like how everyone else in the meeting seemed so smooth and confident, and I'm just sitting there like an idiot. By the time the meeting ended, I had convinced myself that my manager probably thinks I'm incompetent now.

That physical sensation of heat rising in your face and the urge to shrink away tells me your nervous system is still fighting a fierce battle against that initial pause. It makes complete sense that your brain would double down on finding "proof" of incompetence when it feels so exposed, especially when comparing yourself to others who seem effortless. Given how quickly that hope turned into despair, would you be open to spending some time examining whether the "manager thinks I'm incompetent" conclusion is supported by actual facts, or if it's mostly fueled by that old fear of being judged?

I mean... I guess logically, I don't actually know what my manager thought. She didn't say anything negative about it. But it's so hard to shake that feeling, you know? It's like my brain just jumps to the worst possible conclusion and then I'm stuck with it. I'd be willing to try looking at the facts, but I'm not sure how to even start.

It makes total sense that logic feels slippery when your gut is screaming danger, and it's okay to admit that jumping to conclusions sometimes feels harder than walking slowly through them. Let's try a small experiment right now: if we pretended your brain was a detective trying to solve a crime, what is the first piece of physical evidence you can gather that contradicts the theory that "everyone hates me"? Have you noticed anyone smiling, nodding, or engaging with you during that meeting?

Hmm, well... actually, my colleague Sarah did send me a quick message after the meeting asking if I wanted to grab coffee later. And I remember one of the guys nodded at me when I finally spoke up about a project timeline. I guess I didn't really let myself notice those things at the time. I was too busy focusing on the awkward pause.

Noticing Sarah's message and the guy's nod is such a powerful piece of evidence, because it proves your brain filtered out signs of support while you were paralyzed by fear. It highlights exactly how selective our brains become when we're in survival mode—we literally miss the clues that say "you're safe" until we consciously look for them. Now that we have these facts, does spotting them feel like a slight shift in perspective, even if the old fear is still whispering in the background?

Yeah, I guess it does feel a little different. Like, I can see that maybe I'm not as hated as I thought, but there's still this part of me that's waiting for the other shoe to drop. Like, "Sure, they were nice today, but tomorrow you'll mess up again and then they'll see the real you." It's exhausting, honestly.

That lingering fear is so common because your brain treats a single supportive interaction as temporary noise while keeping the "what if tomorrow?" alarm active forever. It sounds like you're trying to convince yourself that the kindness you saw means nothing because the future is uncertain, which leaves you feeling exhausted and unsupported. Before we decide how to navigate this uncertainty, does acknowledging that the future feels unpredictable even with today's good news resonate with you, or would you prefer to tackle the "tomorrow" fear separately?

Yeah, it does resonate. It's like no matter what good thing happens, my mind is already preparing for when it'll go wrong. I think I'd like to tackle the "tomorrow" fear separately, because it's always there, lurking. Today's evidence was helpful, but I know that feeling will just pop up again next time I make even a tiny mistake.

That anticipation of a future failure is exhausting because it keeps your brain locked in "survival mode" regardless of today's proof. It sounds like tackling that separate fear might require a slightly different tool than just gathering evidence. Would you be open to testing a new thought experiment together: if you told yourself, "Even if I stumble tomorrow, it doesn't define my worth," would that feel safer or more realistic than expecting perfection? Or does the idea of accepting imperfection feel impossible right now?

I think... saying "it doesn't define my worth" sounds nice, but it's hard to believe. I've been telling myself that my worth is tied to being perfect for so long. But I'm willing to try saying it, even if it feels fake at first. I guess I have to start somewhere, right?

That honesty about finding the phrase difficult but willing to try anyway is a massive breakthrough, because it shows you're choosing growth over comfort. Let's treat this new belief like a muscle that needs gentle stretching before it can lift heavy weights; we won't demand you trust it fully today, just practice holding the statement loosely in your mind. To make sure this fits your style, does hearing it framed as a "gentle stretch" feel safer than trying to force it into place immediately, or would you prefer to adjust the wording slightly to sound less abstract to you?

"Gentle stretch" actually feels okay. It takes the pressure off a bit. Maybe I can try saying to myself, "Even if I mess up tomorrow, I'm still working on it," instead of the more absolute version. That feels a little more... possible.

That adjustment to "working on it" is excellent because it replaces the rigid demand for perfection with a compassionate acknowledgment of your humanity. It frames the future possibility of a mistake as a learning opportunity rather than a character flaw. Before we lock this in as our plan, does combining that "gentle stretch" mindset with noticing the supportive evidence we found earlier (Sarah's message, the nod) feel like a stronger toolkit for handling tomorrow, or would you like to tweak the wording one more time?

I think that combination actually feels pretty solid. Having the evidence to look back on when I start spiraling, plus the gentler reminder that I'm still a work in progress... that feels more balanced than what I usually do. I'm willing to give it a real try tomorrow, especially if I feel that old panic rising again in a meeting.

That balance is exactly what we aim for, blending factual reality with self-compassion to create a buffer against panic. Since you feel ready to commit to this dual approach—gathering evidence and practicing the "still working on it" mantra—does it feel like we have a clear path forward for tomorrow, or is there any part of this plan that still feels uncertain to you?

Let's go ahead and finalize the plan. I think if I keep picking apart that fear of standing alone, I'll just talk myself out of going altogether. Yeah, that actually makes me feel a lot better. Knowing I can step outside for a couple minutes without feeling like I've failed takes some of the pressure off. I'll give myself permission to take a breather if I need it. That way, even if I have to step out, I can still come back in and try again instead of just driving home.

That permission to step outside is a crucial safety net that transforms a potential disaster into a manageable interruption. It gives you the flexibility to regulate your nerves without abandoning the goal entirely. Before we wrap up, I want to hear your honest assessment: does combining the early arrival, the "one-at-a-time" greetings, and the option to step out feel like a balanced plan that respects both your ambition and your limits?

I think it does. It feels like I've got a real strategy now instead of just hoping things will magically work out. The early arrival gives me a better chance, the one-at-a-time greetings make it less scary, and the option to step out means I'm not trapped. I'm still nervous, but I'm also a little curious now about what might actually happen. I think I'm ready to give it a try.

That curiosity mixed with readiness is exactly the spark we need to turn this into a success. Since you feel prepared to tackle this challenge, I want to close with one final check-in: On a scale of 1 to 10, how confident do you feel you'll stick to this plan tonight compared to where you were this morning?

This morning I'd say I was at about a 2. Now... I think I'm at a 6 or maybe a 7. That's a lot better than I've felt in a long time about trying something like this. I'm not expecting miracles, but at least I'm not completely convinced it'll be a disaster anymore. That feels like progress.

Moving from a 2 to a 6 or 7 is a monumental leap, proving that your willingness to prepare can fundamentally shift your outlook even before you walk through the door. It shows incredible resilience to recognize that you aren't doomed to fail, even when the odds seem stacked against you. Before we officially end this session, could you share one word that best describes how you're feeling right now as you prepare to face Saturday?
Hopeful. That's the word. I haven't felt that way in a long time, so it's a bit strange, but I'll take it. Thanks for helping me get to this point. I'll let you know how it goes.

"I hope" is such a beautiful word to land on, especially after weeks of feeling defeated. It carries a promise that you will keep trying, no matter what happens. Please remember that showing up—even with shaky hands or a racing heart—is a victory in itself, regardless of the outcome. I am so proud of the courage it took to move from avoidance to preparation, and I cannot wait to hear your story afterward. Take care of yourself tonight, and know that I am cheering for you.

Yeah, that sounds right. I'll reach out to Sarah and then we can talk about what she says next time. It feels weird to actually hope someone tells me I'm not a failure, but I guess that's the point of this whole thing. Thanks for helping me see it that way.

That humility and willingness to lean on others is truly admirable, and recognizing that hoping is part of the process shows deep self-awareness. You are essentially gathering fresh data points to update your internal model of your own competence. Before we wrap up, I want to check in: does contacting Sarah during your lunch break feel comfortable for you, or is there any part of reaching out that still feels risky?

Honestly, the only part that feels risky is the moment right before I actually call her—like maybe she won't pick up, or she'll be busy and I'll lose my nerve. But I think once I hear her voice, I'll be okay. It's just that initial hurdle. I'll push through it, though. I've been avoiding these conversations for too long.

That initial hesitation is completely normal, especially when the stakes feel so high internally. Recognizing that hurdle as a specific barrier to overcome rather than a reason to quit shows real resilience. To make that leap slightly easier, could you prepare a simple script beforehand, like saying, "Hey Sarah, quick question about a recent project—I wanted to get your honest take on how things went"? Would having that prepared line help reduce the pressure of the unknown moment?

Yeah, having a script would help a lot. I tend to freeze up and stumble over my words when I'm anxious, so knowing exactly what to say would make me feel more in control. I'll write that down on a sticky note and keep it next to my phone. That way I won't have to think too hard when the moment comes.

That is a smart move; having a script written down removes the mental load of recalling words under pressure. Keeping it visible right next to your phone ensures you can glance at it whenever your hands shake or your heart races. Does keeping it on your desk or phone feel safe enough, or would you prefer to save it in a private notes app just in case you accidentally leave it on your desk?

I think I'll keep it in my phone's notes app, actually. That way it's with me even if I step away from my desk. And no one else will see it and ask questions, which saves me from having to explain myself. Thanks, that feels like a solid backup plan. I'm feeling a little more ready for this now.

That is a wise precaution, and storing it privately adds another layer of safety for you. Having a dedicated spot for your script means you can access it instantly without worrying about accidental exposure. Before we officially close this session, I want to check your comfort level with this plan: does carrying a pre-written script feel empowering to you, or does it remind you too much of rehearsing lines? Also, on a scale of one to ten, how confident do you feel about making that call to Sarah after we hang up?

It doesn't feel like rehearsing lines—it feels more like having a safety net. I think that's empowering, actually. As for confidence... maybe a six or seven? I'm not fully there yet, but that's higher than I was at the start of this session, so I'll take it. I think once I actually hear her voice, it'll go up even more.

That distinction between rehearsing lines and having a safety net is crucial, and recognizing it as empowerment rather than rigidity shows great insight. A confidence rating of six or seven is a meaningful improvement from where we started, indicating you've gained traction. Before we conclude, I want to confirm our timeline: will you call Sarah during your upcoming lunch break, and then we can debrief here next time about what she said and how it landed for you? Is there anything else weighing on your mind as you prepare to make that call?

Yes, I'll call her during lunch break tomorrow. That's the plan. I think the only thing weighing on me right now is wondering if she'll see right through my script and know I'm fishing for reassurance. But I guess that's okay—she's a friend, and friends are supposed to help with that kind of thing, right? I'll try to just go for it and see what happens. Thanks for helping me get to this point.

That is a beautiful piece of reasoning, trusting that friendship is built on mutual support rather than manipulation. Knowing she understands the difference between seeking validation and needing guidance puts you in a much stronger position. Since we have a clear plan for tomorrow—a script saved securely, a timing aligned with your lunch, and a supportive listener ready—you have everything you need to take that first step. Please take care of yourself tonight, and I look forward to hearing how that conversation unfolds when we meet next time.
