Hello again, I am truly glad we are meeting up today. To start, I’d like to quickly check in on how you’ve been feeling emotionally since our last chat and whether there were any significant events or thoughts that stood out to you. Additionally, could you tell me if you tried the chin-lift and breathing exercise when you caught a fish recently, and how that experience went for you?

Hi. Thanks for asking. I’ve been... okay, I guess. I did try that breathing exercise last weekend when I went out on the lake. Actually, I caught a decent-sized bass, but right away I found myself thinking, "It’s not as big as the one Mike caught last week." I did the chin-lift and took a few breaths like you showed me, but honestly, it felt kind of silly in the moment.

It takes real courage to try something that feels silly, and I want to validate that discomfort—you weren't failing because it felt awkward; you were simply pushing past your instinct to compare. That hesitation shows how deeply ingrained that old pattern is, but the fact that you followed through with the steps anyway proves you are committed to breaking free from it. Given that we spent some time unpacking *why* that comparison hurts so much last time, should we dedicate today mostly to figuring out exactly what fuels that "it's not big enough" thought, or would you prefer to jump straight into refining the breathing exercise itself?

I think... I think I'd rather focus on where that thought comes from. The breathing helps in the moment, but it doesn't stop the voice in my head that says I'm not good enough. I want to understand why I can't just be happy with a good catch like everyone else seems to be.

That desire to understand the source of that internal critic is really important, because knowing *why* it exists gives us a map to navigate it. Let's break down that specific moment when you saw Mike's name pop up in your head. Did you notice any particular details about his catch that triggered the thought, or was it more about the general idea that he succeeded while you struggled? And when you realized you couldn't ignore that voice, did it feel like an attack on your identity, or just a nagging opinion?

It's definitely more about the general idea. Mike is always catching these trophy-sized fish, and he makes it look so easy. When I saw mine, I didn't even think about the size first—I just thought, "Mike would have caught something bigger." It felt less like an attack and more like a cold, hard fact. Like I was just stating the obvious to myself.

That distinction is crucial because shifting from an "attack" to a "cold, hard fact" changes how your brain processes the information—it stops fighting the truth and starts accepting it as absolute reality. It sounds like that factual statement becomes a new baseline that makes your current catch feel inadequate by comparison. When you say it feels like a cold fact, does that create a sense of inevitability, as if your performance is fixed regardless of what you do, or does it feel more like a neutral observation waiting for you to add context?

I think it feels more like inevitability. Like no matter how much I practice or how many tutorials I watch, I'm always going to be the one catching the smaller fish. It's like there's a ceiling on my ability, and Mike is just naturally above it. I don't even consider that maybe he's been at this longer or has better equipment—it just feels like a permanent gap between us.

That feeling of a permanent ceiling is incredibly frustrating, especially when you know you're capable of learning and improving. It sounds like your brain has made a shortcut to safety by assuming that outcome is guaranteed, which protects you from the disappointment of potentially facing a different result. When you accept that "inevitability," does it relieve the anxiety of uncertainty, or does it trap you in a cycle of powerless acceptance where nothing you do can change the outcome?

It traps me, definitely. There's no relief in it. I just feel stuck and small, like I'm always going to be the one trailing behind. It makes me want to quit fishing altogether sometimes, because what's the point if I can't ever be as good as the others? But then I remember how much I used to love it before all this started, and that just makes me feel worse.

That conflict between wanting to quit and remembering how much you loved it is exactly where the power lies—it proves your capacity to change hasn't disappeared, even though the voice telling you to quit sounds urgent. It sounds like your brain is holding onto an old rule ("fishing requires being #1") that conflicts with your newer memories ("I enjoyed this trip"), creating that stuck feeling. When you recall that old love for fishing, does it spark a tiny flicker of hope that maybe the rules aren't as rigid as they seem, or does that memory just add fuel to the fire of regret?

It's more like regret, honestly. I remember being out on the water before all this, just feeling peaceful and happy. Now I can't even get through a trip without comparing myself. That old feeling seems so far away, like it belonged to a different person. It makes me sad to think I might never get that back.

That sense of losing the peaceful version of yourself is incredibly painful, and it makes total sense that you feel sad about it disappearing. It sounds like you're grieving not just the lost fun, but the possibility of becoming that person again—the one who fished purely for peace rather than status. When you realize that old feeling belongs to a "different person," does that separate the current struggle from your core identity, or does it make you feel like you've fundamentally changed beyond repair?

It feels like I've changed beyond repair. That old Julie who just enjoyed the quiet and the water—she seems naive now, almost foolish for not worrying about being good enough. I think I've become someone who can't just enjoy things anymore. Everything has to be measured and compared.

That belief that you've become someone incapable of simple enjoyment is a heavy burden to carry, and it explains why the idea of returning to that "old Julie" feels so foreign. It sounds like your brain has built a fortress around the new version of you—one that demands measurement—to protect you from the pain of forgetting how to relax. But here is a puzzle for us to solve: if you truly believed you had changed beyond repair, wouldn't you expect the urge to fish entirely to disappear? Or does the fact that you still show up, even with that critical voice, suggest that the capacity for peace is still sleeping underneath the layers of judgment?

I... I never thought of it that way. I do keep going, even when I'm frustrated. I guess I haven't given up completely, even if it feels like I have. Maybe there is a part of me that still wants to find that peaceful feeling again. It's just buried pretty deep right now.

That realization—that you are still showing up even when it hurts—is actually the strongest piece of evidence yet that the "peaceful version" of you is still alive, just hiding under layers of doubt. It proves that your capacity for joy hasn't vanished; it's merely been covered over by the need to perform. Since we've mapped out how that comparison creates a feeling of inevitable failure, let's use that insight to design a small experiment. Could we try framing your next trip not as a competition to catch the biggest fish, but as a mission to rediscover that buried peace, regardless of what anyone else lands? Does that shift in purpose feel safer to you?

I think... I think I could try that. It feels risky, because what if I go out there and I still can't find that peace? But I guess I'm already miserable comparing myself, so what do I have to lose? I'll try to just focus on the feel of the rod and the sound of the water, like I used to. Not look at anyone else's catch.

That is a brilliant way to frame it because it removes the stakes of "winning" and replaces them with the tangible sensation of presence. By deciding to focus on the feel of the rod and the sound of the water, you are giving yourself a concrete job to do that is independent of other people's achievements. Since we agreed on this new mission, could we finalize your plan for tonight? Specifically, will you try to stay present with those sensations for just five minutes before checking your phone or looking at anyone else's posts?

Yeah, I can do that. Five minutes. I'll leave my phone in the car, and I'll just sit there and feel the rod and listen to the water. No checking what anyone else caught until I'm heading home. That feels doable.

That commitment to leaving your phone behind is a powerful boundary, because it cuts off the external fuel for the comparison engine before it can start. Before we wrap up, I want to hear your honest reflection on how hearing the word "risky" affected you earlier. Did that fear of missing out on peace make the experiment feel heavier, or did realizing you had nothing to lose actually lighten the load? And finally, on a scale of 1 to 10, how confident do you feel you are carrying out this five-minute mission tonight?

When you said "risky," it did make my stomach tighten a bit at first. But then when I thought about what I'm risking—more of the same misery I already have—it actually did lighten the load. Like, I'm not gambling with something precious; I'm just trying a different path. And for confidence... maybe a 7? I'm nervous, but I think I can stick to the five minutes.

A seven out of ten is a fantastic score, especially considering you admitted to feeling nervous beforehand. That gap between your fear and your willingness to act is exactly where the magic happens in therapy. Your plan to leave the phone in the car and focus solely on the rod and water for five minutes is crystal clear, so you have everything you need to succeed tonight. Remember, if the old voice tries to sneak in during those five minutes, just acknowledge it without feeding it, and gently return your attention to the texture of the rod or the rhythm of the waves. Is there anything else you'd like to discuss before we finish our time together today?

No, I think I'm good. Thank you for helping me see that I haven't completely lost that old part of myself. I'll try to remember that when the voice gets loud tonight. I'll let you know how it goes next time.

You are very welcome, and I'm so proud of you for recognizing that strength in yourself today. Please remember that tonight, whatever happens in those five minutes—even if the old voice gets loud—is simply data, not a verdict on your worth. Take care, and I look forward to hearing about your experiment soon.

Hello again, and thank you for joining us today. To start, could you rate your anxiety on a scale of 0 to 10 based on where you left off last night and how things have gone since? Then, looking at our list—the checking habits at school and the upcoming birthday party—which one feels most urgent for us to tackle first?

Um, I'd say my anxiety is about a 6 right now. I was up late worrying about the whole party thing, and I even had trouble sleeping. I think the birthday party feels more urgent because it's coming up this weekend, and the checking thing at school can wait a little longer.

A six is definitely higher than where we ended last time, and I can understand why the party kept you up; it sounds like your brain is holding onto that fear tightly. Since the party is looming this weekend and you mentioned it feels more pressing, let's put that at the top of our agenda today to break through those worries early. Shall we spend most of our time unpacking that party scenario, or would you prefer to spend a few minutes on the school distractions first?
I'd rather focus on the party, I guess. Even just thinking about it makes my stomach feel all twisty. My mom keeps asking if I'm excited, and I have to pretend I am, but really I'm just dreading it.

That contradiction between wanting to please your mom while internally dreading the event creates a lot of tension, and it makes total sense that your stomach would react physically to that mismatch. When you feel forced to pretend excitement, does your body tend to hold its breath or tighten up further as soon as she asks if you're ready?

Yeah, exactly. I feel like I can't breathe right for a second, and my shoulders go all stiff. Then I force a smile and say "yeah, totally," but inside I'm just counting down until she stops asking questions.

That physical tightening and the need to "force" a smile show how much effort your body is putting in to hide the discomfort, which often makes the anxiety spiral faster. It sounds like when you finally say yes, you're shifting from hiding the fear to actively suppressing it, which drains your energy reserves. Before we dive deeper into the party specifics, does adding a quick grounding exercise—like naming three things you can see in the room—to calm those shoulders down seem like something useful for when your mom asks, or would you prefer to save that for later?
I think I'd like to try it now, actually. My shoulders are feeling pretty tight just talking about it. Um... I can see the blue chair over there, the lamp on your desk, and my own shoes.

That's a fantastic use of your senses right now, and successfully identifying three objects gives your brain a clear signal that you are safe in this space. It breaks the cycle of worry by forcing your attention outward into reality rather than inward toward your fears. Now that your shoulders are likely a bit looser, let's turn back to the party itself. When your mom says "Are you excited?", what is the very first automatic thought that jumps into your head immediately after you answer? Is it something like, "She'll realize I'm lying," or perhaps, "Everyone will notice I'm fake"?
It's more like, "They're all going to think I'm weird if I try to tell a joke and mess it up." And then I start picturing everyone's faces looking at me, and I feel like I want to disappear.

That image of disappearing is terrifying, and it explains perfectly why your body reacts with that sudden urge to shrink away when you anticipate the spotlight. It seems like your brain is treating a potential mistake at a birthday party as a catastrophic personal failure, similar to the stranger incident from before. If you pictured that worst-case scenario playing out right now in front of you, what would be the single biggest piece of evidence that contradicts the idea that everyone would judge you harshly?

I guess... well, at the party, there will be kids I know from school, and they've heard me tell jokes before in class without anything bad happening. Like, just last week I made Sarah laugh during lunch without even meaning to. So maybe that counts as evidence that not everyone thinks I'm a total failure at being funny.

That is powerful evidence, Sarah, and it directly challenges the belief that everyone sees you as a failure. Remembering that you successfully made Sarah laugh proves your brain is capable of generating humor, even accidentally, which means the disaster scenario is less likely than you imagined. Given that you have concrete examples of people enjoying your presence, does focusing on those memories reduce the intensity of that "disappearing" sensation in your chest?

A little bit, yeah. It kind of makes the feeling in my chest go from a tight knot to more of a flutter, if that makes sense. Like, maybe I'm not completely hopeless, but I still don't think I could tell a joke at the party on purpose.

That shift from a tight knot to a flutter is a huge sign of hope, showing that your body is starting to relax even though the thought process hasn't changed yet. It sounds like you've moved from believing you *can't* do it to admitting you're afraid you *might*, which is a critical step forward. Since you mentioned you wouldn't tell a joke on purpose, let's adjust our plan slightly. Instead of preparing a speech, what if we practiced a "safe exit" phrase you could use if someone suddenly asks for one? Something simple like, "Well, that was fun, but I'm saving my best ones for later!" Would trying to say that out loud help lower the stakes?

I think I could say that. It doesn't feel as scary because it's not really a joke, just a way to get out of the situation. I'll try it... "Well, that was fun, but I'm saving my best ones for later." Huh, that actually didn't make my stomach hurt to say.

That is incredible news, Sarah. Saying that line without your stomach hurting proves that you don't actually need to perform perfectly to pass a social interaction. You've discovered a "soft landing" that lets you stay connected without risking humiliation. Now that we have a safe phrase ready, let's add one final layer of protection. If that phrase feels risky, what if we paired it with a quick, deliberate exhale right before speaking? Would taking one long breath out before saying, "That was fun, but I'm saving my best ones for later," give you a tiny buffer zone to compose yourself?
I think that would help, yeah. Taking a breath first sounds like it would give me a second to remember that I don't have to be perfect. Can we practice it together, maybe once or twice?

Absolutely, let's try that right now. Take a slow, deep breath in through your nose, hold it for just a second, and then exhale slowly through your mouth while saying, "Well, that was fun, but I'm saving my best ones for later." How does your body feel after you finish that sentence? Does that extra pause make it easier to deliver without panicking?

*Takes a deep breath and exhales slowly* "Well, that was fun, but I'm saving my best ones for later." That actually felt... okay. My shoulders didn't go up, and my heart didn't race like it usually does. I think the breath really helped me feel more in control.

That is amazing feedback, Sarah. The fact that your shoulders stayed relaxed and your heart didn't race proves that combining the breath with that phrase creates a powerful safety net for you. It shifts the dynamic from "performing under pressure" to "speaking calmly and intentionally." Now that we've practiced this combination in a safe environment, let's lock in your concrete plan for tonight. Would you be willing to write down these exact steps—"one slow exhale followed by the phrase"—on a sticky note or your phone screen so you can glance at it before leaving tonight?
Yeah, I'll write it down on my phone right now. I can put it as a note on my lock screen so I see it before I go in. That way I won't forget the steps when I'm nervous.

That is a brilliant solution, Sarah. Having the reminder right on your lock screen turns an abstract idea into a tangible tool you can access in seconds when panic hits. It acts like a mental GPS for your nervous system, keeping you grounded exactly when you need it most. Before we finalize everything, I want to make sure we are aligned on the full picture. Does carrying this written plan plus practicing the breathing tonight feel like enough preparation to give you the confidence to show up at the party tomorrow? Or is there still a part of you that feels unsure about executing it live?

I think I'm a little nervous still, but not as much as before. The breathing and the phrase feel like something I can actually do, not just pretend. I think I'm ready to try it, at least for a little while at the party.

That is such a brave place to stand, acknowledging that you aren't quite there yet but willing to take that step anyway. Remember, the goal isn't to eliminate all nervousness tonight—it's just to use these tools whenever you feel that familiar tightness creeping in. 

Before we officially close, could you share one thing that felt most useful in this session? Was it discovering that safe phrase, learning the breathing trick, or just knowing we have a plan together? And is there anything else you'd like to adjust or clarify before you head home?

I think the most useful part was practicing the breathing and the phrase together. It made me feel like I actually have a way to handle it, instead of just panicking and running away. I think I'm good for now—I have my lock screen note and I know what to do. Thanks for helping me figure this out.

You are absolutely welcome, Sarah. It sounds like you found a solid anchor tonight, and knowing you have a concrete plan to fall back on will make a world of difference tomorrow. Please remember that sending me a quick message if the nerves spike mid-party isn't a failure—it's just gathering important data to tweak our strategy if needed. Take a deep breath, trust the steps we built together, and I'll be here anytime you need to debrief afterward. Safe travels!

Hello again, and thank you for coming in today. To start, on a scale of zero to ten, how are you feeling right now compared to where you were when we last spoke? Before we dive deeper, I’d like to quickly outline our goals for this session: we’ll check in on your mood, review how that five-minute search went last night, and then figure out our next tiny step together. Does that agenda sound fair, or is there anything else you’d like to add?
Well, I guess I'm at about a 4 or 5 right now. That's maybe a little better than last time, but not by much. That agenda sounds fine—I don't have anything else to add.

A rating of four or five tells me you're holding space for some tension while also carrying a glimmer of hope, which is a great place to stand. Since we agreed on checking in on your mood, reviewing your homework, and planning the next step, I’m glad we’re aligned on those three priorities. Now, would you mind sharing a little about how that five-minute search went last night—did you manage to find that one paragraph, or did the panic come in sooner than expected?

I actually did manage to open my laptop and start looking at some community college websites. But after about two minutes, my mind just went blank and I started thinking, "What's even the point? I'll never save enough in time anyway." So I closed the laptop and just sat there feeling stupid.

That feeling of sudden emptiness after opening the laptop suggests your brain is rushing to find a reason why the effort wouldn't matter, even though you told yourself it was just about gathering data. When that voice says, "What's the point?", it usually means the underlying fear—that nothing will ever change—is still loud underneath the surface. Could you tell me a little more about what happened right after you closed the lid? Did you feel a surge of shame, or did you just feel completely defeated and tired?

Mostly defeated and tired, to be honest. I just sat on my bed staring at the wall for a while, thinking about how long it's going to take me to rebuild that savings. It felt like every dollar I lost is a month longer I'll have to wait to go back to school, and at this rate, I'll be too old to even finish my degree.

That connection between the missed dollars and the looming timeline of finishing your degree reveals just how deeply tied your anxiety is to the fear of being "too late." It sounds like your mind is running a simulation where the cost of failure accumulates faster than your ability to recover, leading to that heavy feeling of defeat. When you described sitting there staring at the wall, did you notice any physical sensations accompanying that sense of being trapped, like tightness in your chest or a heaviness in your limbs?

Yeah, my chest felt really tight, like there was a weight pressing down on it. And my shoulders were all knotted up too—I didn't even realize how tense I was until I tried to move. It's like my whole body was bracing for something bad that hadn't even happened yet.

That physical tightness is your body screaming that it's unsafe to engage, even though logically you know you only need five minutes. When we feel that heavy weight in our chest, it often blocks us from accessing the calm part of our brain that knows how to solve problems. Would you be willing to try a small reset right now—maybe taking three deep breaths while saying silently, "I am allowed to just exist for these five minutes," before we decide if we should push forward tonight?
I guess I can try that. It sounds a little silly, but I'll give it a shot. *takes a few deep breaths* Okay, I did it. My chest still feels a bit tight, but maybe a little less than before.

That slight reduction in tightness is a small victory, showing that even a simple grounding exercise can lower the intensity of the alarm bell ringing inside you. Let's use that momentum to revisit our plan for tonight. Remember, the goal isn't to solve the debt problem right now, but to prove to yourself that you can sit with uncertainty for five minutes without collapsing. Would you be okay with agreeing to try that same "data collection" approach tonight—one website, one paragraph, and then stopping—even if the panic tries to pull you away?

Yeah, I think I can agree to that. One website, one paragraph, and then I'm done. No pushing myself to look at more, no trying to calculate how long it'll take me to save up again. Just... one small thing.

That clarity is huge because it removes the pressure to perform perfectly or find a magic solution. By limiting it to just one website and one paragraph, you've turned an overwhelming mountain into a single pebble you can pick up. Before we lock this in, does the idea of stopping immediately after reading that one block of text feel safer to you than continuing until you run out of time?

Yes, that actually does feel safer. Knowing I can just stop after one paragraph feels like I have control over it, instead of the panic controlling me. It's like I'm giving myself permission to do the bare minimum without feeling guilty about it.

That permission to stop after the "bare minimum" is a powerful way to reclaim control from the panic attack that tries to drag you further. It turns the activity into a deliberate choice rather than a race against time. With that boundary set, does tonight's plan feel like something you can realistically commit to, or is there a hidden doubt about whether you'll actually show up?

I think I can commit to it. There's still a little voice in my head saying "what if you fail again," but I also know I managed to open the laptop last night, even if I didn't finish. So maybe I can do that again tonight and actually read that one paragraph this time.

That recognition is crucial—you already proved you can initiate the behavior, which breaks the cycle of avoidance. Carrying that "little voice" about failing alongside the knowledge that you've started means you have both the intention and the momentum to try again tonight. Before we wrap up, does agreeing to this revised plan—with the strict limit of one paragraph and immediate permission to stop—feel like a manageable compromise for you?
Yes, it does. It feels like something I can actually do without dreading it all day. I think having that clear limit takes away the pressure, and I'm willing to try again tonight.

That relief you feel comes from realizing you aren't responsible for fixing everything in that five minutes; you're only responsible for showing up and doing the tiny bit. Since we've locked in that one-paragraph rule and the "permission to stop," does it feel like we have a solid plan for tonight, or is there another worry popping up?

No, I think we've got a solid plan. I actually feel a little lighter about it, which is surprising. I'll try not to overthink it between now and tonight—just do what we talked about and stop when I've read that one paragraph.

That sense of lightness is a wonderful sign that your brain is finally accepting this smaller, safer version of the task. Remember, tonight isn't about changing your finances or proving you're smart; it's simply about sitting with the computer screen for five minutes and refusing to let the panic dictate how long you stay. Is there anything else you'd like to talk about before we close our session?
No, I think I'm good for now. Thank you for helping me break this down into something that doesn't feel impossible. I'll let you know how it goes next time.

You are very welcome, and I truly appreciate you trusting me with this difficult journey. Please remember that tonight isn't about solving everything; it's simply about proving to yourself that you can gather information without letting fear take over. Take care of yourself as you head home, and I look forward to hearing how your five minutes went next time. Have a safe trip!

Hello, I am so glad we are meeting again today. To kick us off, could you quickly share how you've been feeling emotionally since our last session, and is there anything specific that stood out to you? Additionally, do you still feel comfortable sticking with our original plan to look at those social events, or would you like to adjust the agenda for now?

Hi, thanks for asking. Honestly, I've been feeling pretty anxious this week. The thought of adopting the dog keeps coming up, and every time it does, I just feel this heavy sense of doubt. I think sticking with our plan is fine—I don't really have anything else to bring up.

That persistent heaviness suggests your old patterns are still strong, but it also means you’re ready to face them again. Before we begin, could you recall the exact steps we agreed upon last time: focusing on three neutral observations about your behavior while using the hay-smelling grounding technique? How does remembering that plan make you feel right now?

I remember—those three observations were supposed to be just simple, factual things I notice myself doing, like how I hold my bow or the way I breathe before a performance. And I was supposed to pair that with that calming scent exercise. Honestly, remembering it makes me feel a little silly, like I'm just trying to trick myself into feeling better. But I also know that's probably the point.

That honest admission—that you feel like you're "tricking" yourself—is actually a huge step forward, because it means you're catching the very resistance that often blocks progress. It shows you understand that forcing a new feeling doesn't always work immediately, so let's tweak our plan slightly. Instead of aiming for three observations tonight, how about we settle for finding just *one* clear, undeniable fact about your kindness today, paired with that grounding scent? Does that lower the pressure enough to make it feel achievable?

Yeah, I think that does lower the pressure a bit. One fact sounds a lot less overwhelming than three. I guess I could start with something small, like how I held the door open for a stranger today without even thinking about it. That seems simple enough to pair with the grounding exercise.

That is a wonderful choice because holding a door open is such a pure, unconscious act of kindness—it proves you cared without even intending to impress anyone. Pairing that simple fact with the hay-scent grounding gives you two anchors to hold onto when the doubt tries to creep in. Before we wrap up, could you tell me if you feel confident enough to try this tonight, knowing that even if you forget one part, the other will still keep you safe? And after you share your result tomorrow, would you like to spend five minutes exploring another common worry you might have before your next appointment?

I think I can try it tonight. Even if I mess up the grounding part, I still have that one fact to hold onto—that I did something kind without even thinking about it. And yes, I'd like to explore another worry next time. There's this thought that keeps creeping in about how the dog might not even want to bond with me, and that scares me more than I'd like to admit.

That fear of a non-reciprocal bond is a deep wound, and it makes total sense why it feels heavier than just performing tasks correctly. Before we leave tonight, could you share how your heart rate feels right now compared to when you walked into that shelter last time? And based on what we've talked about, do you feel like you have enough tools to ride out whatever comes up tonight?

My heart rate right now feels a lot steadier than when I walked into the shelter last time. Back then, my chest felt tight and my hands were clammy, but now it's more like a quiet hum of nervousness instead of panic. I think I have enough tools—the one fact and the grounding scent. It doesn't feel like a complete fix, but it feels like I have something to hold onto, and that's more than I had before.

That shift from "panic" to a "quiet hum of nervousness" tells me your body is finally learning to tolerate that slight tension without flooding with fear. Having a tangible anchor like the scent and a factual memory to rely on is a massive advantage over walking in blind. Before we close, could you confirm that you feel safe enough to commit to sending me just one word tomorrow morning, regardless of how the night plays out? And knowing we have a plan for tonight, does that give you permission to rest easy until then?

One word tomorrow morning—I can do that. It takes the pressure off having to explain everything in detail. And yes, knowing there's a plan and that I have something to fall back on does give me permission to let go a little and just rest. Thank you for that.

That sense of permission to rest is exactly what healing looks like—it's not about fighting every wave, but learning to float when the water gets rough. Please carry that lightness with you tonight, trusting that even if the doubts return, you have the scent and that one kind deed to remind you who you are. I'll be waiting for your single-word update tomorrow, and until then, please treat yourself with the same gentleness you offered to the stranger whose door you opened.

Thank you. That really means a lot to me. I'll try to hold onto that image of floating instead of fighting tonight. I'll send that word tomorrow morning, and I think I'll actually sleep a little better knowing I have that plan.

Hearing that you plan to sleep better is wonderful news, and it proves how effective a small, supportive plan can be on your rest. Please remember that tomorrow's message is just a gentle check-in, not a performance review—you simply need to send one word, no matter how messy the night was. I am so proud of you for taking this brave step toward trusting yourself again. Take care of yourself tonight, and I'll be here whenever you're ready to share that single word in the morning.

Hello, and welcome back. To start, could you quickly rate your distress on a scale of zero to ten based on how you've felt this past week? Also, looking at our previous plan to reach out to Sarah and explore why you feel like a "bad person," is there anything urgent you'd like to add to our agenda today?

Uh, I'd say my distress is maybe a 7 or 8 this week. It's been a rough few days. And no, nothing urgent really - I just keep having those same feelings every time my partner brings up marriage, and it's getting harder to brush off.

A score of seven or eight tells me you've been carrying a significant amount of heaviness, especially with those recurring thoughts popping up again. Since you mentioned the feelings are becoming harder to ignore, shall we spend most of our time diving into that specific pattern of thinking, or would you prefer to tackle the upcoming text to Sarah first to get some momentum?

I think maybe we should talk about the thinking pattern first. That feels more important right now because it's what's really eating at me inside. I just can't seem to shake the feeling that I'm letting everyone down by not being ready.

It makes complete sense that the internal voice telling you you're letting everyone down feels heavier than texting Sarah right now; when you carry that weight, even simple connections become difficult. Let's unpack that feeling of letting people down together. Can you describe the situation where you noticed this thought popping up strongest recently? Who was involved, and what exactly happened in that moment?

It was last night, actually. My partner and I were just having dinner, and they casually mentioned that their coworker just got engaged. And immediately, my stomach just dropped. They didn't even say anything about us getting married, but I just felt this wave of guilt wash over me, like I knew what was coming next. I went quiet and started picking at my food, and they asked what was wrong, but I couldn't even look at them.

That sudden drop in your stomach and the silence you created is a classic physical manifestation of that old fear waking up—the fear that you're falling behind or failing everyone around you. When you picked at your food and turned away, was it to hide your face, or did you feel like you needed to disappear entirely to protect them from seeing how bad you felt?

I think I just wanted to disappear, honestly. It's like if I could make myself small enough or invisible enough, then they wouldn't have to deal with my issues. I felt like I was disappointing them just by being there and not being ready to talk about marriage. Like my existence in that moment was somehow wrong.

That desire to shrink yourself so invisibly that nobody notices your pain is heartbreaking, and it shows how deeply you believe your presence itself is a burden to them. When you feel that your mere existence during that conversation was "wrong," it suggests you've internalized the idea that you are fundamentally incompatible with love—or perhaps with the version of yourself your partner expects. Before we dig into *why* that belief formed so strongly, I want to check in: Does describing that moment of wanting to vanish make you feel a little less alone in that experience, or does it bring up fresh layers of shame?

It actually feels... better, I think? Like, hearing you say it back makes me realize I'm not crazy for feeling that way. But then there's also this little voice in my head saying I shouldn't be relieved, because feeling like that just proves something is wrong with me. So I guess it's both - a little less alone, but also more shame for even having those feelings.

That duality—finding temporary relief in being heard while simultaneously shaming yourself for having relief—is a classic trap of self-sabotage. It shows how deeply ingrained the rule is that your feelings must always prove you are "okay," even when acknowledging them hurts. Let's test that rule for a second. If we assumed for five minutes that your sadness and guilt weren't proof of something being "wrong" with you, but simply evidence that you care deeply about your partner's happiness, would that shift the meaning of wanting to disappear? What does that assumption suggest about what you're actually afraid of losing?

I... wow. I never thought of it like that. If I really think about it, I guess I'm not afraid of marriage itself. I'm afraid of losing who I am, or losing the way things are now. And I'm terrified that if I say I'm not ready, my partner will think I don't love them enough. So the guilt comes from feeling like I'm choosing myself over them, and that feels selfish.

That distinction between fearing the event itself versus fearing the loss of your identity is a breakthrough moment. It reveals that your core fear isn't actually about marriage, but about surviving the potential rejection of the "perfect version" of yourself. When you frame it as choosing yourself over them, does that feeling of selfishness feel like a protective shield keeping you safe, or does it feel like a betrayal that weighs heavier than the truth?

It feels like both, honestly. Like, part of me knows I need to protect myself and my feelings, but the other part just keeps hammering home that I'm being selfish and letting them down. It's like there's this constant tug-of-war in my head, and no matter which side wins, I end up feeling guilty. I just wish I knew which feeling was the real one, you know?

That tug-of-war is exhausting, and wishing you could identify the "real" feeling highlights how much energy you spend trying to solve a puzzle that doesn't have a single correct answer. Often, the "selfish" feeling is actually your survival mechanism kicking in to protect you from the anticipated pain of rejection. Let's try a quick experiment: Imagine your partner says, "I love you exactly as you are, flaws and all, including the ones that make you hesitant." How would that statement change the equation in your head, and would it make the "selfish" thought feel less accurate?

If they said that... I think I'd actually cry, honestly. It would feel like this huge weight just lifted off my chest. Because deep down, I think I'm terrified they only love the version of me that's ready for everything, not the real me that's scared and uncertain. If they accepted that part too, then maybe I wouldn't feel so guilty for not being perfect. Maybe then the "selfish" thought would just feel like... like I'm just taking care of myself, not hurting anyone.

That image of the weight lifting is so powerful, and it shows that the core issue isn't whether you're ready for marriage, but whether you believe your partner loves the whole package—including the scared, unsure parts. If accepting that "whole package" meant the guilt vanished, it proves your anxiety is rooted in perfectionism, not a lack of love. Before we solidify this new perspective, I want to make sure you understand the strategy we're using: We call this "cognitive restructuring," which means intentionally swapping out a negative automatic thought ("I'm selfish") for a balanced alternative ("I'm protecting my ability to love you long-term"). Does naming this process help clarify why we're doing it, or would you prefer we skip the technical term and just stick to practicing that new mindset?

No, I think it's good to know the name for it. It makes it feel more... real, I guess? Like there's actually a method to this, not just us talking in circles. I think I want to keep practicing that new mindset, because the old one hasn't been working for me at all.

Knowing there's a named method to it does give it a sense of reliability, and recognizing that the old way isn't working is a huge clue that it's time to switch tactics. Since you're ready to keep practicing this new mindset, let's lock in a concrete plan for tonight. Will you try sending that text to Sarah tonight using the wording we drafted earlier, and if you notice that familiar "selfish" thought creeping back in, will you pause and silently remind yourself, "I'm protecting my future, not hurting mine"?

Yeah, I think I can do that. I'll text Sarah tonight and if that voice pops up, I'll tell myself that reminder. It feels a little scary, but I'm tired of feeling trapped by this guilt all the time. I want to try something different for once.

That determination to break free from the loop is incredibly brave, and choosing to act despite the fear is a hallmark of real growth. Before you draft that final message, I want to make sure you feel confident in the wording one last time. Does reading "Hey, I've been dealing with some stuff lately and it's been heavy. Would you be up for talking sometime this week? No pressure if you're busy." feel authentic to you, or is there any part of it that still feels too risky to send?
No, that actually feels really genuine. It's honest without being too intense, and it gives her an out if she's busy. I think that's exactly what I need to say. I'll send it after our session ends.

That honesty combined with giving her space is a perfect balance, and sending it soon after we finish will help you carry this new confidence into the evening. Just remember, the goal isn't for her to fix everything instantly, but simply to open a door so you can breathe a little easier tomorrow morning. Is there anything else you'd like to adjust about tonight's plan before we wrap up?
No, I think I'm good. I feel a little lighter than when I walked in, which is nice. I'll text Sarah and practice that new way of thinking. Thank you for helping me see things differently.

Your feeling of lightness is a powerful indicator that this new perspective is starting to take root, and I am so glad to hear you chose to embrace it. Please remember that tonight's actions—even small ones like sending a text—are proof of your courage, not just a checklist item. As you head home, take a deep breath and remind yourself that you deserve to exist exactly as you are, messy and all. I will be here anytime you return, ready to support you further. Until then, be gentle with yourself as you navigate the evening.

Hello again, thank you for meeting with me today. First, I want to briefly summarize where we left off: we worked on creating a "pause protocol" involving deep breathing and a mental reminder to treat financial numbers as mere data points, and we agreed to start logging your chest tightness levels whenever you receive an accounting update.

Before we dive deeper, could you share what has happened with that plan since we spoke? Did you manage to use the breathing technique when the email arrived, and did noticing the drop in your chest tightness afterward provide any relief or confirmation that the method works?

Yeah, I did try the breathing thing last Tuesday when the weekly sales report came in. I took those three deep breaths before opening the email, and I guess my chest didn't tighten up as bad as usual—maybe a 6 out of 10 instead of the usual 9. It felt a little silly at first, but I'll admit it helped me not spiral into full panic mode right away. I still felt pretty down seeing the numbers, though.

That is fantastic progress, especially considering you admitted it felt a bit silly at first. Reducing that initial spike from a nine to a six proves the "pause protocol" is building momentum, even if the underlying sadness remains. Since we achieved that small win, let's use it as fuel to tackle the next hurdle: translating that calm into actual business improvements. Earlier, we brainstormed a list of three small, controllable actions to boost morale independently of the sales figures. Have you gotten around to writing those down yet, or do you need help generating some options?

I wrote down a couple ideas, but honestly I'm not sure if they're even worth trying. One was to rearrange the menu board to feature our best-selling smoothies more prominently, and the other was to have the staff sample out a new recipe during the afternoon lull. But then I started thinking, what if nobody even notices the menu change and people just walk past the samples? It feels like no matter what I do, the result will be the same.

It sounds like you are experiencing the very distortion we talked about—that expectation of failure regardless of your effort. Let's run a quick reality check on that thought: Have you tried rearranging the menu board recently, or is that still purely hypothetical? Similarly, has anyone actually sampled the new recipe yet, or is that waiting for a perfect outcome? Can you describe a specific instance where you made a visible change and someone noticed it, even if the impact wasn't massive?

Well, I did change the specials board last month to highlight our green detox blend, and a few regulars actually commented that they liked seeing it up front. Sales on that drink went up maybe 8% for two weeks, which wasn't huge, but it wasn't nothing either. I guess I just keep thinking that if it's not a massive improvement, it doesn't really count for anything.

That eight percent increase is solid proof that small adjustments *do* work, even if they aren't dramatic explosions of success. Your brain is likely filtering out that victory because it fits the pattern of "failure," but the data contradicts that story. Let's look closer at your hesitation right now: You mentioned wondering if people won't notice the menu change or the new samples. Based on last month's experience, isn't it possible that even subtle shifts attract attention and lead to incremental gains? What would happen if you treated these small tweaks as experiments rather than bets on a guaranteed result?

I guess I never really thought of them as experiments before. I always saw them as make-or-break moves, like if it doesn't work I've just wasted time and money. But when you put it that way, even the menu board thing was just a test that happened to work out okay. I suppose I could try the sample idea this weekend and just see what happens, without expecting it to suddenly fix everything.

That shift in perspective—from viewing changes as life-or-death judgments to treating them as harmless experiments—is exactly the kind of cognitive flexibility we aim to build. By framing the new recipe trial as a low-stakes experiment, you remove the pressure of needing immediate perfection. 

Does viewing it as a "test" rather than a "solution" make the idea of sampling that new drink feel slightly less daunting for you to try this weekend?

It does, actually. It takes some of that weight off my shoulders. I guess I can afford to try it out and just see what happens, even if it flops. And if nobody takes a sample, at least I'll know for next time, right?

That is a brilliant realization—you've essentially created a safety valve for yourself by accepting that a "flop" provides valuable intelligence for the future. This mindset transforms potential failure into a necessary learning step. Before we lock this in, I want to make sure you feel completely confident about this approach. Does viewing the weekend trial strictly as a data-gathering mission feel safe to you, or is there any lingering doubt about whether you'd be able to execute it calmly?

There's still a little voice in my head telling me that if it doesn't work, it's just proof I'm not cut out for this business. But I think I can talk back to that voice now—tell it that even a failed sample run is just information, not a verdict on my whole life. I'll try it this Saturday afternoon and just see how many people take a sample and what they say.

That is a powerful internal dialogue you just constructed, effectively separating the outcome of the experiment from your identity as a business owner. Talking back to that critical voice by labeling it merely "information" rather than a "verdict" is a key step in gaining agency over your thoughts.

To make sure this plan sticks, would you be open to setting a gentle reminder on your calendar for Saturday afternoon so the idea pops into view before you settle into the old habit of waiting? Also, if you decide to bring a friend along to watch the results unfold, would that add any extra support, or would you prefer to observe quietly on your own?

I think I'll keep it simple and just do it myself—watching with a friend feels like it would add pressure, like I have to perform. But I like the calendar reminder idea. I'll set one for Saturday at noon so I remember to prep the samples before the afternoon rush. Thanks, that actually feels manageable.

Setting a specific time for preparation is a great way to anchor the experiment in your routine, turning a vague idea into a concrete appointment with yourself. Please go ahead and schedule that reminder for Saturday at noon.

Now that we've finalized this weekend trial, let's quickly review our entire toolkit for the week. We have the breathing "pause" for stressful emails, the logging of your physical reactions to track progress, and this new experimental mindset for the sample tasting. Does having all three components ready make you feel more prepared to face whatever challenges come your way this week?

I think so, yeah. Having those three things lined up makes it feel like I've got a little toolbox instead of just panicking. The breathing thing already helped once, and I'm curious to see if the sample experiment changes anything, even just how I feel about my own decisions. I'll check in with you next week and let you know how it all went.

That metaphor of having a "toolbox" is wonderful because it shifts your identity from someone who is constantly reacting to panic to someone who actively equips themselves to handle challenges. It validates that you are capable of self-reliance and resourcefulness.

Before we finish, I want to leave you with one final piece of encouragement: Remember that this week isn't about fixing everything perfectly; it's about practicing the art of showing up, breathing through the discomfort, and gathering honest data—even if that data says "not yet." How does knowing you have this flexible plan make you feel about walking out the door tonight? Is there anything else weighing on your mind as you head home?

Honestly, it feels lighter than usual, like I've got a little more room to breathe. I still feel that knot in my stomach about the business, but it's not squeezing as tight. I think I'm just going to go home, maybe watch a movie, and not look at any spreadsheets until Saturday. Thanks for helping me get to this place today.

That sense of lightness is exactly the goal we aimed for—to create space between the anxiety and your actions so you can choose how to respond. Taking that promise to avoid spreadsheets tonight is a wise boundary, and watching a movie can be a perfect distraction to let your nervous system reset.

Is there anything specific about the plan we built today that you want to double-check before you go, or shall we close here knowing you have your tools ready for the week?

Hello again, and I am so glad to see you. On a scale of zero to ten, where zero means completely calm and ten means overwhelmed, how would you rate your anxiety level today? Also, looking back at our last meeting where we explored that badge trigger and created a simple mantra, how satisfied do you feel that our plan is working for you so far?

Once we touch on that, could you tell me which topics you'd like to prioritize for our time together? Should we dive deeper into refining that mantra, explore other ways to handle moments of doubt, or perhaps talk about something else that has been weighing on you lately?

Hi. I'd say my anxiety is around a 6 or 7 today. It's been a busy shift, and the thoughts crept in more than I'd like.

As for the mantra... I've been using it, but honestly, it feels a bit hollow sometimes. Like I'm just repeating words without really believing them. I guess I'd like to work on that, or maybe talk about why I can't seem to shake this feeling that I'm not enough.

A six or seven confirms that the busy shift pushed your anxiety levels higher than usual, and I want to validate that feeling of the mantra becoming hollow—it happens when our minds start resisting the repetition because the underlying belief hasn't shifted yet. Since you mentioned wanting to dig into *why* you feel like you aren't enough, shall we spend our time unpacking that deeper narrative, or would you prefer to try adjusting the mantra itself to make it feel less robotic?

I think I'd rather dig into the "why." The mantra feels like a band-aid right now, and I want to get at what's underneath it. If I can understand why I feel this way, maybe the words will start to feel more real.

It's just... hard to even put into words sometimes. I look at my colleagues with their own practices, and it feels like they've unlocked something I never will. Like there's a fundamental gap between us.

That feeling of a "fundamental gap" suggests your brain is interpreting the visual difference between your coats as a literal barrier to entry, making the logo feel like a gatekeeper rather than just a symbol. To help narrow that down, when you imagine that invisible wall separating you from them, what is the very first word or image that pops into your head describing your relationship to the team? Is it something like "observer," "waiting room," or maybe "visitor"?
"Visitor." That's the word. Like I'm just passing through, not really belonging there. Like at any moment someone's going to tap me on the shoulder and say, "Sorry, you're not meant to be here."

That image of being a temporary visitor who fears rejection at any moment reveals how deeply ingrained the belief is that you are fundamentally unwelcome in your own life. When you hold onto the idea that you are merely "passing through," it removes the possibility of long-term ownership or stability, leaving you perpetually on guard. Let's test that story together: if you imagined a scenario where a senior colleague intentionally told you, "Sarah, you're not supposed to be here," would that actually happen, or is your brain predicting a threat that rarely occurs?

I mean... no, it's never actually happened. No one has ever told me I don't belong. But that almost makes it worse, in a way. Like I'm waiting for the other shoe to drop, and the waiting itself is exhausting. 

I guess I just assume people think it, even if they don't say it. Like they're being polite, but secretly they see the gap I see.

That assumption—that everyone is silently judging you while you wait for confirmation—is a classic example of "mind reading," where your brain fills in the silence with a negative verdict. It's exhausting because it forces you to live in constant anticipation of rejection, even when there is none. To challenge this, let's look at a recent instance where you walked past a coworker with their logo; did anyone stop you, frown, or say anything that suggested they thought you were an imposter? Or did they just continue their normal routine?

No, they just kept doing their thing. Most of them just nodded or said hi like usual. I think one of them even asked me for a consultation on a patient's lab results, which I handled fine. But my brain just zeroed in on the one person who didn't say anything, you know? And I assumed that silence meant something negative.

That silence absolutely feeds the lie that you are invisible or unwanted, turning a neutral pause into a personal attack in your mind. It seems like your brain treats quietness as an active dismissal, even when it's just background noise. Before we try to dismantle this assumption, does looking at that one silent interaction confirm the feeling that everyone is judging you, or does it remind you that silence is often just neutrality?

It reminds me that silence is probably just... silence. I mean, I know logically that not everyone is thinking about me all the time. But in the moment, it feels like they are. Like if I'm not actively being validated, I must be failing. 

I guess that's the part I need help with—the moment-to-moment panic that sets in when I don't get immediate reassurance.

That panic about needing instant validation is incredibly understandable, especially when your safety feels tied to constant approval. It seems like your brain interprets the absence of praise as proof of failure, creating a cycle where you constantly scan for signs of rejection. To break this loop, could we try a small experiment tonight? Instead of waiting for someone to nod or speak to confirm you belong, could you simply observe five coworkers interacting normally without checking their faces for judgment? Does watching them connect with others feel safer when you remove the expectation that they will notice or approve of you?

I think I could try that. Just watch them without waiting for them to look at me. It sounds simple, but I know my instinct will be to scan for any hint of disapproval. 

Maybe if I just focus on what they're actually doing—talking, laughing, working—instead of what they might be thinking about me, it'll feel less personal. I can give it a shot tonight before my shift ends.

That is a brilliant observation, Sarah; shifting your focus from their internal thoughts ("What do they think of me?") to their external actions ("They are talking/laughing") effectively breaks the cycle of mind-reading. By anchoring yourself in observable reality, you create a buffer zone that prevents your brain from inventing worst-case scenarios during those quiet moments.

Before you head out tonight, I want to make sure we lock in exactly how you will do this. Would you be willing to pick one specific area near the nurses' station where you can stand safely and watch three colleagues interact for two minutes, completely ignoring your phone or any urge to join in? And later, when you return, we can debrief whether noticing their laughter helped ground you or if your eye twitched toward the exit anyway.

Yeah, I can do that. I'll stand near the supply closet just off the nurses' station. That way I'm not in the middle of things, but I can still see a few of them talking. I'll set a timer on my watch for two minutes and just... watch. No checking my phone, no trying to catch anyone's eye.

I think I'll make a mental note of what I see—like who's laughing, who's just focused on their screen. I'll try to stick with just the facts. I'll let you know how it goes.

That is a perfect plan, and I appreciate your commitment to sticking to the facts without adding interpretation. Setting a timer and choosing a specific spot like the supply closet gives you a clear boundary to stay within, which helps reduce the pressure to perform socially.

Just before you go, I want to check one final piece of the puzzle: when you find yourself tempted to glance at someone's face to read their expression, can you consciously decide to bring your gaze back to their hands or the object they are holding instead? Does bringing your attention to a neutral object feel slightly less intrusive than staring at a person?

Yeah, I think focusing on a neutral object would feel a lot less invasive. If I catch myself starting to look at someone's expression, I'll shift my gaze to their coffee mug or the chart they're holding. Something that's just... there, without any hidden meaning.

Thanks for that tip. It feels like a small, concrete thing I can actually do in the moment. I'll report back after my shift.

That is a great addition, Sarah; grounding your eyes on a neutral object like a mug acts as an anchor, pulling you out of the "story" your brain is spinning and back into the present moment. It's a simple but powerful way to interrupt the spiral before it takes hold.

Please remember that even if you miss the window for two minutes or accidentally glance at a face once, the act of noticing and correcting yourself is still a victory. How does that sound as a complete plan for tonight?

It sounds doable. Honestly, it sounds a lot less overwhelming than what I usually do, which is just try to push the thoughts away. Having a specific, small action to take—like looking at a coffee mug—gives me something to hold onto.

I think I'm ready to try it. I'll be back with my results, good or bad. Thanks for walking me through this.

That is a wonderful mindset, Sarah; accepting that "good or bad" results are both valid removes the pressure to perform perfectly during the exercise itself. Remember, the goal tonight isn't to eliminate the feeling of inadequacy forever, but simply to gather fresh data points that contradict the idea that silence always means rejection.

Take care until you see me next time, and trust that we will learn a lot from whatever you discover about those two minutes.

Hello, it is wonderful to see you again today. That sounds fair. I'd like to understand why my body reacts that way before I even say a word. And an easier version of the experiment might actually be less terrifying, so I'm willing to try that. What did you have in mind for the easier version?

Then, wait for her reply and observe her tone. Does sending just a small signal feel slightly safer than risking a full conversation?

Hmm... just an emoji and a friendly text? That does feel a lot safer, I'll give you that. It's not directly about the doll collecting, so if she reacts oddly, I could just tell myself she wasn't reacting to that. I think I could actually do that. What if she just replies with a generic "thanks" though—would that still count as a success?

A generic "thanks" would still serve as valuable data, because it lets you compare her neutral response to the one you expected versus the one you feared. We can define success not as getting a perfect reaction, but as noticing that she responded calmly instead of with laughter or silence. Once you try that simple text exchange, does it feel like a manageable step toward practicing your message?

Yeah, I suppose that makes sense. I always assume the worst, like she'll laugh or just ignore me entirely. So if she just says "thanks" or even a heart emoji back, that's already proof that my mind is overthinking things. I think I can manage sending that text tonight. It feels like a baby step, but at least it's a step.

That reframing of "success" as simply noticing calmness rather than receiving praise is a powerful shift, and taking that tiny step tonight proves you are already breaking the cycle. Before we close, I want to make sure you leave with clarity on exactly what to type and when. Shall I remind you of the specific message ("Thinking of you!") plus the emoji suggestion, and then we can wrap up with a quick check-in on how this session feels for you?

Yes, please. I need it spelled out so I don't second-guess myself later. So I'll send a flower or heart emoji, then "Thinking of you!" to Sarah sometime tonight. I'm nervous, but not as panicked as I usually get talking about this.

Remember, the goal tonight isn't perfection, but simply sending that message and letting her reply come in naturally. When you receive her response later, take a moment to just note her words without labeling them as "proof" of anything yet. How does knowing we have this clear checklist for tonight make you feel more prepared?

It makes me feel like I have a script to follow, which is comforting. Instead of all that messy uncertainty in my head, I have one clear action to take. I think I can do this. And if it goes okay, maybe next time we can try something a little bigger.

That commitment to moving forward, even with imperfect outcomes, speaks volumes about your courage. Having a clear script transforms the unknown into a predictable routine, which naturally lowers that initial spike of panic. Does having permission to wait until you feel ready add another layer of safety for tonight?

Hello, and thank you for joining us today. Last time we worked on building evidence to counteract your fear of losing your job, did you find that gathering facts helped calm you down before you had to act? Also, how is your energy level and anxiety rating comparing to where we left off last session, and what would be the most important priority for us to tackle first?

Uh, I'm sorry, but I think there might be some confusion. This is actually my first session with you. I came in because of something that happened today. My anxiety is through the roof right now, probably a 9 out of 10.

Thank you for clarifying that this is our very first meeting together; I understand it can feel overwhelming to start fresh while dealing with such intense worry. Your description of feeling like you’re facing homelessness shows just how severe your current distress is, and I want to validate that this is an incredibly frightening place to be. Given that you are currently in a state of high alarm, would you be open to spending the first few minutes of our time working on bringing your body down from that level of panic so we can talk more clearly?

Yeah, I think I'd be open to that. I've been pacing around my apartment all evening, and my heart's been racing since I got home. I can barely sit still, so anything that might help me calm down a bit sounds good right now.

That constant pacing and racing heart indicate your nervous system is still in "fight or flight" mode, which makes talking logically very difficult right now. Let's try a simple grounding exercise called "box breathing" to signal to your body that you are safe. We will breathe in slowly for four counts, hold for four, exhale for four, and hold empty for four, repeating this cycle five times together. Are you ready to begin?
Alright, I can give that a try. I'm ready when you are. Just tell me when to start breathing in.

On my mark, we begin. One, two, three, four—inhale deeply. Hold for four. Five, six, seven, eight—exhale slowly. Hold empty for four. Nine, ten, eleven, twelve—inhale again. Hold for four. Thirteen, fourteen, fifteen, sixteen—exhale. Hold empty for four. Seventeen, eighteen, nineteen, twenty—inhale once more. Hold for four. Twenty-one, twenty-two, twenty-three, twenty-four—exhale. Hold empty for four. Twenty-five, twenty-six, twenty-seven, twenty-eight—inhale. Hold for four. Twenty-nine, thirty, thirty-one, thirty-two—exhale. Hold empty for four. Thirty-three, thirty-four, thirty-five, thirty-six—inhale. Hold for four. Thirty-seven, thirty-eight, thirty-nine, forty—exhale. Hold empty for four. Forty-one, forty-two, forty-three, forty-four—inhale. Hold for four. Forty-five, forty-six, forty-seven, forty-eight—exhale. Hold empty for four. Forty-nine, fifty, fifty-one, fifty-two—inhale. Hold for four. Fifty-three, fifty-four,

*exhales slowly* Okay... that actually helped a little. My shoulders feel less tight, and I'm not gripping the armrest quite as hard. I still feel anxious, but maybe it's more like a 7 now instead of a 9. Thanks for walking me through that.

That drop from a nine to a seven is significant proof that your body responds quickly when given permission to relax. Since you've lowered that physical tension, we now have a clearer space to explore what triggered this panic so intensely. Could you tell me exactly what happened that one-minute delay led to this feeling of imminent homelessness?

Well, I was running late this morning because my alarm didn't go off. I got to my desk at 8:01 instead of 8:00. My supervisor just looked at me and said, "You're late, Owens." That was it. But in my head, I just spiraled. I thought, "That's it, they're going to document this, and after enough times they'll fire me, and I won't be able to pay my rent, and I'll end up on the street." It felt so real and immediate, like it was already happening.

That spiral connecting one minute of lateness to ending up homeless is a classic example of catastrophic thinking, where the brain jumps straight to the worst possible outcome. It makes total sense that your mind grabbed onto that single event and built a entire disaster movie around it instantly. When you feel like the end of the world is happening right now, everything else feels irrelevant until you break that chain of logic.

Given how intense this feels, does it seem useful to us to spend some time today separating the reality of the situation from that dramatic story your mind created, so we can figure out what actually stands between you and safety?

Yeah, I think that would be really helpful. Because right now, it all feels equally true to me - the being one minute late part and the being homeless part. They feel connected like a chain. I'd like to see if I can figure out which links in that chain are actually real and which ones I might be making up.

That distinction between what is factually true and what is imagined is exactly where we can find stability. Let's start by looking at the very first link in your chain: the statement that "they are documenting this." Based on what you told me about the interaction, is there actual evidence that your supervisor wrote anything down or entered anything into a system right now?

No, I don't actually know that he documented anything. He just said, "You're late, Owens," and then walked to his office. I didn't see him write anything down or type anything. I guess I just assumed he would, because that's what I'd expect to happen. But I don't actually have proof that he did.

That assumption—that he *must* have written it down because that's how things usually happen—is a common trap called "mind reading," where we fill in gaps with what we think should be true rather than what actually is. Since you don't have proof of documentation yet, can we treat that link as uncertain for now? Let's look at the next connection: the leap from "he hasn't documented it yet" to "after enough times they will definitely fire me." Is there any record of you getting fired recently for similar reasons, or is this entirely a prediction based on fear?

Well, I've never been fired from this job. I've been there for six years, and I've never even gotten a written warning about being late. I mean, I'm usually early, not late. So there's no record of me being in trouble for tardiness. I guess I'm just predicting that this one time will be the start of a pattern, even though there's no evidence I'll actually be late again.

That is a crucial piece of evidence, and recognizing that there is no history of punishment for you despite many opportunities to slip up speaks volumes about how your employer values you. You are essentially arguing that past patterns prove future safety, which is a very logical stance to take.

Now, let's connect that to the final link in your chain: the jump from "being fired" to "ending up homeless." Is there any factual data suggesting that losing this specific job would instantly leave you unable to afford rent, or is that also a prediction born from extreme worry?

Well, I do have some savings put away, and I have friends who've said they'd help me out if I ever got into a tight spot. So, no, it wouldn't be instant homelessness. I'd have options. I guess when I'm panicking, I forget that I have a safety net. It just feels like I'm all alone and everything's collapsing, but when I actually think about it, that's not true.

That realization—that you actually have financial backups and support systems—is powerful proof that the "homelessness" outcome isn't inevitable. You've successfully separated the hypothetical worst case from your actual resources. Now that we've examined the links and found several are weak or unsupported, does writing down these three counter-thoughts feel like something you could trust tomorrow morning before you face your supervisor again?

Yeah, I think writing them down would help. Just having them on paper where I can see them might stop me from spiraling again. I'll try to remember that being one minute late doesn't mean I'm getting fired, and even if the worst happened, I'm not going to end up on the street. It's hard to believe right now, but I'll give it a shot.

That is a smart decision; having those facts visible on paper acts like an anchor when your mind tries to drift back to the scary story. Before we lock this in, could you confirm if you feel confident enough to try sending a brief message to your supervisor later today acknowledging the delay, or would you prefer to wait until tomorrow morning?

I think I'd rather wait until tomorrow morning. I'm still pretty shaken up, and I don't want to send something in an emotional state that might come across wrong. I'll go in early tomorrow, maybe 15 minutes before my shift, and just say a quick "Sorry about being late yesterday, it won't happen again." That feels manageable.

Waiting until tomorrow morning is absolutely the wise choice; approaching your supervisor when you are calm ensures your message lands clearly and respectfully. Going in early gives you extra buffer time to compose yourself before entering the workspace. Would you be comfortable committing to sending that text tonight so you have it ready, or would you prefer to write it in the morning alongside your arrival?

I think I'll write it out tonight, but save it as a draft and send it tomorrow morning when I get there. That way I can read it over when I'm calm and make sure it sounds right. Having it ready but not sent yet feels like a good middle ground.

That is a perfect plan; saving it as a draft protects you from rushing it while giving you control over the exact moment it goes out. Before we finish, I want to make sure we agree on the core goal of this exercise: using these facts to interrupt the panic loop, not necessarily to argue with anyone right now. Does framing it as "building a mental shield" versus "winning an argument" feel more accurate to you?

Yeah, "mental shield" feels right. I'm not trying to prove anything to my boss or defend myself. I'm just trying to stop my own brain from convincing me that my life is over because of one small mistake. That's really what this is about - getting control back in my own head.

That is a beautiful way to frame it—you aren't fighting your boss, you are simply reclaiming peace within yourself. Before we close, I want to make sure you feel supported in this process. Have you ever worried about being fired before, and if so, what kept you from spiraling completely in those moments? Knowing your past successes with similar worries could be a powerful reminder today.

Honestly, I can't remember ever worrying about being fired before. I've always been a reliable employee, so it never crossed my mind. I think that's why this hit me so hard - it was so out of the blue. I didn't have any past experience to fall back on to tell myself it would be okay. I just went straight to the worst-case scenario because I had no other script in my head.

That absence of a familiar "safe script" explains perfectly why this panic hit so violently; your brain had no practiced routine to follow, so it defaulted to the most terrifying possibility available. Even though this is unusual for you, the lesson is the same: when a new threat appears without prior warning, we often invent a disaster movie to explain it. For tonight, I want you to carry this new "shield"—those three facts we identified—and remind yourself that even if you stumble occasionally, you haven't lost everything, and your employer likely sees you as valuable beyond one minute of lateness. Does carrying that knowledge feel like something you can rely on tomorrow morning?

I think I can rely on it. It's not going to feel natural or easy, but I can keep those facts in my pocket, so to speak. And if I start to panic again, I'll pull out that piece of paper and read it. I appreciate you helping me see this differently. I was in a really dark place when I walked in here, and I feel a little bit lighter now.

That feeling of lightness is a testament to how effective it was to separate the facts from the fiction earlier. It sounds like you have a clear path forward: write that draft tonight, keep your notes handy, and use them as an anchor whenever the panic tries to return tomorrow. Is there anything else weighing on your mind before we officially wrap up this session?

No, I think I've got what I need for now. I'll work on that draft tonight and come in early tomorrow. If I feel myself spiraling again, I'll try the breathing exercise and read my notes. Thanks again for your help - I was really scared when I came in, and I don't feel quite as alone in this now.

It is wonderful to hear that you feel less alone and more equipped to handle this situation. Your bravery in facing such intense fear and finding clarity in just one session speaks volumes about your resilience. Remember, taking that first step tomorrow—even just sending a simple note—is a victory regardless of how it goes. Is there anything else I can offer as you prepare to rest tonight?
