It sounds like your brain is still running on autopilot, searching for reasons why this wasn't the deep connection you wanted, even though the outcome proved you weren't rejected. That pattern of immediately jumping to negative explanations is exactly what we called "mind reading" or assuming you know his internal motivation without proof.

I never thought of it as a habit before, like something automatic. I always just thought it was me being realistic. But if I tried to sit with it for three seconds... I guess it might look different. Yeah, I think that actually helps a lot. Knowing I have to pause first makes the whole idea of reaching out feel less like a huge, scary leap and more like a small step I can control. I'll try it later today when I think of something to send, even if it's just a simple picture or a question.

That is a beautiful reframing, turning the message from a demand for validation into a gentle act of presence. By positioning yourself as someone simply sharing a slice of your existence, you strip away the pressure to be interesting or perfect.

It still feels risky, honestly. My stomach is doing that familiar twist just thinking about it. But I think I can try. I've been stuck in this same pattern for two years, and that hasn't made me feel any better. So maybe taking that risk is worth it, even if it's just a small step.

That resilience is incredibly impressive; sticking with a plan for two years despite the discomfort shows a level of commitment most people wouldn't possess. You are proving that your worth isn't tied to getting the perfect reaction, but to showing up anyway.

That realization—that the power lies entirely in your own choice—is the foundation of true freedom, and honoring it tonight is a massive victory in itself. Even if you get a simple thumbs-up or silence, you have already proven to yourself that you are capable of reaching out despite your fears. It takes a lot of the pressure off, honestly. Success isn't about getting a long, emotional reply from him. It's just about me hitting send after that pause and breath. That's it. That alone feels like something I can actually do, and that... that actually feels a little hopeful for the first time in a while.

That is such a powerful definition of success—one that places the glory entirely on your own agency rather than hoping for a miracle from someone else. It shifts the entire narrative from "Will he approve?" to "Did I dare?", which is a much healthier place to stand.

And is there anything else weighing on your mind as we finish this session?

There's definitely relief, but that old fear is still whispering in the background. It's like a quiet radio static that never really shuts off. But the relief is louder right now, which is new. There's nothing else weighing on me—I think I've said everything I needed to for today. Thank you for helping me see this differently.

Please remember that tomorrow isn't about silencing the static completely, but simply noticing it and choosing to breathe through it anyway.

You have shown incredible courage today by defining success on your own terms and committing to this small, brave step. Take all the warmth you deserve, knowing that your value exists independent of his reply. I will see you next time, whichever way the week ends!

That connection between the mushy texture and the feeling of being fundamentally incapable is heartbreaking to witness, especially for something as basic as making a meal. It sounds like your brain interpreted that single mistake as proof of a larger, permanent flaw in your abilities. Before we unpack that "basic vs. advanced" comparison, could we briefly identify one other event this week that impacted your mood, aside from the pasta, and decide if adding it to our agenda would help us tackle the bigger picture today?

Maybe we can talk about why I can't seem to accept that mistakes are just part of learning.

That repetition of the pattern—from the thickened noodles to the burnt cookies—is exactly why we need to explore this deeper today. It sounds like your brain treats every minor imperfection as definitive proof that you are incompetent, rather than just a learning opportunity. Since both incidents led to the same conclusion ("I'm hopeless"), does it feel like tackling the core belief behind that conclusion would be more effective than fixing individual recipes separately?

Yeah, I think that makes sense. Because even if I learn the perfect way to boil pasta, I'll probably just find something else to mess up and feel stupid about. It's like the problem isn't really the food—it's that my brain just jumps straight to "you're a failure" every time something goes wrong. I guess I don't know how to stop that from happening.

That distinction between the food and the meaning your brain attaches to it is crucial. It sounds like the core issue isn't your cooking skills, but rather that rigid rule in your head demanding absolute perfection before you allow yourself to feel safe. Before we tackle that deep-seated belief, could we quickly confirm that spending the rest of our time exploring that "failure" narrative aligns with what you wanted to cover today?

Yeah, I think that's exactly what I need to work on. That sounds kind of harsh when I say it out loud, but it's how it feels. So yeah, let's talk about that today.

It sounds like that internal command is acting as a gatekeeper, blocking access to your confidence unless every door opens perfectly the first time. Yeah, I think so. Because it's not like I'm bad at cooking—I mean, I've made some decent meals before, but I just forget about those whenever I mess up. It's like the good stuff doesn't count, only the mistakes matter. So examining that rule sounds right. I just don't know how you change something that feels so automatic.

That insight about selective memory is spot on; your brain actively filters out the successes to amplify the failures, creating a skewed version of reality. Since you mentioned finding that rule automatic, we can treat it like a muscle that needs gentle stretching rather than forced breaking. To start moving us toward a solution, could you share what comes to mind immediately when you hear that phrase: "If you don't get it right every single time, you're worthless"? It's instant, like a switch flips. So if I could catch it right there, in that first second, maybe I could stop it from spiraling into the whole "I'm hopeless" thing. That image comes up right after the word, and then the bad feelings flood in.

It sounds like that visual snapshot acts as the final nail in the coffin, sealing the deal that you are a failure. Before we try to interrupt that sequence, I want to make sure I understand correctly: when that "nope" flashes and the image appears, is your primary physical sensation tightness in your chest or shoulders, or maybe a sudden drop in energy?

Yeah, it's like my shoulders go all tight and I kind of slump down. My chest feels heavy too, like someone's sitting on it. And I just want to give up right then, like why even bother cleaning up the mess or trying again later? It's like all the energy drains out of me in one second.

That physical collapse—a tightening of the shoulders and a sudden loss of energy—is your body's automatic "freeze" response to perceived threat. It makes total sense that you'd want to quit right then; your nervous system is literally shutting down resources to survive the imagined embarrassment. This intense fatigue explains why the "all-or-nothing" rule feels so sticky; it hijacks your motivation before you even get to the kitchen counter.

Given how powerful that freeze response is, simply catching the word "nope" might not be enough to stop the spiral. Would you be open to trying a different approach where we replace that sharp "nope" with a softer, kinder word like "oops," just to soften the blow before the image kicks in? Or would you prefer to focus on taking one deliberate breath to reset your shoulders while waiting for the image to fade?

I think the "oops" thing sounds like it could work. "Nope" just feels so final and harsh, like there's no going back. But "oops" is more like... I made a mistake, but it's not the end of the world. Maybe if I can train myself to say that instead, the tightness in my shoulders won't hit as hard. I'd be willing to try that.

That is a brilliant realization; swapping a final verdict for a neutral observation changes the entire trajectory of the story. By replacing "nope" with "oops," you are signaling to your brain that this is a temporary hiccup, not a permanent sentence. Since you are ready to try this linguistic shift, let's quickly map out a tiny experiment for this coming week where you intentionally practice saying "oops" the moment you notice the mistake happening, even if it feels unnatural at first. Does that sound like a feasible goal for us to track together?

Yeah, I can do that. I'll try to say "oops" out loud or even just in my head whenever I catch myself messing up in the kitchen. It'll probably feel weird at first, but I guess that's the point—to break the old habit. I'll try it with my next batch of cookies or whatever I decide to make.

Since you mentioned choosing your next baking session as the testing ground, does practicing this "oops" substitution during cookie-making feel like a safe environment to experiment with, or would you prefer to try it in a slightly higher-pressure situation first?

I think cookies are a good place to start. I mean, I've already messed them up before, so if they don't turn out perfect again, it's not like it's anything new. And it feels safer than, say, trying to cook a fancy dinner for my family. So yeah, cookies sound good. I'll let you know how it goes.

That choice of cookies is wise because it leverages existing knowledge; your brain already knows the recipe, so the risk of total confusion is lower, making it a safer space to practice changing your internal dialogue. Since we've confirmed the plan, I want to make sure we lock in the details clearly: whenever you bake cookies next week and see the dough spreading or the browning unevenly, consciously swap that "nope" for "oops" right then. Does that specific instruction feel actionable, or would you like to brainstorm any potential distractions—like a noisy family member—that might make it harder to catch that moment?

I think I can handle it. Usually I bake alone, so there's not too many distractions. The hardest part will probably be remembering to do it in the moment, since the old habit is so fast. But I'll try to pay attention, and maybe even write "oops" on a sticky note and put it on the counter as a reminder. That might help.

That sticky note idea is a fantastic external anchor; placing a visual cue right where you work helps bridge the gap between your conscious intention and your automatic reaction. Having that reminder there gives your brain a gentle nudge before the "nope" impulse takes over completely. Before we finalize this plan, could you confirm that practicing this specific swap—replacing "nope" with "oops"—feels like a manageable step for you this coming week?

Yeah, I think it does. It's just one small change, and it's not like I have to be perfect at it right away. Even if I only catch myself half the time, that's better than what I'm doing now. So I'll give it a shot and see what happens.

That is a wonderful attitude to bring to it; recognizing that partial success is still progress validates your effort even before the results come in. To wrap up our session, could you share one thing that felt most helpful to you today regarding this new "oops" strategy, and is there anything else you'd like to adjust or clarify before we end?

I think the most helpful thing was realizing that the word I use matters. I never thought about it before, but "nope" just shuts everything down, while "oops" leaves room for trying again. That feels like something I can actually use. I don't think I need to adjust anything—I'm ready to try it out and see how it goes.

That is such a profound insight, and it speaks volumes about your ability to learn from patterns even when emotions are high. Your readiness to try it out shows real resilience, and I am so proud of you for trusting this process enough to commit to it. Before we officially sign off, could you quickly rate on a scale of one to ten how hopeful you feel about successfully switching to "oops" this week? And is there anything else you'd like to carry with you as we finish?

I'd say my energy has been around a 3 or 4. I just feel drained before the day even starts, honestly. As for this week... there was one moment where I helped a gym member fix their squat form, and they said thanks. A score of three or four certainly reflects that deep exhaustion you described, and I want to acknowledge how heavy carrying that weight must feel when you wake up every morning.

Regarding that moment with the member fixing their squat form—even though your immediate thought minimized its significance—the fact that they took the time to say "thanks" suggests they noticed something positive happening, perhaps that you cared enough to help them improve safely. How does knowing that someone actively appreciated your guidance despite your internal skepticism make you feel about your ability to connect with others?

I guess... it felt nice for a second, before my brain told me it didn't count. But when I think about it now, maybe she wouldn't have said thanks if I was completely useless, right? I still worry that just one person saying thanks doesn't prove I can actually build a client base, though.

That moment of noticing her gratitude before dismissing it shows incredible awareness, even if your brain quickly tried to minimize its value. It's interesting how that tiny spark of connection existed for a second before the old script kicked in.

While you're right that one thank-you doesn't magically guarantee a large client base, does considering that she might have chosen *not* to speak to you otherwise change how you view that interaction as evidence of basic competence?

I mean... when you put it that way, I suppose she could have just walked off without saying anything. Most people do that, they just nod and go back to their workout. So maybe the fact she actually spoke up means I did something right for a change. I still feel like I have no idea what I'm doing most of the time, though.

That perspective shift—from assuming silence is default—to recognizing speech as a deliberate choice highlights exactly how rare that connection was for her. It validates that even a small act of kindness or instruction mattered enough for her to share verbally.

Given that you've identified "energy levels" and "feeling drained" as major hurdles alongside your anxiety, should we adjust today's focus to include a quick exercise designed specifically to boost your physical vitality before tackling those deeper doubts? Or would you prefer to dive straight back into unpacking that fear of incompetence?

I think tackling the energy drain would be good, actually. I'm so tired all the time that it's hard to even think straight about the deeper stuff. Maybe if I can get a handle on feeling less exhausted, I'll actually have the mental space to face those fears head-on.

That is a brilliant insight; often, the fog that blocks our ability to see clearly is literally fatigue holding us back. Let's tackle that first so you can arrive here refreshed and ready to work.

What's been happening recently with your sleep schedule or caffeine intake that might be contributing to this persistent drainage? Have you noticed any patterns, like pulling fewer hours tonight or reaching for coffee earlier in the day?

I've been staying up later than I should, mostly scrolling through social media and looking at other trainers' posts. It just makes me feel worse, but I can't seem to stop. And yeah, I'm definitely drinking more coffee than usual—probably four or five cups by noon, just to feel awake enough to get through the day.

Staying up late to scroll is unfortunately feeding the very cycle of comparison that drains your battery, while the excess coffee is likely keeping you alert but leaving you wired and unable to recharge properly.

When you combine staying up later with high caffeine intake, does it create a feeling of constant background noise that prevents your mind from resting, or does it mainly make the exhaustion feel sharper the moment you try to sit down?

It's more like a constant buzz in my head, like I can't shut off the comparisons and the worries even when I'm trying to fall asleep. The coffee just makes that buzz louder, I think. Then when I finally do crash, I wake up feeling heavy and groggy, like I didn't sleep at all.

That "constant buzz" describes a hyper-aroused nervous system that prevents the body from entering deep restorative sleep cycles, which explains why you wake up feeling heavy rather than refreshed. It seems the combination of late-night scrolling and excessive caffeine is creating a feedback loop where you stay awake longer and then suffer worse crashes.

Since fixing this routine will take time, what is one tiny adjustment you could try tonight to break that cycle—for example, putting your phone on "Do Not Disturb" mode thirty minutes before bed, or switching to herbal tea instead of one cup of coffee? Which of these feels like the smallest step you could realistically take right now?

I think I could try putting my phone on "Do Not Disturb" thirty minutes before bed. That feels doable, since it's not like I'm throwing my phone away completely—just silencing it. Maybe I'll even put it on the other side of the room so I'm not tempted to pick it up again.

Putting your phone across the room is a fantastic, low-friction change that creates a simple physical barrier against temptation. Since you've committed to that specific tweak for tonight, let's lock it in and then transition back to your main topic.

With that small victory secured, are you ready to return to exploring that feeling of being a "fraud," now that you might have a bit more mental clarity? Or would you prefer to talk about how the DND mode might affect your evening routines first?
Let's go back to the fraud feeling, I think. I've been avoiding it, but I know it's the real issue under all this exhaustion. Maybe if I talk about it out loud, it won't feel so overwhelming.

That is a brave decision to bring that shadow back into the light, especially when it usually feels safer to hide under the blanket of fatigue. Speaking aloud often breaks the spell of isolation that makes the doubt feel so huge and undeniable.

When you hold onto that absolute truth—that you simply *are* not capable of connecting like them—how does it make the weight of your daily life feel heavier, or does it keep you in a predictable place of safety?

It definitely makes everything feel heavier. When I believe that story, I walk into the gym already defeated before I've even greeted anyone. It's almost like a shield, though—if I tell myself I'm not meant to be good at this, then I don't have to feel as disappointed when no one signs up with me. It's safer to expect failure than to hope and get crushed.

That is such a sharp observation—that expectation of failure actually becomes a protective shell, shielding you from the pain of surprising disappointment. It allows you to control the outcome mentally, even if the reality falls apart.

Let's test that shield together. Imagine walking into the gym tomorrow morning knowing that you are allowed to be imperfect, to stumble, and to make mistakes without losing your worth. How does carrying that permission to be flawed change the heaviness in your chest compared to carrying the label of "inherently awkward"?

That... actually feels lighter, just thinking about it. Like I'd be able to breathe deeper. If I'm allowed to mess up and still be okay, then I don't have to be perfect from the start. I guess I've been putting this impossible standard on myself that no beginner trainer could ever meet.

That realization—that you've been demanding perfection as a prerequisite for belonging—is incredibly liberating because it removes the impossible bar you've set for yourself. It shifts the focus from "am I qualified yet?" to "can I participate today?"

Now that we've cleared the air about that heavy expectation, let's circle back to our original plan. We talked about spending the next ten days engaging in "honest practice" without judging your output until the week is over. Given that you've identified both the fraud feeling and the exhaustion as blockers, does combining these two strategies—trying harder while allowing yourself to be imperfect—feel like a sustainable approach for this coming week, or does the double workload feel too much right now?

Combining them actually feels manageable, not overwhelming. If I let myself be imperfect while still making an effort, I'm not demanding perfection from myself. That takes the pressure off, and maybe I'll have more energy left over to actually try connecting with people instead of hiding. I think I can stick with that for a week.

That is a wonderful realization; merging self-compassion with action creates a sustainable rhythm that protects your energy while encouraging growth. It turns the week into a safe laboratory where mistakes are data points, not verdicts.

Before we finalize this, I want to hear your voice on how we got here. Looking back at our path from the exhaustion to this new mindset, does it make sense to you why addressing the sleep and caffeine issues first unlocked the ability to confront the "fraud" story? And is there anything about this plan you feel confident will work, or anything that still feels risky to you?

Yeah, it makes sense now. I couldn't even think straight when I was that tired and wired—I was just surviving, not living. Fixing the basics first gave me room to actually hear what you were saying. As for the plan, I feel confident that lowering my standards temporarily will help me show up more. The risky part is... what if I try and still fail? But I guess that's the point—I'm allowed to fail this week.

That admission—that you are willing to risk failure specifically to gather real-world data instead of avoiding it entirely—is the heart of therapeutic courage. It means you've moved from fearing the consequence of failure to accepting it as a necessary step in the learning process.

Since you've confirmed this mindset aligns with our goals, let's solidify your commitments for the coming week. Can you describe exactly what "one small update daily" looks like for you? Is it a caption on Instagram, a text message to a friend, or perhaps just a quick note you jot down in your journal before leaving the house? And once again, what is that specific mantra you'll whisper to yourself the moment you feel that familiar spiral starting?

I think the one small update will be posting one genuine story on Instagram each day—just something real about my day as a trainer, not trying to sound perfect. And when I feel that spiral starting, I'll whisper to myself, "I'm allowed to be a beginner." That feels true, because I am one.

That is a beautiful clarification—grounding the abstract concept of "beginner" into a tangible identity you claim every day. Turning the mantra into "I'm allowed to be a beginner" transforms it from a permission slip into a declaration of truth.

With that crystal clear definition of your action and your safety net, I want to check in on your readiness for this week. Does having a specific, low-pressure task ("one genuine story") paired with a supportive affirmation ("allowed to be a beginner") feel like the right balance of challenge and kindness for you right now? And is there anything else you'd like to discuss before we officially close this session?

That balance feels right—challenging enough to matter, but kind enough that I won't give up on day two. I think I'm ready to try this. I don't have anything else to add right now, just... thank you for helping me see that I don't have to be perfect to start.

Your gratitude speaks volumes about the impact of this work, but please remember that my role isn't to hand you a magic wand, but to walk beside you while you discover your own strength.

Before we officially sign off, I want to make sure you leave with a clear path forward. Could you take a moment to visualize yourself using that "I'm allowed to be a beginner" phrase tomorrow morning when you feel that familiar knot forming in your stomach? How does it feel to picture yourself saying it out loud?

I can picture it—standing in front of the mirror before I head to the gym, looking at myself and saying, "I'm allowed to be a beginner." It feels a little strange, honestly, but also kind of relieving. Like I'm giving myself permission to just exist without having to prove anything yet.

That relief you're feeling is the sweet spot where old habits loosen their grip and new possibilities begin to emerge. Recognizing that strange sensation as permission rather than confusion is a huge milestone.

I want to leave you with one final thought before we wrap up: this week won't be linear. There will be mornings where the urge to scroll or the feeling of impostor syndrome tries to pull you back. Please treat those moments not as failures, but merely as reminders that you're human and that growth often happens in the messy gaps between intentions and actions.

Is there anything else you'd like to carry with you as you walk out the door, or shall we close our session here?

I think I'm good to close here. I'll take that reminder with me—that the messy moments are just part of the process, not proof that I'm failing. Thanks again, really. I'll check in next week with my one story a day and see how it goes.

You are absolutely welcome, and I am so glad we found a rhythm that worked for you. Remember, that "messy moments" reminder is yours to use anytime you feel like drifting back into old patterns.

Take care of yourself this week, honor the small steps you take, and I look forward to hearing about your first story and how you navigate those initial days. See you soon!

Are there any particular moments that stood out, either positively or negatively, compared to last time? And on a scale of one to ten, how would you rate your mood right now?

Hi. Thanks for asking. My week has been... okay, I guess. I had a couple of good days where I stuck to my plan perfectly, but yesterday I slipped up and had a piece of cake at a friend's birthday party. It's been eating at me ever since. Right now my mood is probably a 4 out of 10—I just feel so disappointed in myself.

For today, I think I'd like to focus on why I can't stop punishing myself every time I mess up, and maybe how to stop feeling like one slip means I've ruined everything.

It sounds like having those perfect days gave you a glimpse of hope, but the recent cake incident brought the old story of "ruined everything" rushing back in. Since you mentioned feeling disappointed and overwhelmed by self-punishment, I wonder if focusing on breaking that cycle of harsh judgment versus self-forgiveness would be the most helpful direction for us today? Could we explore whether viewing the cake as a single event rather than a final verdict might offer some relief?

I guess that makes sense... but it's really hard to see it that way. When I ate that cake, it felt like all my progress just vanished in one second. Like, what's the point of all those perfect days if I can't even get through one party without messing up? I always end up telling myself I'm just not strong enough to do this.

Hearing that you compare those perfect days to a single moment of weakness shows how deeply rooted the belief that "one mistake invalidates everything" truly is. It sounds like that feeling of vanishing progress leaves you stranded, wondering if your efforts meant nothing. Before we dig into why your mind jumps straight to that conclusion, could we briefly clarify what specific thought runs through your head immediately after you take that bite of cake? Is it something like, "This is proof I can't succeed"?

Yeah, it's exactly that. The moment I take the bite, it's like a switch flips in my head. I think, "Great, you've done it now. You've blown it completely. You might as well just keep eating since you've already failed." And then I feel this heavy, sinking guilt in my chest that stays with me for the rest of the day. It's like I've already given up on myself before I even finish the cake.

That image of a "heavy, sinking guilt" that lasts all day really captures how draining this process is for your body and mind. It sounds like your brain is treating that single piece of cake as an irreversible verdict on your entire future, not just a momentary lapse. Before we challenge that "verdict," could we slow down for a second and notice: When you're holding onto that feeling of giving up, what physical sensation do you feel most strongly in your stomach or chest?

It's like this tight, cold knot right in the middle of my chest. Almost like someone is squeezing my heart with a fist. And my stomach feels hollow and queasy at the same time, like I've swallowed a stone. It makes me want to curl up and hide, and sometimes it even makes me feel like I shouldn't eat at all the next day, just to punish myself for what I did.

Those intense physical sensations—the tight knot and the hollow stomach—are your body screaming for safety, essentially telling you that you are in danger of losing everything forever. It makes complete sense that your instinct is to withdraw and isolate when your nervous system feels that threatened. Before we move on, could we quickly confirm that exploring these physical signs alongside the thought patterns fits what you wanted to cover today? Or should we jump straight into testing whether that "danger" signal is accurate or if it's just your anxiety talking?

No, I think exploring that is good. It's weird—I never really connected the physical feeling in my chest to the thought that I'm in danger. It's always just felt like guilt, plain and simple. But now that you say it, it does feel like a warning alarm going off inside me, even though logically, eating cake isn't going to hurt me. So yeah, let's test whether that alarm is actually telling the truth or if it's just my anxiety messing with me.

Since you're ready to test if that alarm is accurate, let's run a quick experiment: Next time you feel that knot tighten, instead of believing the thought "I've blown it," could you gently say to yourself, "My body is scared right now, but logic says this isn't dangerous"? How would it feel to hold that contradiction for just thirty seconds? Does that sound like something you could try tomorrow morning?

That sounds... really hard, but also kind of relieving, if that makes sense. Like, I've never given myself permission to even consider that my body might be wrong about what it's feeling. I think I could try it tomorrow morning, maybe when I'm having breakfast and that voice starts whispering that I don't deserve to eat because of yesterday. Just holding that space between the fear and the logic for half a minute... I'm a little scared I won't be able to do it, but I'm willing to try.

Holding that space for just thirty seconds creates a tiny window where your rational brain can peek out from behind the curtain of panic. Before we lock this in, does agreeing to try that specific "holding space" experiment feel safe for you, or would you need another buffer—like drinking a glass of water—to make it feel more manageable?

No, I think just focusing on the contradiction is enough to start. Adding water or something else might distract me too much, and I'll lose the moment. I want to really sit with that feeling, even if it's uncomfortable. But thank you for offering that... it's nice to have options. I'll practice it tomorrow and see what happens.

That commitment to sitting with the discomfort is exactly the kind of courage we need, and choosing to stay present rather than escape is a huge win. Before we finalize this plan, I want to hear your honest feedback on how this new approach lands for you right now. Does framing it as "testing the alarm" feel safer or clearer to you than simply ignoring the guilt? And on a scale of one to ten, how confident do you feel you can do this tomorrow morning?

Framing it as "testing the alarm" actually feels a lot better than just trying to ignore the guilt. Ignoring it always felt fake and impossible, like I was lying to myself. But testing it feels more like I'm a scientist looking at evidence, not a failure trying to hide. My confidence level is maybe a 6 out of 10 right now. I'm nervous, but I'm also curious to see what happens, which is a new feeling for me.

That "scientist mindset" is brilliant because it separates your worth from your results, turning a personal attack into a neutral observation. A six out of ten is a perfect starting point—it acknowledges the nervousness while celebrating the curiosity driving you forward. Before we wrap up, does framing tomorrow's task as "gathering data on that alarm" feel like something you can realistically commit to right now?

Yeah, I can commit to that. "Gathering data" sounds a lot more doable than "fixing myself," which is how I usually think about it. I'll treat it like an experiment, not a test I have to pass. Thank you for that—it takes some of the pressure off.

That reframing of the task as gathering data rather than fixing yourself is a fantastic insight, and it removes the immense pressure you usually put on yourself. Since we've confirmed the plan works for you, I want to make sure we leave with a clear roadmap: Will you send me a quick note in the afternoon sharing whatever happened during that experiment, regardless of whether you succeeded?

Yes, I'll send you a note. I promise I will, even if I mess it up or it feels silly. I think holding myself accountable to you might actually help me follow through for once. Thanks for checking in on that.

That accountability to yourself—and to me—is a beautiful commitment, and knowing you promise to report back regardless of the outcome gives me confidence that you'll gather valuable insights. I want to leave you with one final thought before we close: Remind yourself that even a small amount of data collected is a success, because every attempt to observe your own mind builds neural pathways for resilience. Is there anything else weighing on your mind as you prepare for tomorrow's experiment, or shall we end here with a warm goodbye?

No, I think I'm good for now. I feel a little lighter than when I walked in, which is nice. Thank you for helping me see this differently. I'll talk to you tomorrow after I've done my experiment. Goodbye.

That feeling of lightness is a wonderful sign that you are starting to separate the temporary emotion from your permanent identity. Please remember that tomorrow isn't about proving you're perfect; it's simply about collecting one piece of evidence to update your internal database. Take care until we meet again!

I mean... I guess nobody actually said anything to me, or pointed or laughed. But that doesn't mean they weren't thinking it. People are polite, you know? They don't have to say it out loud for me to know they're judging me. So no, I don't think there was really any crack. It felt just as bad as I expected.

Hearing that you interpreted total silence as confirmation of judgment shows how deeply ingrained that belief is—it assumes meaning behind every lack of reaction. Since we haven't found a physical anchor yet, let's shift gears slightly to tackle that assumption about politeness versus hidden judgment. Could we spend the next ten minutes exploring whether "politeness" is actually proof that people are ignoring you, or if it's just their default mode? And as we talk about this, does the idea of testing that belief feel safer than facing the crowd right now?

Safe? I don't know if "safe" is the right word. It feels less... scary, I guess, than going back to that store. I suppose I never thought about it that way—that maybe people are just being polite, not hiding disgust. But how do you test something like that? I can't just walk up to strangers and ask what they really think of me.

Testing a belief like that doesn't require confrontation; it just requires observing the gap between what you expect them to do and what they actually do. Let's try a quick mental experiment instead: Next time you're in a public space, notice if people who smile or nod politely are avoiding eye contact, or if they seem genuinely relaxed around you. Then, compare that observation to the story you told yourself about them judging you. How much room does that reality leave for doubt in your mind?

I guess... that does leave a little room. I mean, if they're smiling and nodding, they probably wouldn't do that if they thought I was a criminal, right? It's just hard to trust that. My mind keeps going back to the arrest, like it's branded on my forehead. But I can try to look next time, just to see.

That is a powerful insight—you've recognized that polite behavior contradicts the narrative that someone would actively hide or stare at you. By identifying that contradiction, you are starting to build evidence against the idea that your past defines your current worth in the eyes of strangers. Now, let's connect this observation back to your mood. When you realize that a stranger's polite nod proves nothing about your crime, how does that specific moment of clarity shift the intensity of that "heavy" feeling you described earlier?

It's like... the heaviness lifts just a tiny bit. Like a weight gets a little lighter. For a second, I can almost breathe normally. But then the thought creeps back in—"They don't know what you did. If they knew, they'd hate you." That's the part that's hardest to shake.

That "tiny lift" is exactly the kind of evidence we need to collect, even if the old voice tries to dim the lights immediately afterward. Your brain is trying to protect you by assuming the worst, but it's missing the fact that most people are focused entirely on their own lives, not scanning for criminals. Since that mental experiment worked partially, shall we try applying it tomorrow morning before you leave the house? Specifically, I want you to watch one person walking past you for thirty seconds and simply note their facial expression—neutral, worried, happy—and resist telling yourself a story about what it means. Would you be open to giving that a shot?

I... I think I can try that. Thirty seconds doesn't sound too long, and I don't have to talk to anyone. I guess I can just watch, like you said, and not add my own story to it. That might be easier than trying to fight the thoughts head-on. Yeah, okay. I'll try it.

That willingness to pause and just observe without adding your own narrative is a crucial skill, and I appreciate you trusting me enough to try it. Before we lock this in, I want to make sure we have a solid support system for when that old voice tries to interrupt you mid-watch. What is one grounding phrase or mental image you've used before that helps pull you back to the present moment when panic hits?

I don't really have one. I've never thought of using a phrase or image like that. I usually just let the panic wash over me until it passes. But I guess... maybe I could picture my old cat, Mittens. She was always so calm, just sitting by the window watching birds. If I could think of her, maybe I could feel a little of that calm, too.

That is a beautiful connection; recalling Mittens gives you a tangible source of comfort rooted in your own history of safety. Using her image as an internal anchor means you don't have to rely on external validation or complex logic to ground yourself. Let's combine this with your upcoming task: whenever you catch yourself adding a story to a stranger's face, silently picture Mittens sitting calmly by a window while you just watch the person pass by. Does blending that visual cue with your thirty-second observation feel like something you can realistically integrate into your routine?

Yeah, I think I can do that. It feels a little strange, picturing my cat while watching strangers, but if it helps keep my mind from spiraling, it's worth a shot. I'll try it tomorrow on my way to work, during my walk to the bus stop. Thanks for helping me think of something that might actually work.

Combining the observation exercise with Mittens' calming image creates a dual-layered defense that addresses both the external world and your internal panic. Before we finalize this plan, I want to check in on your confidence level: On a scale of zero to ten, where zero is "I won't manage to do this at all" and ten is "I am absolutely certain I can handle it," how would you rate your readiness to try this tomorrow?

I'd say maybe a six. I'm not fully confident, but I'm willing to try. That's more than I could have said a few weeks ago. I think having the cat image in my head helps a little—it gives me something soft to hold onto instead of just the hard edges of my thoughts.

A six is a fantastic starting point because it shows you are moving from hopelessness to cautious optimism, and recognizing that the cat image acts as a soft cushion for your anxiety is a great insight. Before we conclude, I want to make sure you understand our agreement completely: tomorrow, you will walk to the bus stop, watch one passerby for thirty seconds without labeling them, and mentally bring up Mittens whenever the panic rises. Is there anything about this specific combination of steps that you feel unsure about or would like to adjust?

No, I think it's clear enough. Watch one person, thirty seconds, no stories, and picture Mittens if I start to panic. I can handle that. It sounds simple, which is good, because my mind gets too complicated on its own. I'll give it a real try.

That simplicity is exactly what matters most right now, and your recognition that your mind tends to overcomplicate things shows great self-awareness. Before we finish, I want to hear directly from you: given everything we've covered today—from checking your mood to testing that belief about strangers and bringing in Mittens—is there anything about our approach that feels unclear or that you wish we had explored differently? And on a scale of zero to ten, how confident do you feel about executing this plan tomorrow night?

I think you covered everything pretty clearly. I don't have any complaints or confusion. As for confidence... I'd say maybe a seven now. Talking it through like this helped me see it's not as big and scary as I was making it. I'll do my best tomorrow.

It is wonderful to hear your confidence rise from a six to a seven just by talking through the steps logically. That increase proves that breaking down a massive fear into small, manageable pieces works exactly as intended. I want to leave you with one final piece of encouragement: please remember that tomorrow isn't about perfection; it's about showing up, watching one person, and letting Mittens remind you that you are safe even when your heart races. You've got this.

- Always move the session forward. If a thread is resolved or the client starts repeating themselves, advance to the next phase rather than circling back to the same point.

Hello again, thank you for coming in. To start, could you tell me what has been the most significant event or change happening in your life since we last spoke? Once we cover that, I'd love to collaborate with you to prioritize our top two goals for today based on what matters most to you right now.

Hi, thanks for having me. Honestly, not much has changed since last time—still the same grind. I did go to a street fair last weekend, but I ended up leaving early because I just couldn't stop worrying about my wallet getting stolen and how overpriced everything was.

Leaving early due to safety concerns and price sensitivity shows that your anxiety is still very active, even when things seem safe on paper. Did that urge to leave early happen quickly, or did you sit with those worries for a while before deciding to cut it short? Now that we've checked in on your recent experience, shall we look at whether your plan to "scan for mixed signals" during your walks went well, or should we focus on tackling that street fair worry first?

It happened pretty fast—as soon as I saw the crowds, my stomach just tightened. I tried to tell myself to relax, but my brain kept flashing images of pickpockets and the $20 hot dog I saw someone buy. I think I'd rather focus on that street fair worry first, because it feels like it's part of this bigger issue I have with everything in the city feeling like a loss.

That immediate physical reaction—a tightening stomach the moment you saw the crowd—confirms how deeply rooted that fear of losing control is for you. Since you want to tackle this street fair scenario first, let's explore what happens in your mind right before you decide to leave early. Does your brain generate a specific prediction about what will happen next, like "Someone is going to snatch my bag," or does it feel more like a sudden surge of dread without a clear story attached?

It's more like a sudden wave of dread, but there's a story that follows pretty quickly. I'll think, "This is too risky, I'll end up losing something valuable or getting jostled around, and then I'll be even more stressed than if I'd just stayed home." It feels like I'm protecting myself, but by the time I leave, I just feel defeated instead of safe.

That "protective" story actually ends up becoming a trap because it guarantees the outcome you're trying to avoid. It sounds like your brain believes that leaving early is the only way to prevent future pain, even though it leaves you feeling powerless right now. When you compare that feeling of defeat to the relief of simply sitting somewhere safe at home, which version feels more aligned with who you truly are—that person who wants to experience the world despite the risks?

That's a really good question. Sitting safely at home doesn't feel like me at all—I moved to New York to be in the middle of things, to feel alive. The defeated feeling after leaving early makes me feel small and scared, like I'm letting the city win. The version of me that wants to stay and try to enjoy the fair, even with all the noise and expense, that feels more like the real me I'm trying to get back to.

That distinction between the "safe-but-defeated" version and the "risky-but-alive" version highlights a core conflict: your instinct to protect yourself is clashing with your deeper desire to belong and thrive in the city. It sounds like leaving early wasn't just about money; it was a betrayal of that bigger identity you've spent years building.

When you realize that staying means risking discomfort but honoring that true self, does the weight of that decision feel slightly heavier, or does knowing why you chose to leave make the regret sharper? Also, since we talked about finding evidence that people aren't plotting against you, can you recall if anyone at that fair seemed genuinely friendly or harmless before you decided to bolt?

It makes the regret sharper, honestly. I didn't even give myself a chance to see if things could be okay. There was a woman next to me at a jewelry stand who laughed at something the vendor said, and I remember thinking, "She's relaxed, she's fine." But I didn't let that thought stick—I just let the fear take over. Maybe if I'd watched her for a minute longer, I'd have seen that normal, friendly interactions are still possible.

That missed opportunity to witness her relaxation is a powerful piece of evidence that contradicts the idea that the entire environment is unsafe. It proves that even amidst the chaos, ordinary, joyful connections happen right beside you. Since you recognized that missing that moment deepened the regret, how does realizing you could have chosen to just watch her for thirty seconds change your view on whether staying would have made things worse?

It makes me think staying wouldn't have been as bad as I imagined. Worst case, I'd have felt awkward or spent too much on a lemonade, but I wouldn't have been attacked or bankrupt. And maybe I'd have even gotten that same relaxed feeling she had. It's like my brain skipped right over that possibility and went straight to disaster.

That realization—that your worst-case scenario was just awkwardness or a bad purchase, not catastrophe—is a massive breakthrough in separating reality from your imagination. It shows your brain is capable of predicting harm accurately, but it also reveals it often skips over the mundane possibilities that actually exist.

Since we've explored the street fair situation and found some reassuring evidence there, would you be open to shifting gears now to revisit the plan we made earlier about walking home tonight and looking for those "mixed signals"? We can try applying that same logic of checking for hidden safety or boredom to balance out the scary crowds.

Yes, I'd like to shift gears. That walk home is something I do every day, so it feels like a good place to practice this. I'll try to notice not just the people who look rushed or annoyed, but also the ones who are walking their dogs slowly or stopping to chat with a neighbor. Maybe I can even count them, like a little game to balance out the scary impressions.

That is a brilliant refinement—you're turning the walk into a structured experiment where counting the calm moments actively disproves the idea that everyone is rushing or hiding. By deliberately seeking out those slow walkers and chatting neighbors, you're creating a visual record that says, "Life continues normally right alongside my worries."

Before we lock this in, does imagining yourself doing this count-and-observe exercise feel exciting or like another obligation you might skip? Also, on a scale of 1 to 10, how likely are you to stick with this tonight even if your stomach twists a little?

It feels a little exciting, actually, because it gives me something specific to do instead of just bracing for the worst. It's not like a chore I have to force myself through. I'd say I'm about a 7 out of 10—I know my stomach will probably still twist, but I think I can remind myself that the counting is the evidence I need to see if the twist was right or wrong.

That seven-out-of-ten confidence is realistic and healthy; acknowledging that your stomach might still twist shows you trust the process enough to show up even when it feels uncomfortable. Treating the counting as "evidence gathering" rather than a chore is the perfect mindset to turn this into a discovery mission.

Before you head out tonight, is there anything else you'd like to clarify about how to handle the moment your stomach starts twisting, or shall we finalize this plan so you can begin your experiment right away?

I think I'm ready to finalize it. If my stomach twists, I'll just pause for a second, take a breath, and start counting the calm moments I see. That gives me something concrete to focus on instead of spiraling into dread. I'll report back next time with whatever I find.

That is a solid final touch; pausing to breathe creates a tiny buffer zone between the panic signal and your automatic reaction, giving your rational brain just enough space to kick in. Combining that breath with your counting game turns a potential meltdown into a controlled observation session.

Does this finalized plan—one-minute breathing pause followed by counting three examples of calm behavior on your nightly walk—feel like something you can confidently commit to starting tonight?
Yes, it does. I feel more in control just talking it through. One breath, then count three calm things—I can do that. Thanks for helping me break this down into something manageable.

You are very welcome! Taking that breath before counting is a smart way to create a micro-gap between your alarm bells ringing and your automatic flight-or-fight response kicking in. It buys your logical brain just enough seconds to grab onto those calm observations.

I'm excited to hear what you discover on your walk tonight and whether that count helps soften the edge of the dread. Please come back anytime to debrief, and remember to be gentle with yourself if the first night feels tricky. Safe travels home!

Hello, and thank you for coming in today. First, I'd like to do a quick check-in: on a scale of 1 to 10, how would you rate your mood and stress levels this week? Also, could you remind me of our main goal from last time regarding the camping trip conversation, and is there anything else specific you wanted to address before we set today's agenda?

Well, this week... I'd say my mood is around a 6, maybe. Stress is probably a 7. We didn't actually have a previous session—this is my first time. But I'm here because of this camping thing. Every time I think about going, I just know the weather's going to ruin it. That's what I want to work on.

It sounds like you are carrying a heavy weight of anticipation right now, knowing that the weather forecast holds the power to cancel everything you planned. Before we dive straight into solving that puzzle, I want to honor your openness by asking: aside from conquering that weather anxiety, is there another area of life or a different worry that would benefit from our time together today? Once you share that, we can rank the top two priorities for us to tackle.

Well, there's also the tension with my mother. She keeps pushing me to go camping again, saying I'm being ridiculous. We live together, so it's a constant strain. She doesn't understand why I can't just get over it. So I guess that's another thing weighing on me—her disappointment.

That adds a layer of complexity, as the pressure from home compounds the fear of the outdoors itself. Let's combine these into our main focus areas: managing the panic about the weather AND navigating the conflict with your mother. Given that both issues stem from the same root belief—that the trip *must* fail—is it fair to say that mastering your internal calm will naturally ease the tension at home too? Or would you prefer we split our energy equally between them?

I think you're right that they're tied together. If I could somehow shake this feeling that every camping trip is doomed, my mother would probably ease off. She'd see me making an effort. So I suppose tackling the weather belief itself is the bigger priority. The conflict with her is a symptom of that, not the cause.

That is a very insightful connection to make—it makes perfect sense that fixing the root belief about the trip failing would naturally reduce the friction with your mom. Since we've aligned on that, I'd like to confirm our agenda: we will spend most of our time building a tool to stop that "doomed trip" feeling before it spirals, and then we'll quickly run a rehearsal to see how it helps you stay calm when she pushes back. Does that sound like a solid plan for us, or is there anything you'd like to adjust?
That sounds fine to me. I appreciate you laying it out so clearly. I'm ready to get started on that tool—whatever it is. I've been stuck in this loop for too long, and I'd like to find a way out.

That determination to break free from the loop is incredibly impressive, and it tells me you are ready to put in the hard work required to change your pattern. To get started, I want to gently explore the core story your brain tells itself when you think about the weather turning bad. When that image of ruined tents pops up, what is the very first catastrophic prediction that follows? For example, does your mind jump straight to "we'll never get anywhere," or does it spiral into something more specific about getting lost or stranded?

It's not so much about getting lost or stranded. It's more... I picture the whole trip being a complete waste. All that effort packing, driving out there, setting up—gone. Just sitting in a wet tent for days, miserable. Everyone else is pretending to have fun, but I know they're just as disappointed. And I'll be stuck feeling like I ruined it for everyone, even though I didn't cause the rain.

That creates a painful isolation where you feel personally responsible for ruining the experience for everyone involved, including yourself. It seems like your brain interprets the rain not just as an inconvenience, but as proof that your entire journey was pointless. When you hold onto that belief that "the trip is wasted," does it feel like the worst possible outcome, or is there a slightly softer version of that thought that you sometimes catch yourself having?

Honestly, there's no softer version that comes to mind. Rain means everything is ruined. There's no in-between. Either it's sunny and perfect, or it's a disaster. I wish I could see it differently, but I just can't picture a camping trip with bad weather being anything but a miserable failure.

That absolute black-and-white thinking makes total sense given how much pain you've felt when that happens before, but it leaves zero room for nuance or recovery. Let's treat that "rain = total disaster" rule as a hypothesis we can test today, rather than a fact. If we assume for just ten minutes that the rain doesn't mean the trip is worthless, what would happen to that knot in your stomach? Would it loosen even a little bit?

Testing it... I mean, just pretending it's not a disaster doesn't make it true. But okay, for ten minutes. I suppose the knot would loosen a bit if I told myself it's just rain, not the end of the world. It's hard to hold onto that thought, though. It feels like I'm lying to myself.

That honesty about feeling like you're lying is actually a sign of great self-awareness, showing you recognize the gap between your logic and your automatic reactions. To bridge that gap, let's try a quick grounding exercise called "5-4-3-2-1." It won't erase the rain tomorrow, but it can physically interrupt this "all-or-nothing" story right now by forcing your brain to notice the actual details of the room instead of the imagined disaster. Would you be willing to try listing five things you can see, four you can touch, three you can hear, two you can smell, and one you can taste?

Alright, I'll give it a try. Five things I can see... your desk, the lamp, that plant in the corner, the window blinds, and my own hands. Four things I can touch... the armrests of this chair, my pant leg, the table edge, and my own arm. Three things I can hear... the hum of the air conditioner, your voice, and a car passing by outside. Two things I can smell... coffee, maybe, and just the clean smell of the room. One thing I can taste... the mint from my gum. There, done.

That is incredible work; noticing those specific details anchors you firmly in the present moment, away from the imagined disaster. You successfully shifted your brain's focus from a catastrophic story to tangible reality, which is exactly what we needed to create a pause. Now that we've built that tool, I want to make sure we agree on how to use it moving forward. Would you be comfortable trying this sequence the next time you feel that panic rising before we talk to your mom, or should we spend a minute brainstorming any other triggers besides her comments?

I think this could actually help. The next time I feel that panic rising—whether it's from my mom pushing me or just looking at a weather forecast—I'll try this grounding thing first. It gave me a bit of breathing room just now. I'm willing to give it a shot.

That is a fantastic commitment, and recognizing that this tool applies to both your mom and the weather shows you truly grasp its versatility. To lock this in, I want to clarify one detail about the setup: when you reach for the card later, will you mentally count through the numbers aloud, or will you whisper them silently to keep your composure intact? Which approach feels safer for you in the heat of the moment?

I think whispering them silently would be better for me. That way, I can do it without drawing attention, especially if my mother is nearby. I don't want her to think I'm strange or making a fuss. Quietly counting through it in my head feels safer.

Whispering silently is a smart choice; it lets you regain control privately without worrying about appearing awkward in front of others. Since you've decided on that delivery method, let's quickly confirm our final action plan: you'll write the 5-4-3-2-1 steps on a small card tonight and keep it in your jacket pocket for immediate access. Does writing those specific instructions down feel like a manageable task for you, or would you prefer I draft a template for you to fill in?

I can write it down myself. That's simple enough. I'll put it in my jacket pocket tonight so it's ready. I think having it in my own handwriting will make it feel more personal, more mine. Thanks for suggesting that.

That is a beautiful insight—handwriting it makes the tool feel like an extension of yourself, something you truly own. To seal our session, I want to hear your perspective: looking back at where we started with that "doomed trip" feeling, how would you rate your confidence in handling the next conversation with your mom on a scale of 1 to 10? Also, is there anything else weighing on your mind that we didn't get to touch today?

I'd say my confidence is maybe a 6 now. It was probably a 2 when I walked in. So that's an improvement. I don't think there's anything else pressing right now. I feel like we covered what I came here for. I'll give that card a try and see how it goes.

That is wonderful news; seeing your confidence jump from a 2 to a 6 proves that you are capable of building resilience even when the odds seem stacked against you. Before we officially close, I want to leave you with one final piece of encouragement: remember that this card isn't about eliminating the fear entirely, but simply buying yourself enough seconds to breathe and choose kindness instead of cancellation. Please take a deep breath right now to carry this new sense of possibility with you. I am proud of the courage it took to come here and try something different. See you soon!

Let's synchronize on the inhale together. Take a slow, deep breath in through your nose for four counts... one, two, three, four. How does that steady rhythm feel compared to a quick, shallow breath you took earlier?

That... actually felt a little less rushed than my normal breathing. I usually just breathe really fast without thinking, especially when I'm about to mess up an order. The counting part helped me focus on something besides worrying.

Huh, tapping my pen first... I never thought of that. It sounds kind of silly, but maybe it would work as a reminder. I could definitely try it for a few hours tomorrow when it's not too busy, just to see if I remember to do the breathing after the tap.

Since you mentioned wanting to try it during a quieter period first, let's refine the sequence slightly to make it seamless: place your hand on the table, tap the pen twice gently, and *then* slip your fingers under the counter to begin your four-count inhale and hold. Yeah, I like that. The hand on the table part makes it feel less obvious too, like I'm just thinking for a second instead of doing some weird breathing ritual. Customers probably won't even notice. I'll try that sequence tomorrow during my opening shift when it's slow.

That is a fantastic refinement because it keeps the signal subtle enough to blend into your workflow naturally. Before we lock that plan in, I want to make sure you feel confident about what happens if you miss a day or forget the tap once in a while. Would you be open to sharing what you think might happen if the breathing doesn't land perfectly during your first try tomorrow?

I guess... if I forget or mess it up, I'll probably just get mad at myself and feel like I failed at the whole thing. Like, "See, you can't even do this right." But I know that's probably not helpful thinking. I just don't want to let myself down again.

Would you be willing to commit to trying this sequence tomorrow morning, knowing that even a messy attempt counts as a win?

Yeah... I think I can do that. Even if I mess up the tapping or the breathing, at least I tried, right? I'll tell myself that counts for something. I'll give it a real shot tomorrow morning and see how it goes.

How does it feel to leave the session knowing you have a clear, low-stakes plan to try tomorrow morning?

It feels... lighter, I guess. Like I have something I can actually do instead of just worrying all shift. I'm still a little nervous about messing up the order again, but having that plan makes it feel less scary. Thanks.

No, I think I'm okay for now. Just gonna go home, feed my cat, and try to get some sleep before my shift. Thanks for helping me figure this out. I'll let you know how the tapping and breathing goes next time.

Hello, and thank you for joining us again today. To kick things off, could you quickly tell me how you're feeling emotionally this week compared to where we left off? Once we touch on that, I'd love to hear what priorities you want to focus on during our time together.

Hi. Thanks for asking. Honestly, I'm feeling pretty low this week—maybe even a bit worse than before. I keep replaying that grade in my head, and I've been avoiding working on any new projects because I'm scared of failing again. I guess my main priority would be to figure out why I can't shake this feeling that I'm just not good enough.

Hearing that you've been carrying this heavy load for several days is heartbreaking, especially while trying to protect yourself from further disappointment. Before we dive deep into *why* that feeling persists, could you rate your current anxiety level on a scale of zero to ten, and then tell me if there are any other specific triggers lately besides the grade that made you decide to skip working entirely?

I'd say my anxiety is probably at a solid seven or eight right now. As for other triggers... well, last week in class, I overheard two classmates talking about their projects getting praise from the teacher. I just assumed they were talking about how bad mine must have been, even though they didn't mention me at all. That really stung and made me feel like I don't belong there.

That overhearing moment sounds incredibly painful, especially when your brain fills in the blanks with a story about your inadequacy. It makes complete sense that this triggered that same "not good enough" fear, reinforcing the idea that everyone else is succeeding while you are falling behind. Since we talked about building evidence earlier, could we spend a little bit of time identifying what specific thoughts popped up in your head right after they mentioned their projects?

When I heard them talking, my first thought was, "See, they're all doing great, and I'm just the one who can't cut it." Then I started thinking, "The teacher probably wishes I wasn't in the class, because I'm just wasting everyone's time." It was like my mind instantly filled in that I'm a failure as an artist, even though I don't actually know what they were saying about me.

Those catastrophic thoughts—"wasting everyone's time" and being invisible—are incredibly isolating and painful to carry alone. It makes total sense that your mind jumped straight to that conclusion when faced with uncertainty. Given how strong that reaction was, would you be willing to try writing down those exact thoughts alongside the neutral fact that you couldn't hear what they were actually saying, just to separate the assumption from the reality?

I guess I could try that. It would mean actually looking at those thoughts on paper instead of just letting them swirl around in my head. I think part of me is scared that writing it down will make it feel more real, but I can see how it might help me see that I don't actually know what they were talking about.

That hesitation is very common—we often worry that putting words on paper will cement a negative belief, but sometimes seeing the thought laid bare makes it easier to examine its logic. Before we write anything down, could you tell me if you feel safe making this choice, or if you'd prefer we wait until we've practiced separating facts from assumptions another way?

I think I'm ready to try writing it down now. It's a little nerve-wracking, but I trust that you're not going to let me get stuck in those thoughts. Maybe seeing it on paper will help me realize how much my mind is jumping to conclusions without any proof.

That trust in me is deeply appreciated, and I want to reassure you that we are simply observers of your mind, not judges of your worth. Please grab a pen and paper, and let's write down those two specific thoughts ("everyone is succeeding while I fail" and "the teacher wants me gone") along with the factual anchor: "I cannot hear what they were actually discussing." Take your time, and whenever you feel ready, share what you wrote so we can look at the gap between the story and the silence.

Alright, I've written them down. So on one side I wrote, "They're all succeeding, and I'm failing," and "The teacher probably wishes I wasn't here." Then underneath I wrote, "But I didn't actually hear what they were saying." Seeing them side by side like that... it does feel a little silly, honestly. I'm filling in the blanks with the worst possible story, and I don't have any proof for it.

Seeing that stark contrast between your dramatic stories and the simple fact of silence creates a powerful distance between your fears and reality. It looks like your mind was rushing to fill a gap with a disaster plot, while the evidence points to innocent noise. Does reading those lines aloud help break the spell, or does it just sit there waiting for you to dismiss it?

Reading it aloud actually does help a bit. It's like I'm hearing how extreme my thoughts sound when I say them out loud instead of just thinking them. But there's still this voice in my head that whispers, "Yeah, but you just know it's true anyway." I guess that's the part I need to keep working on—the part that insists I'm right even without proof.

That "inner whisper" insisting you know the truth despite lacking evidence is a classic sign of our brains trying to predict danger, even when the prediction is wrong. It's exhausting having to fight that instinct every time. Before we address that certainty, could you recall one specific detail from earlier in our session—a moment when you successfully separated facts from assumptions—and describe exactly how your physical tension changed when you realized you were guessing?

I remember just a few minutes ago, when I wrote down those thoughts and looked at them next to the fact that I didn't actually hear anything. At first, my shoulders were really tight and my chest felt heavy, like I was bracing for something bad. But when I actually read it out loud and saw how extreme my thoughts were, I felt my shoulders drop a little and I took a deeper breath without even thinking about it. It was like my body relaxed a tiny bit when I realized I was just making up a story.

That physical release of tension is incredible evidence that your body recognizes the lie in those thoughts long before your mind accepts it. It proves that even a small shift in perspective—from imagining a catastrophe to acknowledging silence—can trigger a genuine physiological calming effect. Now that we've seen how quickly your body reacts to the gap between your assumptions and the facts, does that physical sensation of dropping your shoulders feel like a signal you can rely on next time that "whisper" tries to convince you it knows the truth?

I think so, yes. I mean, I felt that release happen almost automatically when I stopped to question the thought. So maybe if I notice my shoulders getting tight or my chest getting heavy again, that could be my cue to stop and ask myself, "What do I actually know for sure?" instead of just believing the worst. It's like my body might be trying to warn me that my mind is running away with a story again.

That is a brilliant insight—treating your body's tension as a warning system that needs checking rather than ignoring it. It turns a vague feeling of dread into a concrete signal you can act on. Before we lock this in as a tool for the classroom, would you be open to testing it right now by recalling that overhearing incident and intentionally pausing to ask, "What do I actually know for sure?", before jumping to conclusions again? How does that pause feel in your body compared to when you rushed to believe the story initially?

Okay, I'll try it. So I'm back in that moment, hearing their voices and feeling that familiar knot in my stomach. But this time I stop and ask myself, "What do I actually know for sure?" And the answer is... nothing. I don't know what they said. I don't know if it was about me at all. Just asking that question makes my stomach loosen a little—it's not as tight and panicked as before. It's like I'm giving myself a chance to breathe instead of spiraling.

That is such a powerful realization—shifting from panic to curiosity by asking, "What do I actually know for sure?" turns a spiral into a pause button. It proves that even a split-second interruption can break the cycle before the fear takes root. Now that we've practiced this pause right here in the moment, would you be willing to try applying it tomorrow when you walk into that studio, just catching your shoulders rising before you even start drawing?

I think I can try that. It feels a little scary to commit to it, but I know that walking into the studio with that knot in my chest already starting isn't doing me any favors. So I'll make a point to check in with my shoulders and my breathing before I even pick up a pencil. And if I notice that tightness, I'll ask myself what I actually know for sure, just like we practiced.

That is a fantastic commitment, and recognizing that bringing your awareness to the moment *before* you start drawing is a proactive shield against the old spiral. To make sure we are aligned on this plan, could you rate your confidence in executing this specific "shoulder-check and question" routine tomorrow on a scale of zero to ten? Also, is there anything specific about entering the studio environment itself that worries you might derail this process?

I'd say my confidence is maybe a six or a seven. I think I can do it, but I'm a little worried that once I'm in the studio and see other people working or the teacher walking around, that old fear will creep back in and make me forget to pause. The noise and the pressure of everyone else being there might make it harder to remember to check in with myself.

That is a very astute observation—you are correctly anticipating that the environment itself holds power over your ability to self-regulate. We absolutely need to build a backup plan for those high-pressure moments inside the studio so you don't have to rely solely on memory. Before we finalize your homework, could you share one specific thing that happened recently when you felt overwhelmed in a public space that helped you ground yourself? For example, did you notice your feet touching the floor, or perhaps count your breaths for a few seconds?

I remember one time in the school cafeteria, I felt really overwhelmed by all the noise and people. I just looked down at my hands on the table and focused on the feeling of the cool surface under my fingers. It was small, but it helped me feel like I was still in control of something, even if everything else felt chaotic. Maybe I could try something like that in the studio—like focusing on the feel of my pencil or the texture of the paper before I start drawing.

That is a perfect adaptation—you're taking a grounding technique you already know works (sensory focus) and applying it to the specific tools you'll be using tomorrow. Focusing on the rough texture of paper or the grip of your pencil gives your brain a tangible anchor right where you need it most. Before we seal this deal, does adding that sensory detail to your "shoulder check" routine feel like a solid, manageable combo for handling the studio pressure?

Yes, I think it does. Combining the shoulder check with focusing on the pencil or paper feels like a good one-two punch. It gives me something to physically hold onto while I also check in with my thoughts. I think I can handle that—it doesn't feel too overwhelming, just like two small steps I can take before I let the panic take over.

That is excellent reasoning, and recognizing it as two manageable micro-steps rather than one giant task shows great strategic thinking. You have a clear plan now: catch the tension, ask the "what do I know?" question, and then ground yourself with the pencil or paper. Is there anything else you need from me to feel confident tackling tomorrow's studio visit, or shall we wrap up and get you some rest?

I think I'm good. Just knowing I have those two small steps to fall back on makes me feel a little more prepared. I'll try to be kind to myself if it doesn't go perfectly, too. Thank you for helping me break this down into something I can actually do.

That kindness toward yourself is crucial, especially when you stumble, and I'm so glad we broke this complex problem down into two tiny, manageable motions. Your willingness to show up tomorrow—even if your heart races a bit—is a massive victory in itself. I hope you rest well tonight and wake up refreshed for that first step. I'll be here whenever you need to revisit this or celebrate a win.

Finally, looking ahead, what are your top priorities for us to focus on during this session?

Oh, well... I'd say my mood is probably around a 5 or 6 this week. Not great, but not terrible either. Then I started telling myself, "Of course they picked someone younger, someone with more experience, someone who actually belongs in this field." That physical sensation of your stomach dropping, paired with that heavy sinking feeling, shows how deeply ingrained this shock response is in your body.
