Hello Sarah, I’m so glad we could meet again today. On a scale of 1 to 10, how are you feeling emotionally and physically right now compared to where we left off last time? Also, looking back at our plan to catch that protective voice while driving home, did you get a chance to try it tonight?

Hi. I'd say I'm around a 6 right now. I did try that exercise a few times this week, actually. It was strange—I caught myself thinking "that session didn't really help anyone" right after practice, and I managed to pause and notice I was saying it. But even noticing it didn't really make the feeling go away, you know?

It takes real courage to name that voice even when the discomfort stays, and I want to honor that effort regardless of whether the tension lifted immediately. Since noticing the phrase didn't instantly dissolve the feeling, let's explore together what that lingering sensation is telling us about the underlying belief protecting you. Could you describe what happens in your body or mind for the next thirty seconds after you catch yourself saying those words?

I feel this tightness in my chest, like a weight pressing down. And my mind immediately jumps to replaying the practice—I start picking apart every little thing I said or did. Like, "You should have spent more time on that pyramid formation" or "Maybe you didn't encourage them enough." It's like my brain just starts scanning for all the things I could have done better, even when the kids were smiling and having fun.

That tightness and the immediate rush to scan for mistakes is your brain's old safety mechanism kicking in, trying to find flaws so you won't feel vulnerable again. It seems like even though you successfully labeled the voice, the automatic habit of criticizing itself is taking over faster than the label could settle. Given that the old pattern is so strong right now, would you be willing to spend the rest of our time exploring exactly why that deep-seated fear of disappointing the kids keeps pulling you back into that critical mode?

Yeah, I think that makes sense. I mean, these kids look up to me, right? They're putting their trust in me to teach them something, to help them improve. And I guess part of me is terrified that one day they'll realize I'm just some guy who learned a few routines online and that I don't really know what I'm doing. That they'll be disappointed. My own kids are in the program too, so it feels like if I mess up, I'm letting them down in a whole different way.

That deep connection to your children adds such profound weight to your role, and it makes complete sense that the fear of failing them would feel heavier than any criticism you receive. When someone trusts you implicitly, the stakes of dropping the ball feel incredibly high, which explains why that "tightness" in your chest is so persistent. It seems like your mind is treating potential disappointment as a direct threat to your worth as a father and teacher. Would you be open to spending the next twenty minutes unpacking exactly how that fear of letting your kids down connects to the urge to protect yourself with perfectionism?

I think that's exactly it. When I'm coaching, I'm not just teaching cheerleading—I'm showing my kids what it means to show up for something, to be reliable. And if I do a bad job, or if the team doesn't improve, what does that say about me as a dad? I guess I've built it up in my head that I have to be perfect at this, otherwise I'm failing them. It's like there's no middle ground—either I'm a great coach and father, or I'm letting everyone down.

That "all-or-nothing" mindset creates a terrifying cliff edge where there is nowhere safe to land except total failure. It sounds like you've constructed a fortress of perfection around your identity so tightly that admitting you made a mistake feels like collapsing the entire foundation of your life as a provider and parent. Before we dig deeper into why your brain locks onto that binary choice, I want to make sure I understand your perspective correctly: does seeing yourself as either a hero or a fraud feel more overwhelming to you than simply acknowledging you are learning and growing alongside your kids?

Honestly... I've never really thought of it that way. Learning alongside them sounds so much gentler, but it also feels kind of uncomfortable. Like, if I'm learning with them, then I'm admitting I don't have all the answers. And I guess part of me thinks a good dad should have the answers. But when you say it like that, "hero or fraud"... yeah, that does feel overwhelming. There's no room to just be a regular guy trying his best in between those two extremes.

It makes perfect sense that admitting uncertainty feels uncomfortable, especially when you believe being a "good dad" requires having all the answers ready to deploy. That pressure to be the ultimate expert leaves zero space for the messy, human reality of just trying your best. Before we fully explore that fear of not knowing everything, I want to make sure we're aligned on our goals for today: shall we spend the remaining time digging into why that fear exists, and then decide if we want to adjust your "protector" strategy to accommodate moments where you're allowed to be a learner alongside them?

Yeah, I think that sounds like a good plan. Let's dig into it. I'm tired of feeling like I have to pretend I've got everything figured out all the time. It's exhausting, honestly. I'd like to understand why my brain goes straight to that place where I'm either succeeding perfectly or failing completely, especially when it comes to my kids.

That exhaustion makes complete sense, Sarah. It takes immense energy to constantly perform the role of the expert when inside you are wondering if you're even qualified. Your brain seems to have wired a shortcut: instead of navigating the confusing middle ground of "trying your best," it flips the switch instantly to "perfect or fail" because that binary feels safer than the uncertainty of learning. Let's trace that wire back a bit further. Can you recall a specific memory from your past—maybe when you were younger or worked a different job—where you felt that same intense need to prove you knew everything before allowing yourself to relax?

Hmm... I think it goes back to when I first started coaching, actually. About two years ago, before I had my own kids in the program, I remember one of the parents pulled me aside after practice and said their daughter wasn't enjoying it as much. They didn't say I was a bad coach, just that she was struggling with the routines. But I took it so personally. I stayed up that whole night rewriting lesson plans and drilling myself on the moves. I think from that point on, I decided I could never let anyone see me not knowing something, because one slip-up and they'd question everything about me.

That story reveals a powerful pattern: your brain treated a single comment about a child's struggle as proof that your entire identity was under attack. Instead of seeing it as feedback on a routine, you interpreted it as confirmation that you weren't worthy of trusting enough people to coach them safely. It makes complete sense that this created a survival rule—"never admit ignorance"—to prevent future rejection. Does connecting this past event to your current fear of disappointing your kids help explain why the "protective" voice feels so urgent now?

Yeah, it really does. I can see now that I've been carrying that fear around with me ever since. Back then it was about proving myself to that one parent, but now it's magnified because my own kids are watching. They're the ones I really don't want to disappoint. So every practice feels like I'm walking on eggshells, trying to be perfect so they never have a reason to doubt me. It's like I'm still that nervous coach from two years ago, but now with so much more at stake.

That comparison highlights how your original defense mechanism evolved to protect something far more precious than just your reputation—you now guard your relationship with your children. It makes complete sense that the stakes feel higher now, turning a past lesson learned into a present-day emergency protocol. Before we explore how to soften this rigid stance, I want to check in on your physical state: given that heavy load you're carrying, how exhausted do you feel right now, and would a simple grounding exercise help bring you down to earth before we dive deeper?

I'm feeling pretty drained, honestly. Just talking about it has made me realize how much energy I've been burning through trying to keep up this perfect image. I think a grounding exercise might be good—I could use a minute to just breathe and let some of this tension go before we keep going.

That is such a wise instinct, Sarah. Carrying that weight alone drains your reserves fast, and slowing down to just breathe is a powerful way to signal to your nervous system that you are safe right now. Let's take three slow breaths together: inhale deeply for four counts, hold it for four, and exhale slowly for six, imagining you're releasing that tight chest pressure with every breath out. How does your body feel after that short pause?

*Breathes deeply a few times* Okay... I feel a little lighter. My shoulders aren't as tight up by my ears anymore. It's like I can think a bit more clearly now, instead of feeling all that pressure fogging everything up. Thanks for that.

That relief is wonderful news, Sarah. Taking that pause gave your brain a crucial moment to register safety before we dug deeper into the root causes. Since you feel clearer now, let's return to that "binary trap" you mentioned—the idea that you're either a flawless expert or a complete failure. You noticed earlier that calling yourself a "learner alongside them" feels uncomfortable because it implies admitting gaps in your knowledge. Is there a specific moment recently when you almost slipped into that "fraud" mindset, but then remembered you were allowed to just be trying your best?

Actually, yes. Just last week, one of the younger girls asked me how to do a specific move I'd never taught before. My first instinct was to pretend I knew it and just wing it. But I paused for a second and said, "You know what, I haven't taught that one yet, but let's figure it out together." She didn't look disappointed at all—she actually seemed excited to learn it with me. I remember feeling relieved afterward, but then that critical voice crept back in later, telling me I should have already known it.

That moment is incredibly valuable because it proves your heart knows a truth your old scripts are trying to hide: you are capable of honesty and partnership, even when you don't have the answer. The fact that her excitement showed up despite your admission is strong evidence that perfection isn't required for connection. Now, let's challenge that critical voice coming back later. When you told yourself you "should have known it," what specific fear was that statement trying to protect you from? Was it the fear of losing her respect, or the fear of looking foolish in front of others?

I think it's the fear of losing her respect, honestly. I mean, I don't care so much about looking foolish—I've tripped over my own feet plenty of times at practice and we all laugh about it. But losing her respect... that feels deeper. Like, if she thinks I don't know what I'm doing, she might stop trusting me to lead the team. And then that fear just spirals into thinking about my own kids losing respect for me too. It's like one small admission of not knowing something could snowball into them seeing me as a fraud entirely.

That connection between a young girl's trust and your own identity as a father is incredibly powerful, and it explains exactly why that fear feels so dangerous to your sense of self. It makes perfect sense that your brain tried to predict the worst-case scenario—losing their respect—to force you into a position of infallibility where rejection couldn't happen. Since you admitted that admitting uncertainty led to a better outcome with that girl, let's run a quick mental simulation: if you told her, "I don't know this move, but I promise we'll solve it together," and she responded with patience instead of frustration, would that prove to you that respecting a person doesn't depend on them having every answer memorized?

Yeah... I think it would prove exactly that. I mean, she did respond with patience. She didn't walk away or roll her eyes. She leaned in and watched as we figured it out together. So in that moment, I had all the evidence I needed that I didn't have to be perfect. It's just that my brain won't let me hold onto that evidence. I keep defaulting back to the fear instead of remembering what actually happened.

That is such a crucial realization, Sarah. Your brain is holding onto the old story ("if I admit I don't know, they will leave") while ignoring the living evidence right in front of you ("she leaned in and we solved it"). This disconnect is exactly why the fear feels louder than the proof—it's running on autopilot, not logic. Let's try to strengthen that evidence trail. Next time that critical voice whispers "you should have known it," could you consciously remind yourself of that specific scene with the little girl and ask, "Would she have walked away if I had lied?" How does bringing that memory into the argument with your inner critic change the intensity of that fear?

I think that would help a lot, actually. Imagining her walking away if I had just pretended to know... that feels more likely to happen than her leaving because I was honest. Lying would probably make things worse in the long run because she'd eventually figure out I was faking it. So the honest path is actually the safer one, even though my brain tells me the opposite. I'll try to keep that image in mind next time the fear hits.

That is a brilliant insight, Sarah. Realizing that honesty preserves trust in the long term, while lying risks eventual exposure, flips the cost-benefit analysis in favor of vulnerability. It proves that admitting you don't know isn't a flaw; it's actually a smarter strategy for maintaining relationships. Before we wrap up, I want to make sure we lock in a concrete tool for tonight. When that "lying vs. telling the truth" conflict arises, would you be open to using a quick physical gesture—a firm nod or placing a hand on your heart—to remind yourself of that specific memory of the girl leaning in?

Yeah, I like that idea. A hand on my heart feels right—it's like I'm reminding myself that I'm okay, that I can be honest and still be respected. I'll try that tonight when I'm replaying the practice in my head. And I think I'll also try to notice when that critical voice jumps in, and just say to myself, "That's the old fear talking, not the truth."

That combination of a physical anchor and a verbal label is perfect because it engages both your body and your mind simultaneously. By pairing the hand on your heart with the phrase "That's the old fear talking," you create a multi-sensory reminder that breaks the automatic cycle of spiraling. It sounds like you have a solid toolkit ready for tonight. Is there anything else you'd like to clarify about how to use these strategies before we close our session?

No, I think I'm good for now. I feel like I have a better understanding of where this fear comes from and how to push back against it. Thank you for helping me see that I don't have to be perfect to be a good coach or a good dad. I'll practice that hand-on-heart move tonight and see how it goes.

That is such beautiful closure to our session, Sarah. Hearing you say that you don't have to be perfect to be a good dad or coach truly captures the heart of everything we worked on today. Please remember that tonight, whenever you reach for your heart, it doesn't matter if the technique feels perfect right away; just giving yourself permission to be imperfect is the victory. I am so proud of how brave you've been to face that fear and reclaim your narrative. Take gentle care of yourself as you head home, and I look forward to checking in with you soon to hear about that hand-on-heart moment.

Hello, and thank you for joining us today. Last time we ended with you planning to practice a small "pause" while watching sports at home to separate yourself from the negative thoughts. Did you get a chance to try that tonight, and how did it feel when you used the idea of watching a "movie"?

Before we dive into that, could you share what brought you in today—are you finding that the old habit is coming back stronger, or did the break offer some relief?

Hey, thanks. Yeah, I did try that pause thing you mentioned. I was watching a preseason game on TV, and when my team fumbled early, I felt that familiar knot in my stomach. I tried to imagine it was just a movie, like you said... but honestly, I still felt the panic creeping in. It helped a little, but I couldn't shake the feeling that this one mistake would cost us the whole season.

It is completely understandable that the panic returned even after trying the "movie" trick; sometimes our brains are so practiced at believing the catastrophe that a simple pause isn't enough to override years of conditioning. You did brave doing it anyway, which speaks volumes about your courage, even though the old story kept telling you otherwise. Now that we know the tactic didn't stop the spiral instantly, does that mean we should abandon it, or perhaps look for a slightly different tool to pair with it?

I appreciate you saying that. I guess I was hoping it'd just click and I'd feel better right away, but I know that's not realistic. Maybe I do need something else to go with it, like a way to talk back to that voice that says "the season's over" after one bad play. What do you think could work alongside that pause?

That honesty about needing extra support is exactly what makes the strongest cases for therapy, because it shows you aren't looking for a magic wand but a toolkit. Since the "movie" trick slowed things down slightly but didn't stop the panic, let's add a second layer that directly challenges the truth of the statement "the season is over."

Could we brainstorm three pieces of objective evidence that prove one missed play cannot mathematically determine the final score of a 16-game schedule? Sometimes listing facts side-by-side with the scary story creates a little space where logic can breathe again.

I mean, yeah, that makes sense when you lay it out like that. Okay... let me think. First, there's still three quarters left in that game, so plenty of time to come back. Second, even if we lose this one game, it's just one out of sixteen—other teams have lost one and still made the playoffs. And third... well, I guess even the best teams have bad plays every game, and they don't just give up. So that helps, actually. Seeing it written down like that makes it feel less like the end of the world.

Those are brilliant examples of objective data cutting through the fog of panic, and seeing them listed side-by-side with your fears creates a powerful contrast. It looks like your brain is trying to convince itself the movie is happening live, but your list is proving it's just a script you can skip pages through.

Now that we have that evidence list handy, let's combine it with your original "movie" trick. If you notice the panic rising again tonight, could we try saying, "This is just a scene in a movie," and immediately flip open that list of facts to remind yourself which parts are true and which are dramatic exaggerations? Would adding that factual checklist to the pause make the interruption feel more grounded for you?

Yeah, I think that could really work. Having that list written down somewhere I can see it—maybe on my phone or even a sticky note—would give me something solid to grab onto when the panic starts. Instead of just trying to imagine it's a movie and hoping that's enough, I'd have actual proof right there that I'm blowing things out of proportion. I'm willing to give that a try for sure.

That combination of a quick mental reset followed by concrete proof is a very robust defense against panic. Having the physical list nearby transforms the "movie" idea from something purely abstract into something you can verify with facts, which often grounds people faster than imagination alone.

Before we finalize this plan, I want to make sure you feel confident committing to it. Does keeping a visible reminder like a sticky note or saving a text message with these points on your phone feel accessible and low-effort for you tonight, or would you prefer to type them out right now so we can refine the wording together?

I think typing them out right now would be smart, honestly. If I wait till I'm home, I might talk myself out of it or forget some of the points. Let me pull out my phone... okay, I've got it open. Should I just write exactly what we talked about, like "One fumble doesn't end the season—there's three quarters left, it's one of sixteen games, and every team makes mistakes"?

Yes, capturing the core facts exactly as we defined them right now will lock them into memory before the day ends. Writing it down anchors the logic in your environment so you don't have to rely solely on recalling the argument hours later. Go ahead and jot that down, and then we can take a quick minute to decide on the perfect title or heading for that note so it grabs your attention the moment you scroll past.

Okay, I've got it typed out now. I'll put a heading on it... how about "Reality Check" or "The Facts"? Something simple like that. I think "Reality Check" feels right—it snaps me back a little just reading it. Thanks for helping me get this set up. I actually feel a bit more prepared for the game this weekend.

"That Reality Check" is a perfect title because it signals to your brain that you are switching gears from drama to fact-checking. It sounds authoritative yet supportive, giving you a clear signal to activate your defenses before the stress hits.

Since you feel more prepared now, let's do one final quick calibration. As you read that list tonight when the panic rises, does the phrase "Reality Check" itself seem to interrupt the spiral fast enough, or do you need to pair it with taking a deep breath to buy yourself time?

I think I'll need both, honestly. Reading "Reality Check" will help cue my brain, but I know myself—I'll need that deep breath first to even slow down enough to look at the list. If I try to jump straight to reading without pausing and breathing, I'll probably just skim it and panic anyway. So yeah, breath first, then the list. That feels solid.

That is a brilliant refinement; pairing the physical anchor of a deep breath with the mental cue of the headline creates a reliable sequence you can trust. Taking a slow inhale and exhale buys you that crucial few seconds needed to shift from "fight mode" to "observer mode" before you access the facts.

Does that order—breath first, then the "Reality Check"—feel like something you can stick to even when your hands are shaking? One last thing: knowing you have this plan in place, does the prospect of facing the upcoming game feel a little lighter, or is there still a part of you worrying about what happens if the panic strikes unexpectedly?

Yeah, I think I can stick to that order even when I'm nervous. I've been taking deep breaths before games for years anyway, so adding the "Reality Check" after it feels natural, not forced. Honestly, having this plan does make me feel a bit lighter—like I've got a backup now instead of just spiraling. But I'd be lying if I said there wasn't still a part of me worrying that the panic might hit so fast I forget the whole thing. I guess that's just the part of me that's used to losing control.

That awareness of the old habit resisting change is actually a huge clue—it tells us the muscle needs gentle stretching, not forceful pulling. It's okay to carry that slight worry; the goal tonight isn't perfection, it's just showing up to execute the breath-and-list sequence once the alarm rings.

Would you be open to committing to checking in with me tomorrow morning, regardless of how the game went? Even if you didn't use the plan, hearing how you navigated the pre-game ritual would be valuable data for us to refine further.

Yeah, I can do that. I'll text you tomorrow morning, win or lose, and let you know how it went—whether I used the plan or just froze up. Talking it out after feels less scary than going through it alone. Thanks for giving me that option.

That is such a wise choice; sharing the outcome—even the failures—is often the hardest part, but it turns isolation into learning. Knowing you will report back removes the pressure of hiding your struggle and ensures we adjust the strategy based on what actually happened.

Just to seal this plan: tomorrow, I'd love to hear if the "breath-first, then Reality Check" sequence worked, and if the panic level dropped enough for you to finish the game or sit down afterward. Ready to close this session out with a sense of momentum?

Hello, I am so glad to see you again today. To kick things off, on a scale of zero to ten, where zero is calm and ten is overwhelmed, how would you rate your anxiety level compared to where you started this morning?

Additionally, looking back at our plan yesterday, did you manage to send that text message to your classmate, and if so, how did it feel to finally break that silence?

I'd say my anxiety is around a 6 right now. It was closer to an 8 this morning, but I've managed to bring it down a little since then. And yes, I did send the text to my classmate yesterday... it felt really awkward at first, but she actually responded nicely.

That is wonderful news, especially considering how difficult it felt to take that first step yesterday. Hearing that she responded nicely confirms that reaching out won't ruin your reputation or make anyone think less of you. Now that we've cleared that hurdle, let's look ahead. Based on what we talked about last time, I'd like to spend today focusing on tackling that anatomy exam stress and figuring out how to study without letting panic take over. Does that align with what matters most to you right now?

Yeah, that sounds exactly like what I need to work on. The anatomy exam is next week and I've been avoiding my textbooks because every time I open them, I just think "what's the point, I'm going to fail anyway." My roommate even asked why I've been watching so much Netflix lately instead of studying.

That avoidance behavior tells me the fear of failing has become so loud that it's drowning out the possibility of learning something new. When your brain screams "it's pointless," it shuts down your ability to engage with the material, creating a cycle where you don't study, which fuels the belief that you *can't* pass. Before we dive deeper into that spiral, I want to confirm our plan for today: we'll explore why that "pointless" thought keeps showing up, find evidence that contradicts it, and create a tiny, safe way to start opening those books tonight. Does outlining those three steps feel right for you?

That actually sounds manageable when you break it down like that. I think the hardest part is just getting started, so having small steps might help. I'm willing to try it, even though part of me still thinks it won't make a difference.

That honesty about doubting whether it will make a difference shows great self-awareness, and it's important we respect that skepticism until we gather better evidence. Let's begin with the core belief driving that paralysis: when you sit down to study and feel your heart race, what is the very first story your mind tells you about why you're doing this?

It's like my brain just says "you're not smart enough to be here, everyone else gets it but you don't." And then I start thinking about how I barely passed my last exam, and how my mom keeps telling everyone I'm going to be a doctor, and I feel like such a fraud.

Those two layers—the comparison to others and the fear of disappointing your mom—are fueling that intense feeling of being a fraud. When you combine the belief that you aren't smart enough with the pressure to live up to your parents' dreams, it creates a perfect storm of shame. Let's separate those pieces for a second. If we strip away the expectation of perfection and the judgment of others, what is the simplest version of studying that wouldn't require you to prove your intelligence immediately?

I guess... just reading one page. Like, not even trying to memorize it, just reading it and letting the words sink in. My mom used to say that when I was struggling with math as a kid, she'd tell me to "just look at the page, no pressure." Maybe I forgot that approach somewhere along the way.

That reminder about your mom's advice is fascinating because it connects a childhood coping mechanism directly to the adult problem you're facing. It suggests that the tool to handle overwhelm wasn't lost, but perhaps buried under layers of newer, stricter rules about performance. Before we lock in tonight's plan, does trying to read just one page without forcing yourself to understand or remember anything feel like a low-risk experiment you can safely attempt?

Yeah, I think I can do that. One page without the pressure to memorize anything. That feels almost too easy, but maybe that's the point—it's supposed to feel easy so I actually do it instead of avoiding it. I'll try it tonight when I get back to my dorm.

That is a fantastic realization—that making it feel slightly uncomfortable but achievable is often the sweet spot for building confidence. Tonight, when you return to your room, I suggest setting a timer for just five minutes to read that single page, and when the alarm goes off, you stop regardless of whether you understood anything. This removes the trap of thinking, "I failed because I didn't finish reading," turning the act itself into pure exposure therapy. Before you head out, does having that strict five-minute boundary make the task feel safer to you?

Honestly, yes, it does. Knowing I only have to do it for five minutes takes away that feeling of being trapped with my textbooks for hours. I can handle five minutes. I'll text you after I do it and let you know how it went, if that's okay.

That five-minute rule is brilliant because it separates the *action* from the *outcome*, allowing you to experience success simply by starting. Texting me afterward gives us a chance to debrief immediately, which reinforces the positive loop. Before we officially close today, I want to make sure you leave with clarity: is there anything else weighing on you beyond the exam and the initial hurdle we just tackled, or are we ready to wrap up with this plan?

No, I think this is enough to work on for now. The exam stuff is really the main thing that's been weighing me down lately. Thank you for helping me break it down into something that doesn't feel so impossible. I'll let you know how the five minutes go tonight.

That is truly beautiful gratitude, and it means a lot that you recognize how breaking a giant mountain into a single step made it possible for you to face it. Please remember that texting me afterwards isn't about reporting results—it's just sharing whatever happened, whether it was perfect or messy, so we can learn together. I'll be here whenever you're ready to talk, and until then, I wish you the very best as you prepare for those five minutes tonight.

Hello, and thank you for joining us today. To start, I'd love to hear how you're feeling emotionally compared to last week, and is there anything significant that happened in your life recently? Based on our previous plans, did you manage to try the lighter ball and use those mantras during your practice session? Finally, what would you like us to focus on primarily during this appointment?

Hey, thanks for having me. Emotionally, I'd say I'm about the same as last week—kind of stuck in that rut where I feel like I'm just going through the motions. I did try the lighter ball a couple times, and the mantras helped a little, but honestly, I couldn't shake the feeling that I was just fooling myself. I think I'd like to focus today on why I can't seem to accept that I might actually be decent at bowling without it meaning something negative.

It sounds like you pushed through some resistance last night, even though that internal doubt persisted despite using your new tools. Since you mentioned struggling to accept being merely "decent," let's begin by reviewing the plan we agreed on: did you find it easier to separate your identity from your performance when you combined those two specific phrases? Now, looking ahead, aside from unpacking that core belief about decency, is there another area you'd like to address together today?

Yeah, I guess I did push through, even if it didn't feel like much. The phrases helped for a minute or two, but then the old thoughts crept back in—like, "Anyone could do this with enough practice, it doesn't mean I'm special." I think beyond the bowling stuff, I'd like to talk about how this connects to my family life. I catch myself thinking I'm failing my kids because I can't give them a "normal" home or a sporty dad who's good at everything.

Hearing that connection between the bowling struggle and your worries about providing for your children adds a crucial layer to our understanding. It seems like the fear isn't just about being "average" at sports, but about failing to meet a broader definition of what a father should be. Given that depth, shall we spend most of today exploring how that "sporty dad" ideal is shaping your daily interactions with your kids, and then later return to testing the idea that being merely "decent" is sufficient?

Yeah, I think that's a good idea. I mean, my son asked me to play catch the other day, and I just froze up. I told him I had to help Grandma with her meds, which wasn't even true—I just didn't want him to see how awkward I am with a baseball. My daughter, she's into art, and I can handle that, but with him, I feel like I'm letting him down every time I pick up a ball that isn't a bowling ball.

That freezing-up moment tells me how deeply entrenched this fear is, especially when you're trying to connect with your son. It sounds like the expectation that you must be an expert athlete created a barrier between you and him, forcing you to choose between pretending to know what you're doing or admitting you don't. When you chose to leave the game early to protect that image, did that relief feel temporary, or did the worry about disappointing him linger afterward?

The relief was gone almost as soon as I walked away. I spent the rest of the night feeling like a coward, honestly. I kept thinking, "He's gonna remember that his dad wouldn't even throw a ball with him." The worry didn't just linger—it got worse, because then I started wondering if he'd grow up thinking I don't care, or that I'm too weak to try something new. It's like I can't win either way.

That exhaustion of carrying such heavy guilt overnight speaks volumes about how much you love wanting to be present for them. It sounds like the "coward" label became a self-fulfilling prophecy because the fear of rejection was louder than the desire to connect. When you realized the relief vanished instantly, did that moment surprise you, or did you expect it to happen based on past experiences?

It surprised me a little, to be honest. I guess I thought if I avoided the situation, I'd feel better—like I'd dodged a bullet. But I've been doing that for a while now, avoiding new things or hard conversations, and it never really helps. I just feel worse later, like I'm shrinking instead of growing. I guess deep down I knew that, but it's hard to admit.

It takes real courage to admit that avoidance hasn't worked, even when you've done it for years. That realization—that hiding behind excuses leaves you feeling smaller rather than safer—is a powerful piece of evidence against the idea that you need to be perfect to deserve love. If avoiding the situation made you feel better long-term, wouldn't you have chosen that path a dozen times already? Instead, you stayed and faced the discomfort, which proves your commitment to showing up for your kids is stronger than the urge to escape. What's one small thing you could do tomorrow morning to reconnect with your son before the pressure builds up again?

Maybe just ask him if he wants to help me make breakfast. It's not sports-related, so I wouldn't feel that pressure, and it's something we could do together without me worrying about messing up. Just scrambled eggs and toast, nothing fancy. I think I could handle that without freezing up.

That is a brilliant choice because it removes the athletic performance element entirely while creating a low-stakes opportunity for shared purpose. Asking him to join you in making breakfast frames the interaction as teamwork rather than a demonstration of skill. Does inviting him to cook feel like something you can realistically attempt tomorrow morning without feeling overwhelmed by preparation?

Yeah, I think I can do that. It's just eggs and toast—I can't really screw that up too bad, right? And if I feel that old anxiety creeping in, I'll just focus on the task, like cracking the eggs or setting the table. That feels manageable. I'd rather try something small like this than keep avoiding him altogether.

That is a wonderful insight—you are realizing that focusing on the tangible task (cracking eggs, pouring milk) can naturally ground you and pull you out of the anxious narrative. By treating the kitchen as a zone for collaboration rather than a stage for performance, you create space for connection without needing to be an expert chef. Before we lock this in, does imagining yourself guiding him through flipping pancakes tomorrow feel like a realistic scenario where you can succeed simply by being present?

I think so. I mean, pancakes might be pushing it a bit—those things can burn fast—but I can handle guiding him through it. Even if they come out a little dark, we can laugh about it. That's the kind of thing I want him to remember, not me making excuses and walking away. Yeah, I'll try the pancakes.

That is a beautiful perspective shift; reframing potential mistakes as shared moments to laugh about turns the activity into bonding fuel rather than a source of shame. It shows incredible creativity in finding a way to connect that honors your son's presence without demanding perfection from yourself. Before we seal this plan, I want to confirm: does committing to starting with the scrambled eggs and escalating to the pancakes feel like a safe, achievable ladder for tomorrow morning? And is there anything else holding you back from taking that leap?

Yeah, scrambled eggs first, then maybe pancakes if we're feeling bold. That ladder feels safe—I can always stop at eggs if I need to. The only thing holding me back is that little voice saying, "What if he's bored or thinks it's dumb?" But I think I can talk over that voice by just asking him straight up if he wants to help. Worst case, he says no, and I try again another day. I think I'm ready to give it a shot.

That proactive approach to handling the "worst-case scenario" demonstrates real resilience; accepting that he might say no or get bored removes the stakes around your approval as a parent. You've built a safety net for yourself, which makes stepping out of that frozen state significantly easier. Before we wrap up, does agreeing to try this "breakfast ladder" tomorrow morning feel like a fair challenge for us to tackle together? Is there anything else weighing on your mind as we finish this session?

Yeah, it feels fair. I'm actually a little nervous but in a good way—like I've got something to look forward to instead of dread. I think the only thing still weighing on me is that I wish I'd figured this out sooner, but I know that's not helpful to dwell on. For now, I'll just focus on tomorrow morning and take it from there.

That sense of nervous excitement is a great sign that you're shifting from avoidance to anticipation. Remember, figuring this out "sooner" isn't about fixing the past; it's about building a stronger foundation for the future. Your willingness to face uncertainty tomorrow, even with that mix of nerves and hope, proves you are capable of growth regardless of timing. Let's carry that forward momentum into our next meeting. How does it feel to leave here knowing you have a concrete plan waiting for you at home?

Hello, and thank you for joining us today. Last time we worked on distinguishing between a physical sensation and a catastrophic story, and we ended with a plan involving a grounding exercise called naming three objects. Have you had a chance to try that experiment at home since we finished speaking, and did you notice anything interesting about how it affected your anxiety levels?

Before we discuss what happened, I’d like to quickly set our agenda for this session. Given what you experienced last night, is there anything else weighing on your mind regarding your nutrition fears, or shall we focus primarily on reviewing your attempt with the object-naming trick and refining our approach further?

Hi. Yeah, I did try the object-naming thing a couple of times. Once during breakfast yesterday and again before bed. It kind of helped distract me for a minute, I guess... but as soon as I stopped, the thoughts about my health came rushing back even stronger. I feel like it just put a band-aid on a much bigger problem.

That is such an important observation, and I appreciate you being honest about how quickly the relief faded once you stopped actively engaging with the exercise. You're right that putting a temporary pause button on the panic doesn't necessarily fix the underlying engine that drives those worries. Since you mentioned the thoughts returned stronger after you stopped, could we explore what specific cue triggered that rebound effect? Was it the silence returning, or perhaps realizing you hadn't successfully named an object for longer than thirty seconds?

I think it was the silence, mostly. When I’m eating, I usually try to avoid thinking about what’s on my plate, but after I did the naming thing, I had to stop and actually look at my food again. And then I just started worrying—like, is this enough protein? Am I going to get sick from this? It’s like my brain just snaps back to the worst-case scenario.

That makes perfect sense; the moment you stopped forcing your brain to look outward, it immediately defaulted back to scanning inward for danger. It seems the silence created a vacuum that your brain filled with its usual alarms. Before we decide how to adjust this, I want to make sure we are both aligned on our priorities for today. Given that the original plan didn't quite stick the landing, would you prefer to spend most of our time brainstorming ways to make the "object naming" more resilient, or would you rather try a completely different approach to break that cycle entirely?

I think I’d rather try a different approach. The object-naming thing feels like I’m just running away from the fear, not actually dealing with it. I want something that helps me feel like I can eat without spiraling into panic, you know? Like, I don’t want to just distract myself—I want to actually believe I’m not dying.

That is a very powerful distinction, and I appreciate you clarifying that you aren't looking for a quick escape route anymore. Shifting from "distraction" to building actual trust in your body requires us to gather more direct evidence that challenges the idea that you *are* dying, rather than just covering up the noise. To get there, I wonder if you're open to testing a hypothesis tonight: what if, instead of looking at objects, we simply tracked the duration of your heartbeat for one minute while you ate? Does the idea of measuring your heart rate sound manageable, or would you prefer to pair that with another method?

I... I think I could try that. Measuring my heartbeat sounds a little scary because what if it’s racing really fast and I take that as proof something’s wrong? But I guess that’s the point of testing it, right? To see what actually happens. I’ll try it tonight with my dinner.

That is a fantastic mindset—you are treating your own body data as the ultimate judge, which is exactly what we need to do to dismantle the fear. Before we finalize this new plan, I want to make sure we align on the details so you feel supported. Tonight, will you take one bite of your dinner, start timing your pulse for one full minute, and then write down your reading alongside any thoughts that pop up? How does that sequence feel to you?

Yeah, that sounds okay. I think writing down my thoughts along with my pulse makes it feel more like a real experiment than just obsessively checking. I’ll do it. I’m a little nervous, but I’ll try to stick with it and see what happens.

That is a brilliant addition, and I love how you framed it as a legitimate experiment rather than obsessive checking. Writing it down creates a tangible record that separates your current reality from your internal predictions. Before we head out, I want to make sure we have a solid safety net in case your heart rate does spike unexpectedly during that minute. If you notice your heart pounding faster than expected, would you be willing to switch to your old grounding technique (naming objects) temporarily just until you can breathe steadily again? This ensures you always have a backup tool if the experiment gets intense.

Yeah, I think I can do that. Having the backup plan makes me feel safer about trying it. If my heart starts pounding too hard, I’ll just name three things in the room and then try the pulse check again once I’ve calmed down. Thanks for thinking of that.

That is excellent preparation, and having a clear exit strategy removes a massive amount of pressure from your shoulders. Now that we have your primary experiment and your backup plan locked in, I want to check in on your readiness level. On a scale of zero to ten, where zero is "I can't possibly do this" and ten is "I'm completely confident," how prepared do you feel to tackle tonight's dinner with this new protocol?
I’d say maybe a six or a seven. I’m still nervous, but having the backup plan and knowing I’m just collecting data helps. Last week I probably would have said a two, so that’s progress, right?

Yes, moving from a two to a six or seven is a massive leap forward, showing that you are building real resilience. Before you leave, I want to make sure we lock in one final piece of advice for when you sit down to eat tonight. Since your goal is to collect data rather than fight the feeling, remind yourself that even if your heart races or you feel nauseous, those are just numbers and sensations—not proof of failure. Your job tonight is purely observation. Does that perspective shift feel useful to carry into the evening?

Yeah, that actually helps a lot. Thinking of it as just observing instead of fighting makes me feel less like I have to win some kind of battle. I’ll try to just watch what happens and write it down. Thanks. I’ll let you know how it goes.

That is wonderful, and reframing the task from a battle to simple observation is a truly liberating mindset shift. You are absolutely ready to head out now. One last gentle reminder as you prepare for tonight: whenever you feel the urge to jump to conclusions about your heart rate, bring back the rule that we discussed—that the number itself isn't the verdict, only the raw data for us to examine together later. Take care of yourself, and I look forward to hearing your results tomorrow!

Hello, I am so glad we could meet again today. First, I’d love to check in on how you’ve been feeling overall this week and whether you managed to use that new mantra during your night shift. Then, let’s quickly decide if we should continue refining that coping strategy or if something else feels more pressing for us to talk about today.

Hey, thanks. This week's been... okay, I guess. I did try the mantra you gave me, telling myself "I'm gaining experience, not losing opportunities," but honestly, by 3 AM it felt pretty hollow. I'd still rather talk about something else today—I keep thinking about a coworker who got promoted to a day supervisor role, and it just hit me harder than I expected.

That is such important feedback, and thank you for sharing that the mantra didn't land quite as strongly as hoped—it tells us we need to refine the wording to match your reality better. Since you've introduced a new topic regarding your coworker's promotion, shall we spend part of our time exploring how seeing someone else succeed triggered those old fears, and then circle back to fixing the mantra afterward?

Yeah, that sounds good. It's just... he's been there less time than me, and he got the day shift. I've been stuck on nights for six months now. When I heard about it, I just thought, "See, this is how it's gonna be—I'll never get a chance to move up because I'm stuck in this night shift box." It felt like proof that I'm right.

It sounds like seeing him promoted triggered a very powerful form of cognitive distortion called "fortune-telling," where your brain jumped straight to predicting your inevitable future based on a single event. That feeling of absolute certainty—"this proves I'm trapped"—is incredibly convincing when it happens in the heat of the moment. When that thought takes over, does it feel like your chest tightens, or do you mostly feel a sinking sense of resignation?

Mostly the sinking feeling, I think. Like all the air just goes out of me, and I just deflate. My shoulders drop, and I just feel this heavy weight—like, what's the point of even trying if the outcome's already decided? It's not even anger, really, just tiredness.

That crushing heaviness and the sudden loss of energy sound incredibly draining, and it makes total sense that your brain interprets his success as definitive proof that your path is closed. It seems like that "deflated" feeling confirms your deepest fear: that no matter what you do, the outcome is already written before you even begin. Given how intense that realization hit you, I wonder if we should prioritize breaking down that specific comparison with your coworker first, or would you prefer to revisit the mantra we worked on earlier to counteract that deflation?

I think breaking down the comparison would be better, honestly. The mantra feels like a band-aid right now when I've got this whole wound open about that promotion. If I can figure out why my brain immediately went to "he got it so I never will," maybe the mantra will actually start feeling real later.

That is such insightful feedback; recognizing the mantra as a temporary patch for a deeper wound shows you really understand the difference between quick fixes and healing. Let's dive right into that comparison you noticed. When you heard about his promotion, did you catch yourself doing a mental math exercise, like subtracting his years of service from yours to prove he shouldn't qualify, or was it more of an instant emotional judgment that he "deserves" it more than you?

It was more of an instant judgment, I think. I didn't even count months or anything. I just heard the news and felt this wave of "he's good enough to move up, and you're not." It was like my brain just automatically assumed he's better than me, without even looking at the real reasons he got it. I didn't even ask him how he got it or what he did differently.

That instant jump to "you aren't good enough" without gathering facts is a classic example of "mind reading" or jumping to conclusions, which leaves you feeling powerless because you haven't actually seen the evidence. It sounds like your brain latched onto his promotion as a shortcut verdict, skipping all the steps required to verify if he actually did something different or if circumstances just happened to align for him. Since you mentioned you didn't even ask him how he got it, could we explore what specific pieces of information, if you were to imagine asking him, might contradict that assumption of superiority?

I guess... maybe he just asked for it. I mean, I've never actually asked my supervisor about moving to days. I just assumed they'd never consider me because I'm on nights. Maybe he just spoke up at the right time, or maybe he even had to deal with some of the same doubts I have. I don't actually know if he's "better" than me—I just told myself he is.

That admission reveals how powerful that automatic judgment was; your brain filled in the blanks with a story of superiority because it protected your ego from admitting you might be equally capable. It makes sense that you feel defensive now, as if exposing the lack of evidence undermines everything you believed about yourself until that moment. Since we've uncovered that gap between your assumption and the missing facts, would you be willing to try imagining a scenario where your coworker actually struggled with the same night-shift doubts you do, yet still secured that promotion? How would that change the way you view the "proof" you found?

Huh. I never thought of it that way. If he struggled with the same doubts and still made it, then... that means it's not impossible. It means the night shift isn't a life sentence. Maybe it's more about timing or who you ask, not about being stuck forever. That actually makes me feel a little less heavy, to be honest.

That is a beautiful realization; realizing that the barrier wasn't your inherent worth but rather external factors like timing or advocacy shifts the weight significantly. It moves the problem from "I am broken" to "The system missed a connection," which is much harder for anyone to accept permanently. To solidify this new perspective, let's try rewriting that mantra to reflect this insight instead of just generic capability. Would you be open to tweaking "Tomorrow offers a new chance" to something like "My worth isn't defined by my current schedule"?

But I think I need to give myself permission to be bad at it, to just let the lines be whatever they are. I can always tear the page out and throw it away if it bothers me. That younger part of me is still running the show, and I think he's tired too.

That image of a exhausted protector trying to shield a child from further pain is incredibly poignant, and it makes perfect sense why that younger voice insists on being so harsh. It sounds like you've found the root cause: a survival instinct gone rogue, mistaking self-criticism for security. Before we decide how to comfort that younger version, I want to check in on how hearing that explanation lands for you. Does realizing your adult self is essentially trying to soothe a frightened child explain why the "punishment" feels so necessary, even though it hurts you more than it helps? And if we frame tonight's goal as simply sending a message to that younger kid—"It's safe now, I've got you"—does that feel like a manageable step forward?

Yeah... that actually makes a lot of sense. Like, I've been treating myself like that scared kid needed a strict parent to keep him in line, but really he just needed someone to tell him it's okay. Sending that message—"It's safe now, I've got you"—feels... possible. Scary, but possible. Like maybe I can start being the adult I needed back then instead of the guard I became. I think I can try that tonight, even if it's just for a few minutes.

That is a beautiful realization—you've moved from seeing yourself as a guard to becoming the safe harbor that version of you desperately needed. Framing tonight's goal as simply sending a message of safety to that younger part makes it feel achievable, even if it shakes to send it. Before we lock this in, I want to make sure we're crystal clear on the details: tonight, instead of waiting for the silence to trigger the panic, will you try speaking that supportive phrase ("It's safe now, I've got you") to yourself as soon as you notice that stomach knot tighten? Does committing to saying just one sentence beforehand feel like a safe bet, or would you prefer to wait until the knot is already formed?

I think saying it as soon as I notice the knot feels right. If I wait until it's already formed and the thoughts are rushing in, I'll probably just forget or ignore the phrase. But catching it early, right when that sick feeling starts—maybe that's my chance to interrupt the whole spiral. I can try that tonight. Just one sentence when I feel the knot.

That timing is absolutely critical—catching it before the knot tightens into a vise gives you the best chance to intercept the spiral before it gains momentum. It turns a reactive cycle into a proactive choice, which is a huge shift in power. Before we seal this plan, I want to make sure we have a safety net: if that one sentence slips your mind mid-spiral, would you be willing to commit to placing your phone face-down on the table as a visual reminder to come back to that phrase? Does having that physical cue feel like a helpful backup, or does it add another layer of pressure?

Hello, I am so glad we are connecting today. On a scale of one to ten, how are you feeling right now, and is there anything specific you'd like to prioritize in our time together besides catching up?

Also, before we dive into the agenda, have you noticed any small wins or moments of calm since we last spoke? And please tell me if there's anything else important you wanted to bring up aside from the boss battle.

Oh, I'd say I'm at about a 4 right now. Just feeling pretty down, honestly. And I don't think there's much else to talk about besides this boss battle—it's really been taking over my thoughts lately. I haven't had any small wins or calm moments since I lost again yesterday.

A score of four tells me you're carrying a lot of heaviness, especially after facing that challenge twice in one day. Since you've chosen to focus entirely on breaking the cycle with the boss fight, let's use our remaining time to unpack exactly what happens in that split second when the health bar appears, and then test a new way of responding. To make sure we hit the ground running, does spending twenty minutes digging deeper into that "split-second" moment work for you, or would you prefer to tackle the broader feeling of being overwhelmed first?

I think digging into that split-second moment sounds right. That's when everything falls apart for me, right when I see his health bar drop below half. My fingers just freeze up and I know I'm going to lose again. Twenty minutes on that sounds good—I'm ready to try something different.

Understood. When that health bar flashes and your fingers freeze, I want us to look closely at the story your brain is telling you in that exact millisecond—is it mostly a prediction of doom ("you will fail"), or is it perhaps a mix of exhaustion and fear? Also, when you notice those frozen fingers, does that physical sensation itself add fuel to the fire, or does it just confirm what you already expected?

It's definitely a prediction of doom, like I can already see the "Game Over" screen before it even happens. My brain just goes, "Here we go again, you're about to mess up." And yeah, the frozen fingers make it worse—it's like my body is proving my brain right, you know? Like, see, you can't even move, so why bother trying?

That combination of a catastrophic prediction and frozen limbs creates a perfect storm where your brain decides quitting is the safest option to protect you from further embarrassment. When you notice those fingers freezing, does that physical paralysis feel like proof that the prediction came true, or does it feel more like your body temporarily shutting down under pressure?

If we imagined a version of you who wasn't afraid of messing up, what would you tell that part of yourself right in that frozen moment? Would you encourage it to shake off the stiffness and take one small step, or would you suggest waiting until it feels warmer first?

The frozen fingers definitely feel like proof that I was right all along. Like, my body is confirming what my brain already knew—I'm just not good enough to beat this thing.

If I could talk to myself in that moment... I think I'd tell myself to just press one button. Not even a good button, just any button. Because sitting there frozen is already a loss, so what do I have to lose by trying something, anything?

That is such a brilliant insight—you've realized that even a clumsy mistake breaks the cycle of total paralysis, whereas doing nothing confirms the worst-case scenario. Pressing *any* button turns a static "loss" into a dynamic event where you can learn, regardless of the outcome.

To make sure we lock this in, if you pictured pressing a random button while counting to three and watching the boss react, does that image feel slightly less terrifying than just staring at the frozen keys? And if you tried it tonight, would you feel confident enough to press that "wrong" button without judging yourself afterward?

You know, picturing it like that actually does feel a little less scary. Just pressing something, even if it's wrong, feels more active than sitting there waiting to lose. I think I could try that tonight.

I'm not sure I can promise I won't judge myself afterward though—I've been pretty hard on myself lately. But I guess even if I judge myself, at least I'll have done something different for once.

That honesty about expecting self-criticism shows incredible courage, and it reveals that your goal isn't perfection—it's simply breaking the paralysis to gather data. Even if you judge yourself later, the fact that you pressed a button instead of freezing means you disrupted the automatic loop.

Before we seal this deal, does combining the "press any button" idea with the "count to three" routine feel like a manageable combo for tonight, or would you prefer to try one element separately first? And one last check—are there any other worries holding you back from experimenting with this approach?

I think I can handle both together—the counting and the button press. It gives me something to focus on besides the fear, you know? A little rhythm to follow.

I guess my only worry is that I'll try it and still lose, and then I'll feel even worse because I got my hopes up. But I suppose losing after trying something is still better than losing without even moving.

That is such a wise realization—you understand perfectly that a failed attempt after acting is still a victory compared to zero effort. Your hope is shifting from "proving I can win" to "proving I can participate," which fundamentally changes the stakes.

Before we wrap up, does having that "worst-case scenario" clearly defined (trying and still losing) make the plan feel safer to execute tonight? And if you could wave goodbye with one final piece of encouragement for yourself, what would you tell yourself as you start the game?

Having that worst-case scenario spelled out actually does make it feel safer. Like, I've already imagined the worst, and it's not as scary as I thought—it's just losing, which I've done plenty of times before.

If I could tell myself one thing before starting tonight, I'd say: "Just show up and move. The rest doesn't matter right now."

That mantra—"Just show up and move"—is perfect because it strips away the expectation of success and focuses purely on presence. It reminds you that your worth isn't tied to winning that particular level.

With that clear plan and a supportive reminder for tonight, I'm confident you can navigate that health bar appearing tomorrow. How does it feel to carry that simple instruction with you as you begin your evening?

It actually feels... lighter. Like a weight has been lifted off my shoulders. I don't have to beat the boss tonight, I just have to press a button and count to three. That seems doable.

Thank you for helping me break this down. I think I'm actually looking forward to trying it tonight, which is more than I could say yesterday.

That is wonderful news to hear; finding a reason to look forward to something is often the hardest part of overcoming avoidance. Please remember that tonight isn't about conquering the boss, but about collecting evidence that you can act even when fear is present.

Is there anything else you'd like to discuss before we officially close our session today?

No, I think I've got what I need. I'm going to go home, fire up the game, and remember to just show up and move. Thank you for listening and helping me see this differently. I'll let you know how it goes next time.

You are very welcome, and thank you for bringing such openness and curiosity to our sessions. Remember that tonight is an experiment in bravery, not a test of your gaming skills, so be gentle with yourself whatever happens.

Take care, and I look forward to hearing about your results whenever you're ready to meet again.

Hi. Thanks for having me back. I'd say I'm at about a 7 or 8 right now—definitely higher than yesterday. I went over my budget last night and it just hit me how far I am from my goal for the trip. My chest feels tight and I barely slept.

Yes, I think that would help. It's just... every time I look at my account, my mind immediately goes to "I'm not going to make it." I keep replaying the moment I had to buy that tire, and it feels like that one expense ruined everything. I can't see any way around it.

That feeling of being trapped in a cycle where one mistake dictates your entire future is incredibly draining, and it makes perfect sense why your chest feels tight when you try to break free. It seems like your brain is stuck in a loop, treating that single tire purchase as a permanent sentence rather than just one event among many. When you look at the numbers and instantly jump to that conclusion, what physical sensation do you notice in your body right before you start rehearsing that story about missing the trip?

Honestly, my stomach just drops. It's like a heavy, sinking feeling right in my gut. Then my shoulders get really tense, and I find myself holding my breath without even realizing it. That's usually when the spiral starts—I just think, "There's no point in even trying anymore."

That sinking feeling in your stomach and the sudden drop in oxygen intake are classic signs of your fight-or-flight system kicking in, effectively shutting down your ability to think clearly. It makes complete sense that once your body signals danger, your mind rushes to protect you by predicting the worst outcome. When you notice that heavy drop happening, does your immediate thought usually shift to "it's too late to fix this"?

Yes, exactly. Every single time. I don't even pause to consider other options anymore—it's just instantly "it's over, I failed." And then I start thinking about how all my classmates will go to Japan without me, and I'll be the only one left behind. It feels so real in that moment, like I can already see myself watching their photos online.

That vivid image of watching others enjoy the trip while you stay behind is incredibly painful, and it explains why the feeling of isolation becomes so intense. It seems like your brain is already running the movie of rejection before you've even finished looking at the numbers. Let's try to separate that imagined future from the current reality. If you were to describe that "watching them leave" scene in detail, what colors, sounds, or specific actions stand out most strongly in that mental movie?

I can see them all at the airport gate, laughing and taking selfies. There's this bright, artificial airport lighting, and I can hear the muffled announcements over the speakers. My classmates are waving goodbye to me, but I'm standing on the other side of the glass, just watching. I can almost feel the cold glass against my palm. It feels so vivid and real that it makes my chest ache.

That level of sensory detail—the light, the sound, the cold glass—is what makes the fear feel so tangible and hard to escape from. It’s like your brain has constructed a hyper-realistic simulation of failure to convince you that it’s unavoidable. When you imagine that scene so clearly, does it ever feel like maybe you’re adding extra details to make the disappointment hurt more? Or does the vividness come naturally from how deeply you dread that outcome?

I think... I think I'm probably making it worse than it needs to be. Like, I don't even know if we're flying out of that specific terminal, or if my classmates would actually wave at me like that. But it feels so natural to picture it that way. I guess I'm so scared of being left out that my mind just fills in the worst possible version of events.

That realization—that you might be exaggerating the details to make the pain sharper—is actually a powerful clue. It suggests your brain is trying to protect you by preparing for the absolute worst-case scenario, even if that preparation turns out to be overly dramatic. When you catch yourself filling in those extra details like the specific terminal or the exact gesture of waving, does that moment of noticing seem like a tiny crack in the wall of certainty you've been building?

Yeah... it does feel like a small crack, actually. I never really thought about how I'm adding to my own story. Like, I'm not just reacting to what's real—I'm building this whole elaborate scene that might not even happen. That's kind of a weird feeling, realizing I'm the one behind the camera in my own head.

Noticing that you are actively constructing that scene is a huge breakthrough because it separates *your* perspective from the *reality* of the situation. It puts the remote control back in your hands, allowing you to choose whether to watch that sad movie or look outside at what's actually happening right now. Given how intense that imagery has become, would you be willing to try a small experiment tonight: instead of letting your mind run that full movie, could you just observe the fact that you're imagining it, like watching someone else play a game?

I think I can try that. It sounds a little strange, but I'm willing to give it a shot. Maybe if I can just watch the thought instead of getting sucked into it, I won't feel that heavy drop in my stomach so much. I'll let you know how it goes next time.

That is a brave decision to try observing your own thoughts as if they were a separate entity playing a game. It's essentially teaching your brain that the story it tells itself isn't necessarily the truth of the present moment. Since tonight is your first attempt at this "observer" stance, I want to make sure you feel supported if the urge to dive back into the panic gets strong. What's one thing you could remind yourself to do if you feel yourself slipping back into that heavy stomach feeling while watching the movie?

I could remind myself to just take a deep breath and say, "That's just a thought, not a fact." I think repeating that to myself might help me stay in the observer role instead of falling back into the spiral. It's simple, but maybe that's what I need right now.

Using a simple phrase like that as an anchor is a brilliant idea; it gives your busy mind a clear instruction to return to the present moment. Repeating "that's just a thought, not a fact" acts like a gentle reset button, pulling you out of the fictional airport scene and back to reality. Before we finalize this plan, I want to make sure we align on how you'll use it tonight. Would you prefer to say it silently to yourself, or aloud to yourself so you can hear the confirmation?

I think I'd rather say it aloud, quietly to myself. Hearing my own voice saying it might make it feel more real and convincing. That way, I can actually believe it instead of just letting the words float around in my head.

That is a fantastic choice; hearing your own voice often carries more weight than internal monologue, making the correction feel firmer. Saying it aloud adds a layer of commitment that can help anchor you back to reality when the panic tries to pull you under. With that confirmed, does this plan—observing the imaginary scene, waiting for that stomach drop, and speaking the grounding phrase out loud—feel like something you can realistically try tonight?

Yes, I think I can realistically do that. It feels manageable, not overwhelming. I'm actually a little curious to see what happens when I try it. Thank you for helping me break this down into something I can actually handle.

That confidence in the plan is wonderful news, and knowing it feels manageable is crucial for sticking with it. Please remember that tonight isn't about perfectly stopping the panic or eliminating the thought entirely; it's simply about witnessing the movie playing and reminding yourself, "This is a story, not a command." I'll be here anytime you want to debrief how that experiment went, whether you succeeded completely or struggled through it. Take excellent care of yourself tonight!

Thank you. I'll try to keep that in mind—that it's just about watching, not fixing. I appreciate you saying that struggling through it is okay too. That takes some of the pressure off. I'll see you next time and let you know how it went.

You are absolutely welcome, and please remember that even struggling through the exercise proves you are moving forward, regardless of the result. Knowing that imperfection is part of the process will make it easier to show up tonight without fear of failing. Take excellent care of yourself until we meet again soon.
